issues.title: Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects
issues.summary: A bipartisan “permitting reform” bill would help expand the grid, but tribal nations fear it would mean “the demolition of our heritage.”
issues.author: Jake Bittle
issues.content_html:
After years of negotiation, Congress is on the cusp of passing a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill that would make it far easier to build power plants and electric transmission lines in the United States. The bill was negotiated by a bipartisan group of senators including Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse, a noted climate hawk, and Republican Mike Lee, an opponent of environmental regulation. It has picked up support from cleanenergyadvocates because it would promote more transmission lines to carry renewable power to cities, speed up review for solar and wind projects, and stop presidents from cancelling offshore wind farms. It has also been endorsed by many conservative, business, and fossil fuel groups, who say it would cut down on environmental red tape and speed up natural gas pipelines.

The bill has divided the climate movement, separating groups focused on decarbonization from those focused on endangered species protection and environmental justice, but the most influential opposition has come from tribal nations. The bill would weaken a historic preservation law that tribes often use to protect cultural and religious sites from development, and numerous prominent Indigenous nations and organizations have said it harms tribal sovereignty.

While the bill cleared a procedural hurdle in the Senate last week, it remains unclear whether it will pass there or in the House. The negotiators who framed the bill say they believe they have the votes, but a number of Democrats in both chambers have opposed the bill. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next Speaker of the House, has criticized what he called the bill’s “failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.” Nevada senator Catherine Cortez Masto, who voted to advance the bill, has said she won’t ultimately vote to pass it, saying she “cannot ignore the concerns” of tribes in her state.

“Projects affecting tribal governments before were already fast-tracked, but now this allows for a super fast track,” said John Bathke, a member of the Navajo Nation, a former historic preservation officer for the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Reservation, and now a professor of Indigenous studies at San Diego City College.

The 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, passed in the wake of nationwide urban renewal efforts that demolished many old buildings, requires the federal government to consider the effect of construction projects on historic and cultural properties. (Most intact objects or properties that are more than 50 years old and have some kind of historical, cultural, or religious significance qualify under the law.) When you’re building a solar farm or a transmission line, that is a big undertaking: The area of review can extend for as much as 5 miles away from the project itself, and major transmission lines can be hundreds of miles long. Even if a project is visible a few miles away when you’re standing in a historic area, that still counts as a potential effect.

While tribal nations have control over infrastructure projects on their reservations, many tribes have cultural, religious, and political claims over areas that are outside their reservation boundaries. The historic preservation law is one of the only tools they have to stop or alter construction projects that might desecrate sacred territories or religious sites.

“Even though a lot of these projects aren’t on reservation land, it’s part of their traditional homeland, it’s part of their spiritual landscape,” said Bathke. “That land still belongs to them and they belong to that land.”

Tribal nations have used this law to limit energy projects that they say would harm their sacred territories. In perhaps the best-known example, the Quechan Tribe of the Fort Yuma Indian Reservation sued the federal government in 2010 over its approval of a 6,000-acre solar farm on federal land in California, one of the first such projects in the United States. The tribe argued that the project would destroy religious sites and buried remains and that the government had rubber-stamped it after just a few meetings. A court sided with the tribe and the solar developer nixed the project, moving to build on private farmland instead. (Bathke was the tribe’s historic preservation officer — the tribal official who helps with historic reviews — during the solar dispute.)

Supporters of clean energy development have long sought to reform the law. They argue that historic preservation review has become a far more sweeping and burdensome process than the authors of the law intended, and that clean energy projects are affected more than any other type of construction. The onus is heaviest for transmission lines — in some cases, the area under review can extend to hundreds of square miles, and entire rivers or valleys can be considered historic sites. Since transmission wires can be seen from miles away, it’s hard to eliminate all visual impacts associated with building them.

“As written, [the historic preservation law] is a modest procedural check on hasty decisionmaking. … In practice, it has grown into a substantive burden on building infrastructure of all kinds,” write Ben Schifman and Aiden Mackenzie, two research analysts at the Institute for Progress, in a report on how the law affects energy development. The Institute for Progress has been a leading advocate for reforming the law and for the bipartisan permitting bill.

To illustrate their argument, Schifman and Mackenzie cite the example of SunZia, an $11 billion transmission line that carries wind energy west from New Mexico to California. The project took two decades to complete. The line had to secure permits from multiple state power regulators, but it also had to undergo a historic review process that covered an area twice the size of Delaware. Among many other things, the government had to consider whether being able to see the transmission line in the distance would harm the historic characteristics of thousands of different sites across multiple states.

While the government undertook this review, a coalition of tribes in the area protested the process. One of their main arguments centered on the San Pedro River Valley, a landform in Arizona that is sacred to the Apache, O’odham, Hopi, and Zuni peoples. The tribes wanted the government to declare the entire valley a historic zone, which could have required SunZia to reroute its wires. The government declined to give the valley that designation, arguing that the tribes had not identified the issue early enough in the review process. The Tohono O’odham and the San Carlos Apache tribes along with a group of environmental nonprofits then sued to stop the line. They failed to halt construction before the wires joined the grid, but the case is still ongoing, and a court could still force the developer to alter the project if the tribes win.

The initial version of the permitting bill limited the scope of the historic review process in several ways in an apparent attempt to avoid future SunZias. It made consultation with tribes effectively optional, allowing the federal government to move ahead with projects in cases where a tribe’s designated historic preservation official took too long to identify important sites. It outlined a definition for “traditional religious or cultural importance,” which had previously been open-ended under federal law. It narrowed the definition of a “visual” impact, requiring that such impacts “direct[ly]” and “significantly diminish” the historic value of a place; this standard is subjective, but it would likely exclude things like being able to see a wind turbine on the horizon. It also prohibited judges from halting construction work on projects if they find a flaw in a historic preservation analysis, as happened in the Quechan Tribe wind farm case; instead, judges could only order the federal government to redo its analysis as construction continued.

These provisions provoked an immediate outcry from several tribal nations and Indigenous groups, who said it would threaten tribal sovereignty. A coalition of several major tribal groups, including the National Congress of American Indians, said that the bill was in “deep conflict with federal trust and treaty obligations” and that Senate negotiators were “proposing to facilitate the demolition of our heritage.”

Some lawmakers who support the bill expressed regret about their failure to incorporate Native interests.

“We didn’t bring the tribes along on this … we could have done better on it in retrospect,” said Republican senator Alan Armstrong, who represents Oklahoma, in an interview with Punchbowl News.

Negotiators amended the bill earlier this month to address these concerns. The bill now makes tribal consultation mandatory throughout the historic review process, which isn’t the case under current law. It also prevents the government from taking over the historic review process when tribal officials are slow to respond. These changes are significant given that the Trump administration is already trying to weaken the historic review process through executive action. The administration’s rulemaking could limit the historic review process even if the permitting bill doesn’t pass.

The tribes and tribal organizations that opposed the first version of the bill say these changes are nowhere near enough. Their primary areas of concern, including the limited definition of visual effects and the ban on injunctions, are still in the new version.

“While this amendment addresses select concerns, the authors ask Indian Country to be grateful Washington chose to take away fewer of our rights in the name of ‘progress,’” said Ira Matt, the head of the the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers and a member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes. He also said the bill erodes “protections we have spent decades fighting to secure” and that those supporting it had demonstrated a “fundamental failure to understand and respect Tribal sovereignty.”

It’s unlikely that lawmakers will strip the historic preservation section altogether. Many of the most suitable areas for clean energy development are on federal land in the West. In order to build enough clean energy to replace fossil fuels, developers will likely have to build projects that pass near tribal cultural sites. In that light, the bill’s historic preservation reform represents the biggest win for clean energy companies since the passage of the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act, which subsidized wind and solar construction and has since been largely repealed.

Some tribal nations believe they themselves will benefit from the bill’s effort to speed up energy permitting. A few tribes have endorsed the bill, most of them tribes that have significant coal and oil resources. The Apsáalooke (Crow) tribe, whose reservation covers 2 million acres in Montana, told Senate negotiators last month that the bill could deliver “a predictable regulatory environment” and greater investment certainty” for “energy-producing tribes.” The tribe has significant coal reserves and has historically been a large coal producer, but its production has declined in recent years. The National Tribal Energy Association, which represents a number of fossil-fuel producing tribes, has also endorsed the bill.

The bill will also strengthen the investment case for solar and wind on tribal lands, said Anthony Walters, a member of the Cherokee Nation and the vice president for government relations at the Alliance for Tribal Clean Energy, which helps tribes develop renewable energy. Walters says the main constraint that many tribes face is getting access to capital, and speedy environmental reviews and more transmission lines would make it easier for tribes to attract the money they need.

Even so, he said the economic benefits of that development could never outweigh the potential destruction of sites that tribes hold sacred.

“The bill would help clean energy development projects across the board, so tribes would see the benefit of that,” he said. “But on the whole, right, we can’t do that at the expense of all the processes that tribes use to protect their interests. It’s a big trade-off.”

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Tribes push back as Congress moves to fast-track energy projects on Nov 17, 2026.

issues.title: Nitrates in drinking water are a ‘public health crisis,’ environmentalists warn
issues.summary: Nearly 120 million Americans are served water with nitrate levels above what public health advocates say is safe. They want the EPA to act.
issues.author: Juanpablo Ramirez-Franco
issues.content_html:
When the federal government set its limit on how much nitrate drinking water can safely contain, the primary concern was blue baby syndrome, a condition that deprives infants of oxygen. In the 51 years since then, research has associated exposure to the contaminant with cancer and other health problems, fueling calls for a stricter standard.

On Monday, a coalition of national and local advocacy organizations including the Natural Resources Defense Council, Union of Concerned Scientists, Prairie Rivers Network, and 11 others filed a petition calling on the U.S Environmental Protection Agency to lower that threshold from 10 milligrams per liter to 1 mg/liter. In its petition, the coalition argued that “nitrates in drinking water are causing a public health crisis across the country.”

“One in three Americans — nearly 120 million people in this country — are currently being served water with dangerous levels of nitrate in it,” said Tyler Lobdell, a senior staff attorney at Food & Water Watch. That figure includes people served water with nitrate concentrations above 1 mg/L — one-tenth of the current federal standard.

Nitrate pollution, much of it linked to fertilizer and manure runoff and leaching from agriculture, is a particular concern in farming regions, where contaminated groundwater can disproportionately impact rural, low-income, Latino, and farmworker communities. Studies have linked exposure with colorectal cancer, thyroid disease, and fetal abnormalities. A 2019 study estimated that up to 12,594 new cancer cases each year are attributable to nitrate in drinking water.

“This change would reflect the best available, peer-reviewed science and would bring substantial health benefits to communities across the country,” according to the petition.

Climate change can exacerbate nitrate contamination as increasingly intense rainfall and flooding washes fertilizer and manure into waterways and groundwater. Drought can concentrate pollutants.

In a statement to Grist, the EPA wrote that it would review the petition but noted that it completed its review of drinking water regulations, including the nitrate standard, in July 2024.

“EPA conducted a robust evaluation of available studies and applicable data for nitrate to determine if any new information provided a basis to support a regulatory revision that would improve or strengthen public health protection,” the statement read. “Based on the agency’s review, EPA determined that the nitrate rule was not a candidate for revision at the time.”

As part of the petition, the organizations commissioned the consulting firm One Water Econ to analyze the costs and benefits of adopting the proposed standard, especially in states most affected by nitrate contamination.

The 43-page report found that slashing the threshold isn’t cheap. The report estimates that adopting the 1mg/L benchmark would cost $94.5 billion over 50 years, which would cover everything from upgrading water treatment plants, maintenance, and replacing equipment. Despite the steep price tag, the analysis found that returns would significantly outweigh the investment, the benefits totaling $364 billion.

“People are paying with their health right now,” Lobdell said. “Costs are accruing right now in the real world, in the form of people losing their loved ones and children being born with abnormalities.”

The states with the largest impacted populations tend to cluster in the West and Midwest and account for 62 percent of the affected population, according to the analysis. Agricultural powerhouses like California, Texas, and Arizona topped that list, with traditional farming states like Iowa not far behind.

In Iowa, approximately 42 percent of residents are exposed to nitrate levels above 1 mg/L, according to the analysis. This summer, Des Moines-area residents faced water restrictions for the second year in a row amid high nitrate levels. Illinois faces a similar problem. Between 2021 and 2023, more than 2 million people were served drinking water that tested above 1 mg/l, said Robert Hirschfeld, the director of water policy at Prairie Rivers Network.

The current 10 mg/L threshold dates to 1975 and was formally adopted in 1991, based largely on the risk of blue baby syndrome. Advocates argue that the standard does not account for subsequent research associating nitrate exposure with other health problems.

The EPA has twice tried to reassess the nitrate benchmark as part of its required periodic review of national drinking water standards. The Obama administration began that process in 2016, but the Trump administration paused it in 2019. The Biden administration restarted it in 2023, before the second Trump administration cut the effort short by eliminating the office responsible for the reviews.

“We’ve done the EPA’s work for it,” Lobdell said.

The petition asks the EPA to take two immediate steps: adopt an interim benchmark for nitrate while it considers the new limit, and enforce other federal protections like the Clean Water Act and rein in industrial agriculture, which Lobdell said has been given “free pass to pollute.”

For communities confronting nitrate contamination, the debate is ultimately about where regulators draw the line between what is legal and what is safe.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Nitrates in drinking water are a ‘public health crisis,’ environmentalists warn on Nov 17, 2026.

issues.title: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.
issues.summary: A technology born in aerospace uses liquid CO2 to wash clothes without water or a dryer. The challenge is making it work in a home appliance.
issues.author: Naoki Nitta
issues.content_html:
Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain.

Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer.

Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons.

Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place.

Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on.

In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat.

Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps, and compressors.

Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank. As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp.

The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing.

For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry.

The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said.

As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint.

Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance?

LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work.

LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts, and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs.

Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.”

Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously.

The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag. CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium.

Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings, and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration, and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said.

Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend.

The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question.

Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution. on Nov 16, 2026.

issues.title: As Texas embraces carbon storage, a Black community questions the risks
issues.summary: Texas now issues permits for companies to store carbon dioxide underground. East Texas residents fear safety risks, and skeptics doubt the climate benefits.
issues.author: Emily Foxhall, The Texas Tribune
issues.content_html:
On a rural road outside Beaumont, a Texas energy giant is preparing to pump carbon dioxide underground to permanently store it and keep the gas from contributing to global warming. The project could be the first of its kind to start operating in the state.

It’s a long-awaited milestone for the oil and gas industry, which has touted carbon capture and storage as an important tool for cleaning up industry emissions. Texas lawmakers threw their support behind the technology, while state regulators spent years seeking permitting authority from the federal government to try to clear projects faster.

The Texas Railroad Commission, which oversees the oil and gas industry, won that authority late last year and approved this Exxon Mobil project in September. But the nearby community of Cheek has asked commissioners to reconsider the permit decision.

The area close to the project is predominantly Black, and many residents are working-class or elderly. People there don’t trust the company’s assurances that it will keep residents and their groundwater safe.

Only a small number of carbon storage wells have been permitted so far across the United States, and some CO2-related accidents have already happened. Experts and community advocates have warned of the risk for pipeline accidents and potential underground leaks. Leaders in Cheek are concerned the injected carbon dioxide could contaminate groundwater or get into the air and suffocate them. They worry emergency responders won’t be equipped to rescue them.

“We’re just shocked that they would want to do this so close to homes,” said Douglas Cormier, the 67-year-old president of the Cheek Texas Community Association, who grew up in the rural town and lives there with his wife near his daughters and grandkids.

Residents explained they don’t want to be the test subjects for the technology, and some experts argue it’s more distracting than effective in fighting climate change. Harvard University History of Science Professor Naomi Oreskes, who studies disinformation and climate change, has called carbon capture and storage “mostly a dangerous distraction.”

A recent investigation by Drilled and ProPublica showed it would take more resources than feasible for carbon capture and storage to reduce emissions enough to avoid extreme warming. Companies have canceled or paused nearly a third of 19 proposed carbon storage projects in Texas so far.

But carbon capture supporters argue that storing emissions is an important part of an “all of the above” approach to fighting climate change. Federal tax credits support carbon capture projects. Locally, East Texas remains attractive because of its existing carbon dioxide pipeline network (owned by Exxon Mobil), its geology, and nearby industrial facilities that might pay for their carbon to be stored.

Exxon Mobil has seven agreements with companies to store the greenhouse gas. The volume of carbon dioxide injected underground through those agreements will equal emissions from 2 million cars.

“The community’s concerns around safety of any sort of an injection project are valid and real and need to be taken seriously,” said Nichole Saunders, senior director and lead counsel for energy transition with the Environmental Defense Fund. “At the same time, the need for more carbon management infrastructure to get to where we want to go on climate is also real.”

So far, the case has raised questions about whether companies and the Railroad Commission are doing enough to address community concerns as a backlog of projects awaits approval.

Agency watchdogs say the commission has a history of failing to keep communities safe from industry risks. It’s also facing pressure from state Representative Drew Darby, leader of the House’s energy resources committee, who told the agency at a September hearing that carbon-capture projects needed to be moving at “utmost pace while protecting the public.”

In a statement to the Tribune, Railroad Commission spokesperson Bryce Dubee said the organization has a record of protecting drinking water while regulating injection wells. Winning the authority to regulate carbon storage “speaks volumes to this expertise,” Dubee said.

Exxon Mobil held early meetings with community members in Cheek. The company’s permit requires it to install automatic shut-off systems for the injection wells, monitor the underground carbon dioxide plume, and post a phone number where the operators can be reached around the clock.

The permitting program requires coordination with local emergency officials, according to the commission. Exxon Mobil sponsors emergency training programs through the Texas A&M Engineering Extension Service in College Station.

“We want community members to know they can count on us to operate responsibly, communicate openly, and put safety first every day,” Senior Vice President Dominic Genetti wrote in a blog post.

But the day following Darby’s comments, after hearing Exxon Mobil hadn’t talked with the community since the residents hired lawyers, Railroad Commission Chair Christi Craddick scolded Exxon Mobil for not supporting residents enough. Some people from Cheek had taken a bus to be there to voice their concern.

“Give them information,” she said. “Be there for their safety. Give ’em a fire truck if that’s what they want.”

Then Craddick voted for the permit.

Community distrust

Photos and posters about the area’s decades-long history hosting local rodeos hang in 81-year-old Preston Frank’s self-made museum in Cheek. Like many who live here, Frank, an upholsterer, inherited the land from his family. He considers it an important way to build generational wealth.

“That’s the reason why we’ve been fighting Exxon Mobil,” he said. “We don’t want them coming in here and diminishing the value of the land.”

Just west of Beaumont off Interstate 10, the unincorporated community of Cheek is split by the highway and railroad, with many homes sitting on large tracts of land dotted with cattle and horses. People wave to each other. On the north side, there’s a Catholic and a Baptist church. Once a year, residents gather for a community picnic at the park.

Exxon Mobil plans to compress carbon dioxide into an “almost liquid state,” pump it thousands of feet deep into the Earth and let it flow into little spaces in the rock, where scientists expect some to dissolve into salty water in those spaces or get stuck like a drink spilled in sand. Residents from the start had concerns.

How does Exxon Mobil know where the molecules will go? What if they don’t behave as expected? What if the project gets abandoned?

Carbon dioxide leaking into water could increase its acidity and cause metals to contaminate it, according to advocacy groups and experts. If it leaks back into the air or a pipeline ruptures and people are caught in a big enough plume, they won’t be able to breathe or run gas-powered cars to escape.

“Contamination of drinking water with CO2, or with metals or chemicals leaching out of rock due to CO2 acidification of the water, could be very costly if the affected aquifer is used by a lot of people,” Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers wrote in a 2007 paper. “[O]nce any aquifer is contaminated, it will remain so.”

The Cheek Texas Community Association signed on in July 2025 with attorneys at the nonprofit Earthjustice, which charges no cost. They fought the permit approval all the way to a state administrative hearing in March this year where they argued Exxon Mobil hadn’t done enough to adequately ensure water and public safety would be protected and wasn’t monitoring a large enough area underground.

“It’s the first one in an area so close to a community, and that’s why the water issues and the safety issues are so paramount here,” said Jen Powis, who leads Earthjustice’s Gulf regional office.

The project also raised familiar concerns over environmental justice, a term used by researchers who have shown communities of color suffer a greater proportion of environmental harm than whiter, wealthier areas. Residents feared Exxon Mobil saw in their homes a place where the company could more easily and cheaply push a project through.

The company already built three unassuming injection wells at the edge of the community. Only some residents in Cheek signed so-called pore space agreements with Exxon Mobil for use of the small pockets in underground rock where the carbon dioxide will be stored and that property owners control under current case law.

“I’m just thinking they found an area where they can do it and not expect a lot of resistance,” said James Strambler, 70, a former IBM technician who moved there around 2017.

After the March hearing, a technical examiner and administrative law judge recommended moving the permit forward to the commission for a vote.

State gains power

Texas’ work to win the authority to permit carbon storage wells dates back more than a decade.

In 2009, Texas lawmakers passed a law authorizing the railroad commission to design a framework for how the state would regulate these projects in a way that upheld federal law. In 2022, the state formally applied to the Environmental Protection Agency for that authority.

At a virtual July 2025 hearing held by the EPA, the Texas Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing 90 percent of the state’s fossil fuel production, said approving carbon capture and injection would be an economic boom for the state.

Gaining permitting power for carbon storage wells was “essential for our state’s economic future and energy leadership,” said Todd Staples, the group’s president, following the hearing.

Supporters of the technology are quick to point out that carbon dioxide makes sodas fizzy and creates the tunnels of fog that Texas football teams run through. They cite a study done by Texas A&M researchers that found the danger of leaks presents “a low probability of occurrence” — a risk that can be monitored and managed.

Advocates also point to the state’s decades-long history of injecting carbon dioxide into wells under a different type of permit as a way to draw more oil out of the ground and also store some of the greenhouse gas, a process known as enhanced oil recovery, which Exxon Mobil has pursued for decades.

“This has been put in place now for over 50 years,” said Scott Castleman, a spokesperson for the Gulf Coast Carbon Capture and Storage Alliance, which represents Calpine, Chevron, and Exxon Mobil. “Certainly, there is more discussion and opportunity for this industry to scale, and so that’s where you’re starting to see projects and interest in areas that may not have seen this before.”

Establishing community trust will “make or break” projects as the industry grows, said Sophia Cunningham, executive director of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative at the Greater Houston Partnership. Best practices include engaging the community early and providing different, meaningful ways for people to give input and discuss possible benefits.

“It’s a technology that can reduce emissions associated with our industrial activities, and so that is a good pursuit and it’s important to support that,” Cunningham said.“But it’s also reasonable to expect that not everybody in a community is going to want that.”

Residents near projects should be asking whether there would be a helpline to call for any issues, or whether truck drivers would observe weight limits for roads and bridges, said Susan Hovorka, a research professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology. In Hovorka’s mind, research and experience have already proven the technology to be safe.

“It’s not utterly without peril, and so people are not foolish to ask,” Hovorka said,“But … their anxiety is sometimes maybe higher than is practical and realistic.”

But there have been serious incidents in other parts of the U.S.

In Mississippi, a carbon dioxide pipeline ruptured in 2020 after heavy rain caused a landslide, releasing a vapor cloud of CO2. A government investigation found that first responders had not been notified about the safety risks and “had to guess” what they were. Dozens of people went to the hospital.

Injected fluid at another facility in Illinois leaked into “unauthorized zones” underground, which most residents learned about in a news article.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry paused the state’s review of new applications to ensure any permit issued would be in compliance with state regulations, citing a need for a review process that considers “the safety of our citizens and environment and that streamlines the process for greater efficiency.” Louisiana has permitted three carbon dioxide wells to be constructed so far but not to begin operating.

In other states with permitting authority as of mid-October, Arizona hasn’t permitted any carbon injection wells. North Dakota has approved eight active injection wells across three projects, and Wyoming has approved five wells in one project.

“The benefit isn’t there,” said Naomi Yoder, an environmental researcher who opposed Texas’ bid to regulate the technology and raised concerns about potential harm to the environment and communities. “So it doesn’t make any risk worth it, and there is risk involved. You can’t possibly sequester enough carbon dioxide to make it worth it.”

Can Texas improve?

In the Texas state hearing in September, the day before Exxon Mobil’s Cheek permit won initial approval, Darby reiterated the importance of supporting the industry. Virginia Palacios, executive director of the agency watchdog group Commission Shift, told him they should also ensure companies pay for equipment and training for emergency responders.

Meanwhile, Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian has vehemently opposed these projects. Christian has argued carbon dioxide is good for plants, rather than acknowledging the robust science that shows burning fossil fuels has caused carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere to rise, driving up global temperatures.

He voted against Exxon Mobil’s permit, saying he didn’t think it was safe.

Newly elected Railroad Commissioner Jon Rosenthal, who will join Craddick and Christian on the three-person commission, told Inside Climate News he supported the state taking over regulation of the wells.

Some projects have meanwhile stalled. Oxy said in its latest earnings call in August that its carbon storage project — the first and only other one approved in the state so far — was coming online “as we look forward.”

Other projects are moving forward, including Exxon Mobil’s second project near a community not far from Cheek, called Nome. The commission is collecting public comment on that project this week at hearings on Monday and Tuesday. Exxon Mobil named this one “Sunflower,” fitting with the Cheek project called “Rose.”

In late October, environmental and community advocates knocked on residents’ doors to invite them to a meeting about how to advocate for themselves. Only one person from the project’s area attended. Several arrived from Cheek, lending advice on what they’d learned while attendees ate pasta and salad.

The meeting hosts characterized the technology as a financial boon to industry and the Railroad Commission while putting drinking water at risk. The colorless, odorless gas can also cause suffocation, presenter Alexis Iwasiw warned the group.

“At high concentrations … it can lead to serious injury or death,” she said.

The next night, Exxon Mobil held an open house in the small Nome City Hall. They served boudin balls and shrimp and offered colorful pamphlets about the company’s safety record, how to respond in an emergency and how drinking water would be protected. They displayed a poster of other pipelines in the area.

As the sun went down, the group of several dozen made its way outside, where the Exxon Mobil presenters enthusiastically launched into explaining how CO2 is safe at certain levels. With a call of “let it rip, tater chip,” they released the gas from a demonstration pipeline, where it puffed out visibly like white smoke.

Mike Doguet, a 72-year-old rice and turf farmer-turned real estate developer, looked on. He believed the company did a much better job communicating with residents in advance here than in Cheek. The company is paying for new firefighting equipment, he said, among other community support. (Cheek community leaders have a list of wants, too, including improved roads, a community center, and an emergency warning system.)

One of the Sunflower project’s injection wells sits across the street from Doguet’s home in Nome, making neighbors wonder if there was oil. Doguet’s daughter lives next door and his son isn’t far. He wasn’t worried about safety.

“In my mind, it’s going to encourage new industry. It’s going to be good for the environment. It’s all positive to me,” Doguet said. “I don’t see the negatives.”

As the presentation went on, a resident from Cheek peppered the Exxon Mobil employees with questions. One of the Exxon Mobil presenters snapped back, telling her they were in the business of keeping substances in pipelines and would always err on the side of safety.

A former Exxon Mobil employee and Nome resident in the crowd, 77-year-old Lawrence Riley, piped up to say that in his decades of experience, he’d never had a pipeline emergency: “They are very, very safe, I am telling you,” he said.

Wearing an Exxon Mobil hat, 71-year-old Mayor Kerry Abney at one point walked through the CO2 cloud. He thought the project was great: Workers were shopping at Big D’s in town, contributing to sales tax, he said. People had a chance to make money in a place where agriculture is tough.

As Abney put it in an interview: “Santa Claus came.”

The Cheek resident watching the plume crossed her arms, looking skeptical.

Carlos Nogueras Ramos and Zach Leggio contributed reporting.

issues.author: Karla Mendes
issues.content_html: On Nov. 16, a group of roughly 20 Indigenous Awá people living in voluntary isolation approached an Indigenous Guajajara village, in Brazil’s northeastern Maranhão state. The rare encounter has mobilized Indigenous peoples and activists concerned about the safety of the Awá, considered the most threatened group on the planet. The motivation for the unusual interaction is unclear, but Guajajara leaders “expressed concern about the physical condition of some members of the group, especially children and older people, who appeared to be very thin,” according to accounts and images posted on social media by Indigenous organizations. The Guajajara reportedly offered the Awá food and other objects; the Awá remained there briefly before returning to the forest. Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, told Mongabay by email that technical teams are monitoring the situation and that it had activated a contingency plan to “ensure that the relevant agencies are prepared to respond appropriately to any developments in the situation, especially regarding the ethno-environmental protection, health and safety of the Indigenous people involved.” Funai added that the peoples’ right to self-determination would continue to be respected. Unlike other isolated peoples who make frequent contact, this is the first time in decades that the Awá of the Arariboia Indigenous Territory “have appeared in this way and made such close contact with other people,” Sarah Shenker, director and senior researcher at the Indigenous rights organization Survival International Brazil, told Mongabay by phone. issues.title: Jason Clay, who persuaded big business to help save nature, has died at 75
issues.summary: In 1988 Jason Clay attended a Grateful Dead concert at Madison Square Garden and met a man who wanted to help save tropical rainforests. Clay, an anthropologist who had worked with Indigenous communities, asked what he did for a living. “I make ice cream,” the man replied. It was Ben Cohen of Ben & Jerry’s. […]
issues.author: Rhett Ayers Butler
issues.content_html: In 1988 Jason Clay attended a Grateful Dead concert at Madison Square Garden and met a man who wanted to help save tropical rainforests. Clay, an anthropologist who had worked with Indigenous communities, asked what he did for a living. “I make ice cream,” the man replied. It was Ben Cohen of Ben & Jerry’s. Clay suggested developing a flavor using nuts gathered from tropical forests. He thought higher payments for forest products might give people a reason to keep the trees standing. Within a year, Rainforest Crunch was on supermarket shelves. Clay set up a trading company and went on to work with more than 50 businesses on some 200 products, generating roughly $100 million in retail sales. At one point, he said, his operation was buying around a fifth of the world’s Brazil nuts. It paid gatherers two or three times the going rate, and other buyers raised their prices to compete. The people gathering the nuts weren’t generally the ones clearing the forests. Ranchers and loggers had little reason to change what they were doing, and Clay eventually called Rainforest Crunch a failure. “We were attacking the wrong driver,” he explained in a 2010 TED talk. He should have been working on beef, lumber and soy. Clay, who died on November 16th aged 75, spent more than three decades at the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), where he worked to change how major companies bought agricultural commodities linked to deforestation and other environmental problems. issues.title: In Zimbabwe, trusted local guardians help communities coexist with lions
issues.summary: Conservation biologist and founder of the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Action, Moreangels Mbizah joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail her work helping reduce human-wildlife conflict between African lions and communities in Zimbabwe. The group began working only six years ago in two wards of Nyaminyami rural district, and since then has recorded a 98% […]
issues.author: Mike DiGirolamo
issues.content_html: Conservation biologist and founder of the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Action, Moreangels Mbizah joins the Mongabay Newscast this week to detail her work helping reduce human-wildlife conflict between African lions and communities in Zimbabwe. The group began working only six years ago in two wards of Nyaminyami rural district, and since then has recorded a 98% reduction in conflict incidents there. Across the districts of Mbire and Binga, conflict has decreased by 53%. To accomplish this, WCA has pioneered a “community guardian” model. Known as “Batabilili,” these guardians are trained by the organization and implement a range of mitigation measures, including helping farmers secure livestock in above-ground kraals, monitoring lion movement, and conducting community meetings. “They are trusted because they come from these communities, and they are their children, their brothers and sisters,” Mbizah says. “They are part of the community fabric, so that makes it really important in terms of the buy-in and the ideas and the decisions that are being made when it comes to lion conservation.” She says this has also helped reduce retaliatory killings of lions for preying on livestock, because community members’ concerns are directly addressed by a trusted member. “There’s no one that is supporting them when they incur these losses. No one comes to see and to support, to provide … emotional or psychological support when a conflict incident happen[s]. issues.author: Associated Press
issues.content_html: MUMBAI, India (AP) — Prince William presented five Earthshot Prize winners with 1 million pounds ($1.3 million) each on Tuesday, recognizing their efforts to tackle the world’s climate challenges. The annual ceremony, held this year in Mumbai, marked the centerpiece of William and Princess Catherine’s three-day visit to India. The Earthshot Prize winners were selected from 15 finalists for their work in areas ranging from clean transport and renewable energy to forest conservation and marine protection. Four were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, for its electric transport initiatives; PFAS-Free France, for its campaign to ban toxic “forever chemicals”; Niue Ocean Wide Trust, for protecting marine ecosystems; and Ørsted, for advancing offshore wind energy. The fifth recipient was the country of Bhutan for its work in conserving Himalayan forests. William, the Prince of Wales, established the prize through his Royal Foundation in 2020 to encourage inventors and entrepreneurs to develop technologies to combat global warming and mitigate its effects. The ceremony at Mumbai’s Jio World Convention Centre brought together Bollywood celebrities, innovators, entrepreneurs and environmental advocates. William and the Princess of Wales, commonly known as Kate, began their visit Monday. The couple have played street cricket in Mumbai, ridden in an electric rickshaw and met leading figures from India’s cricket, fashion and film industries. They are scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday. The trip marks a significant step in Kate’s return to overseas royal engagements. issues.title: Christian Pulisic sinks wild bicycle-kick goal early vs. Haiti in Mauricio Pochettino's final match with the USMNT
issues.summary: Mauricio Pochettino is leaving the USMNT to take over at Manchester United.
issues.author: Ryan Young
issues.content_html:
Christian Pulisic certainly met the moment on Tuesday night to send off his head coach.

The U.S. men’s national team star scored a wild bicycle-kick goal in the first half of their Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals match with Haiti. Pulisic, in the 25th minute of the match at TQL Stadium, started tracking a pass from Weston McKennie in the box. As he reached the ball, with his back to the goal, Pulisic expertly sent it back up and over his left shoulder and into the net.

Naturally, that sparked quite the celebration in Cincinnati.

🚨 CHRISTIAN PULISIC BICYCLE-KICK GOAL 🚨 pic.twitter.com/V5f7oiUiXU

— B/R Football (@brfootball) November 18, 2026

That put the UMSNT up 1-0. They scored a second goal before halftime of the match when Julian Hall found the back of the net in the 43rd minute. That put the USMNT up 8-0 on aggregate at the time, after their 6-0 win over Haiti in the first leg of the quarterfinal on Saturday.

Tuesday’s match was the final one under Mauricio Pochettino’s watch. The 54-year-old has led the USMNT for the past two years, and will take over at Manchester United. It marks a return to the English Premier League for the longtime coach, who previously worked for Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and others on the European club circuit.

Pochettino oversaw 37 matches as the USMNT boss, which included a World Cup run that reached the Round-of-16, where they fell to Belgium on home soil. The U.S. Soccer Federation had reached a new deal with Pochettino earlier this year with the expectation that he would guide the team for four more years and into the 2030 World Cup. But clearly, the opportunity at Manchester United was too good for him to pass up.

While it’s unclear who will take his place, Pulisic certainly did his part on Tuesday night to send Pochettino off on a high note.

issues.title: Andrej Stojakovic took matters into his own hands in the first half at No. 5 Duke
issues.summary: This guy is a superstar.
issues.content_html:
DURHAM, N.C. — When was the last time an Illini player had this good of a first half….in this big of a game?

Senior guard Andrej Stojakovic came back to Illinois with two things in mind: aiming to win a national championship, and looking to rise his stock in the 2027 NBA Draft. After putting Illinois in the lead against No. 5 Duke with a 20-point first half, his stock may have just skyrocketed.

Against a larger-sized Duke squad, few could’ve predicted that Illinois would be leading the points in the paint battle 24-8 at halftime. Stojakovic was responsible for 14 of those paint points, and even hit a contested three. That was a real heat check.

He didn’t just put up those numbers, though, he did it on incredible efficiency. Stojakovic went 8-for-11 from the field in the first half. Illinois’ efficient offense runs through a shot-quality system, assigning gold medals to the best shots (open layups, open threes) and bronze to the worst shots.

After his first few buckets, he decided he was going to take whatever shot he wanted—and it worked.

If he keeps this up in the second half, he could be looking at a career-high in points and help lead Illinois to a massive win. The whole squad is feeding off of the momentum he created, and the Blue Devils look lost.

issues.title: Titans Wan’Dale Robinson on IR, Xavier Restrepo elevated to roster
issues.summary: The Tennessee Titans have placed their top wide receiver, Wan'Dale Robinson, on injured reserve and elevated Xavier Restrepo to the active roster.
issues.content_html:
The Tennessee Titans have placed their top wide receiver, Wan’Dale Robinson, on injured reserve. In a corresponding move, they have also elevated receiver Xavier Restrepo to the active roster.

The #Titans have promoted WR Xavier Restrepo to the team’s 53-man roster and placed WR Wan’Dale Robinson on Injured Reserve.

— Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 17, 2026

Robinson led the Titans in targets (54), receptions (38), and receiving touchdowns (three) through their first nine games. However, he suffered an ankle injury in their Week 10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars, and while the severity has not been fully disclosed, it was severe enough to put him on IR, ruling him out for at least the next four games. Those four games are against the Dallas Cowboys, Jacksonville Jaguars, Washington Commanders, and Detroit Lions.

Sitting with a 1-8 record, Tennessee currently holds the No. 1 overall pick in the NFL Draft after the Los Angeles Chargers finally got their first win of the season. The Titans are rebuilding after trading away defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons and safety Amani Hooker earlier this season. They will also have the Chicago Bears’ first-round pick this year and in 2028 from the Simmons trade, as well as the Buffalo Bills’ second-rounder from the Hooker trade.

issues.title: 'I've never had just a copy-paste season' – A pointed change for Aaron Gate as road evolution continues and track targets linger in distance
issues.summary: New Zealand rider's targets shift with XDS-Astana aims in 2026 which delivers 'a completely different season, but one that I've enjoyed just as much as any other'
issues.author: Simone Giuliani
issues.content_html:
Last year when Aaron Gate stepped into the WorldTour with XDS-Astana there was no question about the team goal, and that was chasing points as the squad knuckled down to deliver a stunning turnaround in the final year of the three-year cycle to avoid relegation from the top tier.

Through that process Gate played his part by taking three ProTour stage wins, an overall victory, plus plenty of podiums and top-10 results while also supporting teammates to many more wins in 2025. It was also a schedule that, for the rider from New Zealand, was dominated by ProTour races, where it was easier to harvest points.

The freedom of escaping the urgent points push for the team, which still finished sixth in the rankings in 2026, meant they could channel those efforts in another direction.

"Once we secured that goal it sort of shifted back to 'OK, how do we win some big races on the world stage?', and 'how do we achieve that as a team'," Gate told Cyclingnews at his season closing race of Le Tour de Langkawi in Malaysia. "And the nice thing is, we didn't lose any momentum."

They did, however, shift a number of pieces around the board and that could clearly be seen in Gate's schedule – with his tally of races suddenly flipping to two-thirds on the WorldTour, doubling top-level races. With that move, also came a change in how Gate was utilised, the impact of which was reflected in his results tally.

"For me personally, it's meant focusing more on supporting my teammates," said the track specialist turned WorldTour rider. "And it's been a great season with a good group of guys "

That support role was also clearly evident at his season-ending race, as the squad rallied around Matteo Malucelli at Le Tour de Langkawi for three stage victories. Last year it was a race where Gate clinched one of his season victories on the final stage, after Malucelli crashed out. This time it was all-in for the Italian sprinter who claimed the final victory for the team.

It meant that Gate walked away from 2026 without a UCI win on the road, a position he is unaccustomed to, but that doesn't mean he is looking back with any sense of disappointment at how the year has played out. In fact, he was quick to name a season highlight as starting the Tour de France for the first time as part of the lead-out support for Max Kanter, along with a number of other marquee race debuts.

"I've really enjoyed doing some bigger races this year," said Gate. "For example, the year before I went to Tour of Hainan and it was, of course, nice to win a stage and be on the GC podium there. But it was also nice this year to finally do Ronde van Vlaanderen and Paris-Roubaix, which were races that I couldn't do because of the calendar clashes the year before.

"So it's been a completely different season, but one that I've enjoyed just as much as any other, from going to some of the higher level races, but of course it is nice when opportunities are there. So it's not like I choose one or the other. I think for me, the enjoyment is in the balance of being able to do both."

One thing for certain is that Gate, who moved from being a track focussed rider to a more road centered athlete through his career, is far from stagnating, with no two seasons looking the same.

"It's kind of the beauty in cycling that you've got this huge variety, and it's something that I think is how I'm still enjoying it at my age," said the 35-year-old, who may have just recently joined his first WorldTour team but has spent well over a decade racing on the road internationally around his track commitments.

"I've never had just a copy-paste season like a lot of a lot of pros do … they can get 10 years down the road and still be doing the same season, more or less, their their whole career. It's nice that I get this variety."

Gate is signed with XDS-Astana through 2027 and trying to "get some longevity" out of his road career, where he hopes to keep showing his worth at the top level by both supporting his teammates as well as going for results himself. The Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race, where he came second in 2024, is one race that he singled out as an event that suits, and where he would like to have "another crack".

Though, looking a little further into the future, the track goals haven't fallen off the radar completely either. The Team Pursuit bronze medallist at the 2012 Olympic Games also has four gold medals from the Commonwealth Games on the track, and was selected as the New Zealand Team flagbearer for the Paris 2024 Olympic Games.

"I've sort of been disappointed with fourth places in the last three Olympics, so it'd be nice to try and go back for another one in Los Angeles and try to win gold finally. It's the thing that's kind of eluded me, so it'd be nice to try again," said Gate. "That's the long-term goal, but for now I'm enjoying the opportunities that the road is presenting."

issues.title: Gran Premio NYC confirmed as fifth UCI men's race in US next year with sponsor search active to add women's event
issues.summary: Pro race piggybacks mass-participation Gran Fondo 'because the cost for the pro race alone would be a million dollars' says GFNY CEO
issues.author: Jackie Tyson
issues.content_html:
The Gran Premio New York City (GP NYC) returns as a UCI one-day race in 2027, as organisers confirmed that a fourth edition is now on the international calendar for Sunday, May 16.

The 1.2-ranked men's race expects to attract a more robust field of North American and international teams as it is no longer an isolated UCI race as Battenkill's 1.2 event on May 22 in Cambridge, New York makes the pair of road races appealing as a doubleheader, separated geographically by less than 200 miles.

Professional teams at GP NYC will start approximately 10 minutes ahead of thousands of amateurs in the Gran Fondo New York (GFNY) on the George Washington Bridge, sharing an 85-mile (137km) road course along the Hudson River, through the towns and scenic countryside of Bergen County, New Jersey and Rockland County, New York.

It is the GFNY, which is the flagship stop of the mass-participation GFNY World Series with events in a dozen countries, that provides the infrastructure for the pro race to take place.

"The pro race only happens because of the Gran Fondo. We have 3,000 riders, so it's a busy day," GFNY CEO Uli Fluhme told Cyclingnews.

"Without the structure of the Gran Fondo and the road closures in place for the thousands of riders, there would not be a pro race because the cost for the pro race alone would be a million dollars. It's feasible because you have thousands of riders paying for the race.

"So all those road closures, and what we tell local governments and police is basically the same thing. They don't mind the pro race, just more colorful jerseys, 10 minutes ahead of the amateurs."

Both GP NYC and Battenkill, as well as a few other US events, include amateur racing on the same courses on the same day, which the director for the upstate New York event likes as a great model for cycling.

"We're super happy to be back on the UCI calendar again, especially with the prestigious GFNY and Gran Premio just 6 days prior and a short drive north to Battenkill from New York City. It's a fantastic opportunity for bicycle racing in the Northeast to showcase the landscapes that both events represent: the magnificence of New York City and the rural terrain of the Battenkill Valley of upstate New York," Dieter Drake, president of Anthem Sports which operates Battenkill, told Cyclingnews.

Having the GP NYC on the international calendar brings the number of UCI road events in the US for men in 2027 to five, with USPro Road Nationals in mid-June providing an additional opportunity for UCI points. For women, however, there are only three events with UCI points – Tour of the Gila, USPro Nationals and Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b AmeriGas. Both Battenkill and Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic provide prize purses and USA Cycling-sanctioned women's categories.

"Of course, we would love to have a women's pro race as well. We've put it out there to sponsors," Fluhme explained. He said the issue was to make the women's race safe as well as affordable.

"If we put women into this, we would be looking at having to start the women an hour ahead of the men, which means an hour extension of closures. We could start them right after the men or together; then we would need to leave an hour gap for the amateurs.

"So we estimate a cost of the women's pro race in addition at $100,000. We have not overcome that hurdle of the finance to get it done."

The official Team Presentation for the men's pro race will take place on the second day of the NYC Bike Expo, May 14-15, held at the GFNY Festival Village in Fort Lee, New Jersey, where the finish lines are based on Sunday. Confirmations of pro teams and more race weekend activities will be made in the coming weeks.

"This is a passion project. It just costs money at this point. But you know, I'm a lifetime cyclist, bike racer; I love pro cycling, so that's why we do this. And I believe in it. I believe in the concept of integrating the two, the Grand Fondo, together with the pro race because the Grand Fondo riders are the fans of the sport."

issues.title: 'Now time to get serious' – Tadej Pogačar wraps up off-season of travelling, running, and fellow pro's wedding, as 2027 preparations set to begin
issues.summary: Slovenian set to start ramping up his time on the bike ahead of UAE Team Emirates-XRG training camp in December
issues.author: Dani Ostanek
issues.content_html:
Tadej Pogačar has announced that it's "now time to get serious" as he calls an end to his off-season ahead of ramping up preparations for a racing return in 2027.

The Slovenian former world champion was forced to end his 2026 campaign prematurely after crashing out of the Vuelta a España. After recovering from his injuries, he has spent recent weeks travelling and enjoying time away from serious training and racing.

Pogačar's latest stop came in Ireland at the weekend, where he and his partner Urška Žigart attended sometime training partner Eddie Dunbar's wedding in Killarney. He wasn't riding his road bike while in Ireland, but was spotted by several locals riding a mountain bike and going for a run in the woods.

"Now time to get serious. But before that, spent some nice moments around the world," Pogačar wrote in an Instagram post on Tuesday.

"Sometimes cycling gives you more than just wins. Thank you Eddie Dunbar and Niamh O'Keeffe for having us there on your special weekend (yes, Irish weddings are long)! It was sound."

In a change from two wheels, running seems to have been a theme of Pogačar's off-season, with a video as part of his post showing him on another run, by the coast.

Next up for Pogačar will be a return to serious training as he prepares for 2027, with a meetup with his UAE Team Emirates-XRG team for a training camp in south east Spain next month.

His early-season schedule isn't yet known, but he is set for a return to the UAE Tour in February, a race he's won on three occasions in the past. Last month, he offered a suggestion of his main goals for 2027 – the Tour de France, Vuelta a España, and the Road World Championships – but the full outline is set to be confirmed in mid-December at the training camp.

issues.title: Rapha Pro Team Shadow winter glove review: A good addition to the Shadow range but perhaps not the best value
issues.summary: The Rapha Shadow range was expanded for this winter
issues.author: Tom Wieckowski
issues.content_html:
Tech specs

Price: $120 / £80 / €95

Weight: 58 grams per pair - Medium

Colour: Black / Laurel

Sizes: XS/S/M/L/XL

Touchscreen compatible: Yes

Rapha resurrected its Shadow range of foul-weather and winter clothing last year, and has expanded it coming into this winter season.

Gloves were included in that expansion, and the brand has released the Pro Team Shadow Winter gloves, which sit alongside the Shadow gloves in the winter lineup.

The Pro Team Shadow gloves are, in the brand’s words, ‘engineered for hard training in cold and damp conditions’.

These are thinner gloves that are designed to offer good dexterity and protection from the elements. They are also, given their ‘Pro Team’ name, designed with more purposeful riding in mind, where hands will stay warmer when you are generating that little bit more heat, but of course, you can use them for anything.

My glove testing for winter is well underway for our best winter cycling gloves guide. Whilst there’s still some warmth left in the sun's rays in my part of the world (UK), I’ve sought out some freezing conditions to put them through their paces.

If you are shopping for a thinner pair of light/mid weight gloves this winter, this review should give you the inside track on some of Rapha's new Shadow products.

Design and aesthetics

These are thinner gloves designed with more purposeful riding in mind; they are also well suited to slightly milder temperatures or riders who don't want or need too much of a bulky glove.

Rapha says it has used its ‘Shadow technology’ in the makeup, meaning the gloves feature its Shadow membrane and a DWR coating. The Shadow membrane is an in-house offering from Rapha.

Rapha lists a temperature range for these gloves of 0-7C / 32-45F. If you are going hard in the cold, that might be ok. It depends on the rider, but if you are looking at these gloves for general fall riding in cooler conditions, I would recommend wearing something warmer below about 5C / 41F.

There’s Japanese OCTA thermal insulation in parts of the inside, and what looks like the same grid-shaped fleece that features on the Pro Team Bibtights and Pro Team Shadow Winter Jacket; it’s good stuff, similar (if not the same as Polartec Power Grid) and has always kept me comfortable.

The gloves pull on, extending a few centimetres up the wrist; I've worn them over and under long-sleeve base layers, arm warmers, jacket sleeves. The length is good.

The index finger is touchscreen compatible, which is just as well as the gloves do need a fair pull to get on, especially if you are slightly damp. Rapha recommends sizing up if you are in between sizes.

Two fingers, the top of the thumb and the palm also have a series of grippy dots applied, and grip is good on brake hoods and bar tape.

The entire thumb is covered in a soft nose wipe material, which is great; it's nice to have in the cold, and I'm glad Rapha has included it.

There are also some pretty specific care instructions on the Rapha website. I assume to look after the PFAS-free DWR, Rapha says to wash in a laundry bag at 30 degrees Celsius, and to rinse twice after washing. You can also tumble dry to reactivate the DWR. If the waterproofing was amazing, I’d be more motivated, but I’m not sure I’m going to have motivation to rinse these things twice after every wash.

Branding is minimal, with a small Rapha wordmark on the outside of each wrist and the recognisable Rapha dashes on the little finger. Black and Laurel (a kind of light grey) colours are available.

Performance

I’ve worn these gloves across a wide range of autumn temperatures, from the low teens to five degrees above freezing and in the rain. One of the first things I learnt about them is that they are not a pair of gloves to choose for anything more than light rain.

Within 40 minutes, I had soaked hands wearing them in medium rain on a gravel ride, my first outing with them. They resisted water for a little while, but were quickly overcome and got pretty waterlogged. My lower overall off-road speed did lead to my hands getting uncomfortable. I felt the thumb-wipe panel was probably one of the main key weak points regarding water ingress.

For intermittent rain or light showers, you may be ok, especially if you are going hard, but they won’t stand up to much water, so bear this in mind.

In the cold, going hard, they perform very nicely. I wore them on my local chaingang in 5ºC, riding hard, and they kept my hands comfortable without getting sweaty, ditto for various sets of uphill intervals, which is pretty much what they say they will do on the tin.

A feature I really like is the nose wipe panel, which covers most of the thumb. It’s really soft, and just helps when you need to wipe your nose in the cold. It’s probably my favourite feature and has been well executed.

Putting the gloves on and off isn't the easiest; for instance, taking them off for uphill intervals and then putting them back on for steadier riding is ok, but that tighter cuff makes it a little trickier.

When you are just trying to crack on, little things like that can be annoying in the winter cold. Breathability is decent, though, so perhaps more riders will just leave them on, and generally I have too.

For general riding, in cooler conditions, they work well too; they are thin enough to provide very good control and dexterity, and do a decent job of keeping your hands warm and comfortable. As an autumn option, or a thinner glove for more intense riding, they do their job well.

Value

These are fairly pricey gloves at $120 / £80 / €95. They are well executed, look good, and do their job well. However, the rain protection is minimal. Switching to a neoprene offering in rain may be the way to go, but that does mean buying another pair of gloves.

These are a competitor to the popular Castelli Perfetto RoS 2 glove; those gloves are designed for a similar purpose using Gore-Tex Lab's Windstopper and a soft internal fleece and retail for £85 / $95. Does that Castelli Gore-Tex Windstopper label just carry a little more weight?

Despite being a similar weight, there perhaps isn't quite the same amount of insulation as the Q36.5 Termico gloves, but those gloves don't have a nose wipe panel or touchscreen compatibility like these ones do.

These are a solid pair of gloves, seemingly good quality and well made, and they do their primary function very well, but you can achieve the same performance for less money.

Verdict

A good pair of lightweight gloves from Rapha that do what they say on the tin. They provide good warmth, dexterity and wind-blocking properties in a neat package.

They look good and fit well, but aren't going to handle too much rain, so don't expect them to.

The Pro Team Shadow gloves will carry you through Autumn and Spring and down to close to freezing if you are riding hard and generating heat and don't want the bulk of a bigger glove.

Testing scorecard and notes

Design and aesthetics

A good design that does what it says on the tin. Some protection in the wet, but not very much. Nice subtle styling.

9/10

Wet weather performance

Not great, wet hands within 60 minutes in the rain. Although these gloves aren't designed to deal with lots of rain.

6/10

Cold weather performance

Good across a wide range of temperatures. These aren't heavy winter gloves, but offer enough warmth when riding harder in some quite cold conditions.

8/10

Comfort and fit

Comfortable with a great thumb nose wipe panel. Id maybe just like the wrist to be a touch stretchier.

8/10

Value

A little on the pricey side, par for the couse for a Rapha Pro Team product. Good gloves, but you can achieve the same for less without doubt.

7/10

Overall

38/50

issues.author: Ben Fisher at Cardiff City Stadium
issues.content_html:
One way or another, Portugal’s No 7 shirt has caused quite the commotion in recent weeks and months, if not years. Perhaps it was inevitable, then, that the first win of the post-Cristiano Ronaldo era would come courtesy of the player wearing the updated jersey, one with a cross through the number to preserve Ronaldo’s eternal legacy, as the Portuguese Football Federation put it. A sumptuous finish by Carlos Forbs, a second-half substitute, was ultimately enough to clinch victory on a topsy-turvy night with Portugal surviving Pedro Neto’s sending-off for two yellow cards.

For Wales, a Nations League relegation playoff double-header awaits in March, with Slovenia, Hungary, Republic of Ireland or Bosnia and Herzegovina – who knocked them out of World Cup qualifying this year – all potential opponents in Friday’s draw in Switzerland. Afterwards Craig Bellamy stressed the importance of keeping elite company to accelerate improvement but reiterated that he will not be in the job beyond Euro 2028, after which his contract expires.

This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly s
issues.author: Robert Kitson
issues.content_html:
Springboks’ achievements are remarkable but their head coach lacks statesmanship, diplomacy and good grace in defeat

So here we go again. Exactly five years have passed since South Africa’s head coach, Rassie Erasmus, first felt the full force of World Rugby’s ire for criticising match officials. And guess what? This most habitual of offenders has just copped another lengthy ban – and deservedly so – for his latest intemperate comments, notable as ever for their total lack of statesmanship, diplomacy or good grace in defeat.

To his acolytes his outspoken nature is part of what makes Rassie such a groot leier (great leader). To many others it simply cements his status as a serial prat. For the avoidance of any doubt everyone respects the remarkable achievements both of Erasmus and his double World Cup-winning teams. It is the rest of the package, sadly, that is too often a major letdown.
