issues.title: Pentagram draws on ancient Greek coinage for Alpha Bank identity refresh
issues.summary: Established in 1879 and headquartered in Athens with more than 200 branches across Greece, Alpha Bank is a universal bank known for personal service, relationship-based banking, wealth management and private banking, alongside recent innovations in digital banking. Beyond financial services, the institution plays a prominent role in preserving Greek culture and heritage, maintaining an extensive [
issues.author: Design Week
issues.content_html:
Established in 1879 and headquartered in Athens with more than 200 branches across Greece, Alpha Bank is a universal bank known for personal service, relationship-based banking, wealth management and private banking, alongside recent innovations in digital banking.

Beyond financial services, the institution plays a prominent role in preserving Greek culture and heritage, maintaining an extensive art and numismatic collection. A silver coin from this collection – the silver stater of Aegina – originally inspired the bank’s 1972 logo. Minted by the first city-state in the Greek world and Europe to produce its own coinage, it was the earliest silver coin used across markets in the Mediterranean and the east.

When Alpha Bank’s senior leadership commissioned Domenic Lippa and his team at Pentagram to develop a new identity system, that ancient coin once again served as the primary reference point. The brief required a design that respected the institution’s history while strengthening its market position, responding to shifting customer expectations and reflecting an ambition to modernise the business. The resulting system needed to resonate with young professionals, affluent clients and wider public and institutional audiences alike.

Developed alongside brand strategy and narrative by Simple Revolution, the positioning centres on the brand idea ‘Building progress, together’ and introduces the campaign line ‘A new together’. Both elements are intended to anchor a futureproof identity that feels human and contemporary while remaining trustworthy and reliable.

Liberating the symbol and custom typography

At the core of Pentagram’s redesign is a redrawn version of the bank’s emblem. The team retained the understated central axis detail of the silver stater and framed it within an expressive roundel that preserves the original coin’s subtle historical asymmetries. Every component of the identity stems from this central mark, spanning the wordmark, custom typography, icon suite, signage, floor numbers and brand patterns.

Lippa explained that developing the final design relied heavily on client collaboration. “I believe within any project we are eternally searching for the truth in the solution,” Lippa said. “To discover the truth, you need a client willing to help you go on that journey. The team at Alpha Bank gave us 110% of their time, knowledge and ambition. Without them, we would never have managed to find what we were searching for.”

He noted that the client’s willingness to push beyond the initial parameters allowed the design team to restore the emblem’s visual integrity. “Alpha was willing to explore different opportunities and, in so doing, was open to pushing the brief further,” Lippa said. “Once that creative door was opened, we could go in different directions, but what I felt quite early was that the emotional strength of the legacy was the symbol. And that symbol had lost some of its quality and balance. I wanted to make the symbol reconnect to its source – the original silver stater.”

To give the emblem prominence, Pentagram separated it from the logotype. “The symbol needed to become the emotional heart of the brand, as it was originally,” Lippa added. “For this to happen, we needed to liberate it from the wordmark. The wordmark itself needed to be less formal but still retain the authority for the bank. After all, this was still a bank. Once these principles were resolved, everything else seemed to fall into place.”

The updated wordmark takes its structural cues from Alpha Sans, a custom five-weight typeface developed with Tom Baber in both Greek and Latin scripts. Inspired directly by the proportions of the coin symbol, Alpha Sans is paired with Alpha Text, a functional secondary typeface built for body copy at smaller sizes.

An expanded palette and versatile brand assets

Pentagram built the enhanced colour system around the existing Alpha Blue, white and Galazio Blue. These core tones are joined by a secondary palette comprising Thalassi Turquoise, Heritage Pink and Alpha Gold, which are used to distinguish sub-brands such as business and private banking. Five additional bright colours have also been introduced specifically for digital applications, including infographics.

“The typeface [Alpha Sans] was based on the proportions of the symbol. The colour palette is a combination of historic and contemporary shades that enables the brand to be dynamic and flexible. Other assets allow the brand to be engaging and at times surprising,” Lippa said.

Those supporting assets include a suite of abstract and logo-derived patterns generated from elements of the symbol and wordmark. Designed to bring visual interest where a more expressive treatment is required, the patterns scale from large-format graphic applications down to subtle textural repeats. A bespoke set of brand icons was also designed to align with the geometry of the new symbol, functioning across large-scale print and outdoor applications as well as compact digital interfaces.

For photography, the identity adopts a stylistic approach centred on everyday moments, focusing on people and their immediate surroundings to create relatable, real-life connections. Depth of field is applied consistently across day and night scenes, as well as portraits and landscapes, to establish visual clarity and immerse the viewer in each frame.

Translating the vision into physical spaces

To extend the visual identity into physical environments, experience design consultancy Dalziel & Pow developed a new approach to Alpha Bank’s branch experience. The concept has debuted at the bank’s branch in Kolonaki, Athens’ luxury retail and cultural quarter, reimagining the traditional banking hall as a warmer, more personal and contemporary space.

Across digital channels and physical branches, the design system establishes a coherent visual language capable of adapting to Alpha Bank’s varied audiences and services while supporting its long-term commercial ambitions.

issues.summary: Crystal Ski, the UK’s leading ski holiday provider, has launched a comprehensive rebrand developed by WPP-owned design consultancy Landor. The project is designed to capture the attention of a new generation of holidaymakers, reaching beyond seasoned skiers to attract people who have never previously considered a mountain break. Following extensive audience research that identified nine […] What t
issues.author: Design Week
issues.content_html:
Crystal Ski, the UK’s leading ski holiday provider, has launched a comprehensive rebrand developed by WPP-owned design consultancy Landor. The project is designed to capture the attention of a new generation of holidaymakers, reaching beyond seasoned skiers to attract people who have never previously considered a mountain break.

Following extensive audience research that identified nine new target groups across existing and potential customers, Landor developed the strategic positioning “Escape to higher ground”. This direction shifts the brand’s focus from the practical logistics and value of booking a ski trip to the emotional and restorative benefits of the mountain environment. The updated strategy positions the category as an antidote to the always-on nature of modern life, offering vast landscapes and cold air to help travellers disconnect.

The Crystal lens

To distinguish Crystal Ski from competitors heavily reliant on familiar tropes of carving through powder and traditional après-ski celebrations, the design team created a visual language rooted in the physical properties of snow. At the core of the identity is the “Crystal Lens”, a signature graphic device inspired by the sixfold symmetry of snowflakes.

Formed by the shape of the letter “Y” in the Crystal Ski wordmark, the lens acts as a framing tool across brand communications. It refracts imagery to reveal different perspectives of a mountain holiday, highlighting a wide variety of experiences from saunas and hot springs to raclette dinners.

Crystalline typography and colour

The redesigned logo incorporates angled letterforms and distinctive crystalline cuts, complete with a diamond-shaped dot positioned above the “i”. For the typography, Landor selected the Season typeface family by Display Foundry, pairing the structured Season Sans with the more expressive Season Mix.

Supporting the primary assets is a new, mountain-inspired colour palette. The adaptable system includes shades named mountain stone, cloud white, evergreen, aurora, glacier, midnight, twilight and alpenglow. Accompanying photography art direction deliberately uses unexpected angles to present alpine settings in fresh ways, working in tandem with a verbal identity that brings emotion and wit to the brand’s messaging.

Broadening the appeal of the mountains

The refreshed identity is rolling out across Crystal Ski’s digital and physical touchpoints, supported by a new creative campaign developed by VML.

Ellie Eyles, head of marketing at Crystal Ski, noted that while the business has built its reputation on making ski holidays easy and inclusive, there is a broader opportunity to capture everything that makes a winter break special – from the excitement of the slopes to the feeling of leaving everyday life behind. She said: “Working in partnership with Landor, we’ve created an identity that builds on the trust we’ve established while giving us a platform to reach the next generation of holidaymakers.”

Emma Ellis, UK managing director at Landor, said: “Crystal Ski already has something many brands are working hard to build: strong recognition, trust and a loyal customer base. The opportunity was to use that strength to unlock future growth, creating desire among people who might never have considered a ski holiday. The category has traditionally focused on the practicalities of skiing, but there’s a much richer emotional story to tell. ‘Escape to higher ground’ builds on Crystal’s reputation for simplicity by capturing the wider emotional appeal of the mountains, giving the brand a distinctive platform for its next phase of growth.”

issues.title: The Outline: Toaster creative chair, a tour of Pentagram NY, and a book cover – 16/11/2026
issues.summary: Welcome to The Outline, Design Week’s weekly roundup of the stories you might have missed. This week, Neville Brody joins Toaster as Creative Chair, Paula Scher gives a tour of Pentagram New York, sound studio father heads to Dungeness to open a new chapter, and more. Business News Sound studio father opens Chapter 01 with […] What to read next: The Outline – IMAX, Alan Cumming, and a coffee table
issues.author: Design Week
issues.content_html:
Welcome to The Outline, Design Week’s weekly roundup of the stories you might have missed.

This week, Neville Brody joins Toaster as Creative Chair, Paula Scher gives a tour of Pentagram New York, sound studio father heads to Dungeness to open a new chapter, and more.

Business News

Sound studio father opens Chapter 01 with a film made in Dungeness

London sound studio father, founded by composers Freddie Webb and Joe Farley, has launched Chapter 01, a new phase for the business, with Can You Hear This?, a short film made on Kent’s shingle coast at Dungeness. The team set up a mobile studio there for several days, captured sounds from the landscape using hydrophones and contact microphones, and turned what they heard into music. Farley calls the result “an unspoken manifesto” for the studio’s approach, which treats sound as a design material from the outset rather than a final layer.

That thinking runs through its commissioned work, from scores built out of recordings of materials and processes for the V&A’s Schiaparelli exhibition, made with design studio Nebbia, to a sonic identity for O2 that started with a recording session of human breath. Chapter 01 continues later this month with an evolved visual identity by Further, built on a grid inspired by varying tempos, and a collection of designed objects. In December, a limited vinyl release designed with Tom Hingston will follow, alongside a listening session at Space Talk in London.

Paula Scher gives Future London Academy a tour of Pentagram New York

Pentagram partner Paula Scher has opened up Pentagram’s New York office for Inside Pentagram, a new film from Future London Academy hosted by co-founder Ekaterina Solomeina. On the tour, Scher reveals that the meeting rooms are named after the founding partners, though “most of the people who work here don’t have any idea” who they were. The staff canteen came about because Colin Forbes calculated that hiring a cook was cheaper than long lunches. The conversation then ranges across her career.

She describes missing her first meeting with her hero Seymour Chwast after her train broke down, and writing The Brownstone, her only children’s book, which is still in print 50 years on. She also recalls showing her Public Theater identity to the London partners, two of whom walked out over its mixed type weights. Thirty-two years on, she still runs that identity from a single poster each year that serves as its manual. Scher also reflects on the decline of design communities in New York. “I think they’re too competitive,” she says. “The community got nastier.”

Appointments

Neville Brody joins Toaster as Creative Chair

Designer and typographer Neville Brody has been appointed Creative Chair at Toaster, the creative product marketing agency founded in 2010 by former Google creatives. Brody, whose work for The Face, Channel 4, Nike and Kenzo has shaped visual culture for more than four decades, moves from Brody Associates to join the agency, formalising a long relationship that began with his role as an advisory member of Toaster’s board. He will work across new and existing client relationships, and will set up Toaster Labs, a lab space exploring the overlap between creativity and technology, human and machine.

The launch builds on Toaster AI Studio, which opened earlier this year alongside Toaster Brand and Toaster Creative. “AI is inevitable,” says Brody. “It can accelerate highly complex and repetitive processes, but when it works by averaging what already exists, it also risks creating a spiral of homogenisation.” Founder and CEO Tom Dunn says bringing Brody’s brand craft together with the agency’s creative, content and AI production capability gives product-led brands “something that has never been more necessary”. Toaster’s clients include Google, Netflix, YouTube and Samsung. Brody was awarded an OBE in 2025 and is Professor of Communication at the Royal College of Art.

Design Bits

Naipe Foundry’s Urca brings Rio glamour to beauty branding

Barcelona-based Naipe Foundry has released Urca, a high-contrast sans serif for beauty, cosmetics and fashion brands that want an alternative to both formal luxury and generic minimalism. Designed by Brazilian founders Ãlvaro Franca and Felipe Casaprima, the typeface is named after a peninsula in Rio de Janeiro that still holds the atmosphere of the city’s mid-century glamour. The area was home to the Cassino da Urca, where Carmen Miranda performed for years, and it stood in for early-1970s Rio in the Oscar-winning film I’m Still Here.

Urca pairs the dramatic thick-and-thin contrast of fashion mastheads with softened, rounded details, aiming to feel polished but approachable. “Think beautiful ready-to-wear rather than sharp stilettos,” says Franca. Its thin strokes are sturdier than in classic high-contrast faces such as Didot or Bodoni, so it stays crisp at small sizes. The family spans nine weights in static and variable formats, supports more than 200 Latin-script languages and includes a fleuron and a manicule. It is available through Adobe Fonts, and direct licences from Naipe start at â‚¬50 per weight.

Monotype adds four new styles to Jonathan Hoefler’s Inkwell family

Monotype has expanded Inkwell, the handwriting-inspired type family that Jonathan Hoefler began designing in 2004, with four new styles: Antique, Formal, Chancery and Ornaments. The idea for Inkwell came from a map Hoefler was designing for his wedding at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, which called for lettering that felt informal but considered, sitting somewhere between official type and elaborate calligraphy. Released by Hoefler&Co in 2017, its seven original styles each span six weights, from the fine line of a technical pen to the force of a permanent marker.

Monotype senior type designer Jordan Bell, who joined the project in 2015, led the expansion. Antique draws on ornamented Victorian lettering, Formal puts a new twist on the classic engraver’s script, and Chancery draws on Renaissance writing with swash capitals. Bell’s own Ornaments set adds emoji, pointing hands, weather devices and cartographic symbols, bringing the family back to its mapmaking origins. “Inkwell has always been a passion project, one built around the joy of making and using type,” says Bell. The new styles add 24 fonts to the family and are available through Monotype Fonts and MyFonts.

Chilly’s opens a build-your-own-bottle pop-up in Soho

Reusable bottle brand Chilly’s has opened Every Part Matters, an interactive Christmas pop-up on Walker’s Court in Soho, built around the modular design of its Series 3 Bottle and Flip. Visitors can build their own products by mixing and matching components and adding laser engraving. The space also breaks the products down into their parts, to show how each one can be customised, replaced, upgraded and returned at the end of its life, with the aim of keeping products in use for longer.

Ready-made products and seasonal collections are also on sale, alongside a refill point and a dedicated area for returning end-of-life products. The pop-up coincides with the launch of a new extended warranty. “For us, thoughtful design means thinking beyond the day someone buys the bottle,” says co-founder and director Tim Bouscarle. He adds that the brand wants people to “leave with a product they’ll value long after the decorations come down”. Founded in 2010 by Bouscarle and James Butterfield as an alternative to single-use plastic bottles, Chilly’s is running the pop-up until 23 December.

Stop Look and Listen sends illustrated poetry book Jack and Jill uphill

Jack and Jill, a folk-horror teen romance in verse by poet Thomas Sharp, is being published as a limited-edition illustrated hardback. Studio Stop, Look and Listen designed it, and its founders, Rosey Trickett and Marc Spicer, deliberately steered clear of the visual clichés that have built up around the folk revival: Barleycorn dollies, blackletter, mummers’ masks and standing stones. Instead, the book draws on the British psychedelic underground press of the 1960s and 1970s, chalk figures, road signs and countryside skies. Millie Turner’s psychedelic illustrations set the tone, and the typography follows the story.

It sits at increasing inclines rather than on a regular baseline, as if trudging uphill. Hand-pressed typographic prints of Sharp’s nursery-rhyme passages are set against the silhouettes of English hills, like white chalk figures, alongside inky gradients inspired by summer night skies. The dust jacket turns the hill contours of a Victorian geologist’s map into inky psychedelia. The 88-page foiled hardback has a first printing of 120 copies and launches on 25 November at Proposition Studios in Bethnal Green, with a reading, design talks and a one-off choral performance.

Desk Curiosities

Tamp Coffee’s Helch cups become a tribute to the late street artist

Chiswick speciality coffee shop Tamp Coffee is giving away takeaway cups featuring artwork by Helch, the West London street artist known for his distinctive lettering, who died just days after the collaboration launched. Tamp’s founder, Dorian Needs, had commissioned Helch to bring his signature style to the shop’s cups as a celebration of local creativity. Following his death, the project has become a tribute, and Tamp chose not to publicise it until now.

Rather than selling the limited-edition cups, Tamp is handing them out to customers with any purchase. “Helch’s work was part of the fabric of West London, and we’d admired his art for a long time,” says Needs. “We wanted to give the cups away rather than put a price on them, so that people in the community can enjoy a little piece of his work and join us in celebrating the legacy he leaves behind.” Tamp opened on Devonshire Road in 2014, inspired by Needs’ time in South America, and has long championed street art in the area. It commissioned the mural on the wall outside the shop, as well as another across the road. The cups are available at 1 Devonshire Road, Chiswick.

Northern Festival of Illustration launches a Young Illustrators Prize

The Northern Festival of Illustration, the biennial Hartlepool festival run by The Northern School of Art, has launched a Young Illustrators Prize for 2027, opening its competitions to 12- to 18-year-olds for the first time. Until now, the festival’s competitions have focused on professional and emerging illustrators. Entrants from the UK and around the world are invited to respond to the theme The Art of Being, a celebration of the everyday wonder of being human, through still images, animation or animated GIFs.

“It could be the art of being hilarious, the art of being creative, the art of being magical, there really are no limits to how they approach it,” says festival director Matthew Burton, a senior lecturer on the school’s Illustration for Commercial Application degree. The overall winner will receive £300, and two highly commended entrants will get £100 each. All three will be able to exhibit at the 2027 festival alongside established artists. Up to ten shortlisted entrants will receive a gift bag and certificate. The prize is free to enter. The deadline is 31 January 2027, the shortlist will be announced on 1 March and the winners on 1 April.

Psychedelics Design Awards 2026 crown a Burning Man gateway and “soilpunk” folktales

The second Psychedelics Design Awards, which bill themselves as the world’s first design competition dedicated to the psychedelics space, have announced their winners. The awards attracted 86 entries from 13 countries, almost twice last year’s number, and nearly 40% entered on a scholarship. The nine winners were revealed at Creative Biome, the fifth Psychedelics Design conference. They include The Sphinx Gate, an immersive rite of passage built for Burning Man, in Architecture and Space, and Bionic and the Wires, a UK project that connects bionic arms to mushrooms and plants so they can make music, in Audio and Music.

SoundSelf, a meditation technology guided by the user’s own voice, took Products and Services. Tractor Beam, a seasonal collection of future farmers’ folktales building a new genre it calls “soilpunk”, won Visual Design and Branding. Drug Science and the Organisation for Indigenous Outreach & Conservation took Educational and Community Impact for their Indigenous-led research into plant medicines. Entries were judged by a 32-member international jury, which included Design Week’s own David Coveney.

Entries for 2027 open early next year.

issues.title: New Godflesh & Jesu with Phoebe too
issues.summary: Some of the many reasons it’s been a great year for post-metal.
issues.author: Jeff Bergstrom
issues.content_html:
The great Jon Wurster (The Mountain Goats, The Bob Mould Band, Superchunk, The Best Show with Tom Scharpling) is a prolific drummer and one of the funniest people on earth. One of my favorite Wursterisms™ is that he utilizes the hashtag #rocknrollweirdness on Instagram when posting images of incongruous moments in rock n’ roll. Whether it’s a picture of The Who holding their Who Are You release party on the Hollywood set of the TV show Battlestar Galactica, Oasis hanging with Wesley Willis, or Motörhead drummer Philthy Animal Taylor and W.A.S.P. guitarist Chris Holmes having ice cream on a nice day, Wurster is a master curator of singular images of #rocknrollweirdness.

It’s rare for an instance of #rocknrollweirdness to land so profoundly with me that it gives me the energy to take finger-to-keyboard for the first time in years. Yet it recently came to my attention that master of heviosity Justin K. Broadrick was recently tapped by mainstream indie icon Phoebe Bridgers to play guitar on two tracks of her August 14, 2026 release Lost Weekend. Justin performs on track #5, “Bobby,” as well as on the ‘hidden’ track “Best Dressed” (track D17 on the vinyl and Track 00 on CD). Broadrick is involved with many different personal projects, each with their own particular signature sonic qualities, so it is important to note that he performs on these tracks under his Jesu moniker. And although I find his contributions to be buried under too many layers of over-production, the Broadrick aficionado can immediately recognize Jesu’s signature guitar sound in the first 15-seconds of “Bobby.” Lost Weekend was the Number 1 album in the UK and debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200. This is almost definitely the first time Justin has been that high in the charts.

But there was more! Phoebe Bridgers then released “On Video,” her song from the new A24 film Primetime. You can listen to it below. Oh and guess what? Justin Broadrick played bass and guitar on that song. As you probably know by now, Phoebe is also in the movie, and has been playing the song on tour.

These aren’t the first instances that Justin and Phoebe’s careers have intersected. Back in 2021, again under the Jesu moniker, Justin remixed Phoebe’s Boygenius bandmate Julien Baker’s track “Favor.” Justin not only executed the remix, but he also played guitars on the track which also features Phoebe Bridgers (and Lucy Dacus) on backing vocals. Check that track out below.

In other Justin K. Broadrick news, we’ve had a few months to let it sink in that the mighty Godflesh has retired from touring due to ongoing health issues plaguing Justin. The good news is that prior to his tour-ending surgery, Justin and Benny had an entire new Godflesh album pretty much already in the can. The album, entitled Decay, dropped on September 25 via Relapse Records and is available in all the formats, including vinyl in all kinds of colors and patterns.

Fortunately, all of the recordings for Decay were completed long before the surgery, vocals included… although the back end of a couple of songs were recorded with the hernia itself, and that was a struggle. I was already aware that the GODFLESH shout, so to speak, was exacerbating the hernia greatly, as was every GODFLESH performance in the lead-up to the surgery once the hernia appeared, and the hernia was mostly caused by year upon year of shouting in GODFLESH. The album was mixed post-surgery, and while I was still in some pain and considerable discomfort, but fortunately GODFLESH is generally me expressing my pain, albeit [usually] mental, philosophical and existential, whereas this was physical pain.

You can listen to “Living/Ending” below and do some heavy duty ordering of the vinyl.

I interviewed Justin back in 2014 and would love to interview him again someday to discuss all of his projects BUT Godflesh. Until that happens, both Guitar World and The Guardian have published very good interviews with him that do a great job bringing fans up to speed with the current state of Justin’s world.

See also: it’s been a great year for post-metal.

issues.title: 5 Artists We Want to See at Louder Than Life 2026
issues.summary: Louder Than Life’s 2026 edition is coming. Check out who we’re excited to see.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
Louder Than Life‘s 2026 edition is this weekend: September 17-20 at Kentucky Expo Center in Louisville, KY. As always, we’re figuring out who we most don’t want to miss. We’ll of course be sticking around for big headliners Tool, Iron Maiden, and My Chemical Romance, but the variety of acts we’re excited about across punk and metal genres this year is vast. Here are five artists that we’re especially looking forward to:

Circa Survive

As Andrew Sacherwrote when the band first announced their return:

Circa Survive went on “indefinite hiatus” in 2022, which came as bummer news considering they had just released some of the best music of their career, and the prospect of a reunion didn’t look very good after singer Anthony Greensaid on HardLore in December that what happened in 2022 was more of a “breakup” than a “hiatus” and added, “I don’t know if the band is ever going to do anything ever again… And even if it did, it wouldn’t be the same. It just wouldn’t.” So, it comes as a nice surprise that Circa Survive just announced their first show in nearly five years! They’ll be playing Louisville’s Louder Than Life festival in September, and Anthony Green will be pulling double duty at that fest, as L.S. Dunes are playing too. (Everyone in L.S. Dunes will be pulling double duty at that fest, as My Chemical Romance, Coheed & Cambria, and Thursday are playing too.

We can’t wait!

Haywire

Boston punks Haywire are one of the most exciting, most fun, and fastest rising hardcore bands of recent times, with banger after banger, and with more on the way soon, as they recently announced their second full-length album, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, due October 2 via their new label home, Roadrunner Records. Their raucous live shows continue to be unmissable, whether in a basement, a boxing ring, a club, or at a fest. See you in the pit.

Missing Link

Staying on the fest’s Friday hardcore stage for a second: playing before Haywire and the recently-announed, no-longer secret guest Knocked Loose, we want to highlight NY heavy hardcore band Missing Link whose intesity blows us away every time we get the chance to catch them (including sometimes with Haywire). Great live show. Don’t mess up and miss them in Louisville.

Hot Mulligan

Louder than Life also brings the pop punk, and the post-hardcore and emo-leaning Lansing, Michigan band Hot Mulligan are doing it better than most right now. Now four full lengths into their career, the band has become a festival staple, somtimes a rare mosh pit-inducing band on a lineup (like when we saw them at Gov Ball and Lolla), and sometimes right where they belong like in between Alkaline Trio and Jimmy Eat World in Louisville in Thursday. Always a super fun time, we can’t get enough of their energy, their humor, and their infectious hooks.

Danzig

The man, the myth, the legend. Danzig on this year’s fest officially brings it over the top for this Danzig-obsesed writer.

Check out the entire lineup HERE, and have fun this weekend.

issues.title: Haywire sign to Roadrunner, announce new LP & video, threw $$ into the crowd at Sound & Fury, keep touring & stuff (BV-exclusive vinyl)
issues.summary: The album was produced by Mat from Citizen and mixed by Taylor Young whose band God’s Hate meanwhile surprised the world with a surprise Sound & Fury set followed by a surprise new EP.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
Boston punks Haywire are one of the fastest rising hardcore bands of recent times, and now they’ve announced their second full-length album, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, due October 2 via their new label home, Roadrunner Records. Citizen‘s Mat Kerekes produced the album. Taylor Young mixed it at The Pit. The album was recorded over three months in Leeds, UK and Toledo, OH, and features appearances from members of Nothing and The Aggrolites, along with other friends of the band.

We’ve teamed up with the band for a BrooklynVegan-exclusive vinyl variant of I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, limited to just 300 copies. Pre-order now in the BV Shop.

The first single from I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye is “Interstate Love Affair,” which comes with a Luis Hernandez-directed video. Watch it below.

It follows Haywire’s 2024 great releases, the Conditioned for Demolition LP and For Better or for Worse EP, and 2025 splits with No Guard and Dropkick Murphys ( “Citizen I.C.E.” included).

Constantly on the road (and in our feeds), last year Haywire completed a goal of playing all 50 states, and played an amazing tour with Drain, No Pressure and Secret World. They’re taking a short unexpected break though. They announced this morning that their Australia tour this week is postponed till later in the year, but they’ll be touring again in the US in September, including a Milwaukee show supporting Turnstile, a run opening for Circle Jerks, and appearances at Louder Than Life, Riot Fest, Four Chord Music Festival and CBGB Fest. October brings Aftershock, Furnace Fest, a free University of Connecticut show and Sick New World, followed by Pressure Point Fest and Warped Tour in November.

Haywire revealed that they’d signed to Roadrunner just ahead of this past weekend’s Sound & Fury fest, then celebrated their new record deal by throwing $5,000 in cash into the crowd during their set on Sunday. Watch footage below.

Sunday at Sound & Fury also included a surprise split set from Twitching Tongues and God’s Hate, both bands of brothers Colin and Taylor Young (the same Taylor who worked on the new Haywire album) (and the new Terror record and a million other records). A day after the surprise appearance, God’s Hate revealed that they were ending their hiatus with a new three-song Won’t Be Disgraced EP.

Mat Kerekes’ band Citizen, meanwhile, just released the great new album Halcyon Blues, and we’ve also got a BrooklynVegan-exclusive “Ether” vinyl variant limited to 400 copies.

Again, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye is out October 2 via Roadrunner, and the BrooklynVegan-exclusive vinyl is limited to 300 copies. Here’s the cover art:

issues.title: 19th-Century Philosopher’s Head Examined
issues.summary: LONDON, ENGLAND—English philosopher Jeremy Bentham suffered from painful toothaches and arthritis of the lower jaw, […] The post 19th-Century Philosopher’s Head Examined appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
LONDON, ENGLAND—English philosopher Jeremy Bentham suffered from painful toothaches and arthritis of the lower jaw, according to a statement released by University College London. Bentham is thought to have been the first person to have legally registered the preference for his body to be used for scientific study after death, including preservation as an “auto-icon,” or “self-image.” After his death in June 11, 1832, Bentham’s remains were dissected and his body preserved in the collections of University College London. A team of scientists led by Tim Causer of the Bentham Project carried out advanced CT scanning of Bentham’s head, revealing the poor condition of his teeth and lower jaw. “I have never been fond of having my teeth drawn, but I have more than once submitted to the momentary torment to rid myself of the enduring one,” Bentham wrote to Sir Robert Peel in 1830. The CT scans also confirmed that Bentham’s brain had been removed during the dissection, but some of the outer brain remained in the skull. The glass eyes added to the head in the creation of the auto-icon were found to have been equipped with an anatomically correct optic nerve. The scan also provided a detailed view of the hole driller in the top of the skull in order to attach it to the rest of the auto-icon. To read about some of Bentham’s theories, go to “Alone, but Closely Watched.”

The post 19th-Century Philosopher’s Head Examined appeared first on Archaeology Magazine.

issues.title: Mesopotamian Chronology Refined with Tree Rings and Ice Cores
issues.summary: TUCSON, ARIZONA—Phys.org reports that a team of researchers led by Charlotte Pearson of the University […] The post Mesopotamian Chronology Refined with Tree Rings and Ice Cores appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
TUCSON, ARIZONA—Phys.org reports that a team of researchers led by Charlotte Pearson of the University of Arizona has refined the timeline for historical events in ancient Mesopotamia. First, the team members radiocarbon dated individual tree rings and analyzed tree ring data from timbers unearthed at archaeological sites in Turkey, in order to calculate precise dates for when the trees were felled. These dates helped the researchers to determine when the buildings had been constructed. Then those dates were linked to historical records from the sites that were tied to specific years in the Assyrian calendar. The scientists also evaluated Babylonian records of Venus, noting that sometimes the planet was hard to see because of haze in the atmosphere. They compared these observations with evidence of volcanic eruptions preserved in polar ice cores. The strongest match was found to be an eruption of the Aniakchak volcano in Alaska around 1628 or 1628 B.C. Combining the data, the researchers suggest that Babylon fell around 1587 B.C. , while severe drought between 1194 and 1192 B.C. may have contributed to the collapse of the Hittite Empire. “Single-year measurements of radiocarbon from calendar-dated tree rings offer new opportunities to refine and improve chronologies,” the researchers concluded. To read about evidence of spy craft in Mesopotamia, go to “In His Majesty’s Secret Service.”

The post Mesopotamian Chronology Refined with Tree Rings and Ice Cores appeared first on Archaeology Magazine.

issues.title: New Analysis of Hunter-Gatherer Remains Recovered on Danish Island
issues.summary: GOTHENBURG, SWEDEN—According to a report in La Brújula Verde, a team led by Anders Fischer […] The post New Analysis of Hunter-Gatherer Remains Recovered on Danish Island appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
GOTHENBURG, SWEDEN—According to a report in La Brújula Verde, a team led by Anders Fischer of the University of Gothenburg and John Meadows of the Leibniz Centre for Archaeology has analyzed Rødhals Man, the 6,000-year-old skeletal remains recovered from a midden on the Danish island of Sejerø in 1956. Previous genetic study of the bones revealed that Rødhals Man belonged to a group of western European hunter-gatherers. Analysis of carbon and nitrogen isotopes in his bones and teeth indicates that he ate a diet heavy in marine fish. Adjusting for the “old” carbon acquired through consumption of marine fish, the bones were radiocarbon dated to between about 3890 and 3770 B.C. , around the time that the first farmers appeared in Denmark. Layers of dentine in Rødhals Man’s teeth yielded additional information about his diet over time. During childhood, he consumed marine shellfish, flatfish, and eels. But in adolescence, the amount of protein from land sources in his diet increased beyond that usually observed in the remains of other Mesolithic hunter-fishers found in Denmark. It cannot be determined if this land food came from hunting and gathering, or from eating cows, sheep, and cereals raised and grown by farmers. The researchers suggest, however, that the land food was provided by farmers, since Rødhals Man was not also consuming freshwater fish, as inland hunter-gatherers were likely to do. Additionally, the team notes that the burial of Rødhals Man resembles that of the first farmers, including a frame made of flat stones. The researchers concluded that Rødhals Man may have adopted some of the farmers’ way of life, though he kept many of his ancestors’ traditions. Read the original scholarly article about this research in Antiquity. To read about population shifts between the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods in Denmark, go to “Ancient DNA Revolution: Danish Turnovers.”

The post New Analysis of Hunter-Gatherer Remains Recovered on Danish Island appeared first on Archaeology Magazine.

issues.title: Souvenir Collection May Have Begun 500,000 Years Ago
issues.summary: TEL AVIV, ISRAEL—Hominins may have begun collecting relics and keepsakes some 500,000 years ago, according […] The post Souvenir Collection May Have Begun 500,000 Years Ago appeared first on Archaeology Magazine .
issues.author: Jessica Esther Saraceni
issues.content_html:
TEL AVIV, ISRAEL—Hominins may have begun collecting relics and keepsakes some 500,000 years ago, according to a statement released by Tel Aviv University. These possible souvenirs include small, colorful pebbles unearthed in Israel’s Qesem Cave, and handaxes made from flint containing fossils or unusual geological formations that were recovered in the Sakhnin Valley. Ran Barkai and Ella Assaf of Tel Aviv University and their colleagues said that tools showing signs of heavy use, whether resharpened or not, have been unearthed at several sites, such as Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave. These objects may have been kept for their aged appearance, the researchers explained. Just like modern keepsakes, the objects may have been retained in order to trigger memories of a place or personal experience. Use of such items over many generations may have increased evolutionary pressures on brain mechanisms involved with memory and sense of self, the researchers argue. Read the original scholarly article about this research in Evolutionary Anthropology. To read about stone balls found in Qesem Cave, go to “Around the World: Israel.”

The post Souvenir Collection May Have Begun 500,000 Years Ago appeared first on Archaeology Magazine.

issues.title: The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs
issues.summary: These aren't your grandpa's steroids.
issues.author: Stephen Johnson
issues.content_html:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

Looksmaxxing teenagers are DIY bio-hacking

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

For a look at how this often ends, check out the Hulu documentary Get Huge that details the death and madness that surrounded “Dr.” Tony Huge, a pioneer in the looksmaxxing world, or subscribe to Coach Kolton’s YouTube channel, where the grim consequences of extreme looksmaxxing are presented in graphic detail.

What are “softmaxxing” and “hardmaxxing?”

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

What does “natty” mean?

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

What are the bicep heart and waist heart trend?

Credit: @montanaandryan, @nurciinguldiiken - TikTok

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

Viral videos of the week: messing with AI job interviews

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

issues.title: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?
issues.summary: Every bar, nightclub, and coffee shop seems to have the exact same style now, and it's (sort of) ChatGPT's fault.
issues.author: Eric Ravenscraft
issues.content_html:
You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font . But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “ thinking models ”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

The hidden “design brief” behind every AI poster

To borrow a classic and implausible example , if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

Credit: Eric Ravenscraft/Lifehacker

“Choices” are still driven by statistical models

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

That one font “choice” might be a misinterpretation

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text .

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model , so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

Every chatbot has a “house style" (even if it's an accident)

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

issues.title: These Are the Best Early Black Friday 2026 Deals on Samsung Devices
issues.summary: Samsung's early Black Friday sales are already live.
issues.author: Jake Peterson
issues.content_html:
We may earn a commission from links on this page. Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication.

Black Friday might be a couple of weeks away, but Samsung is rolling out the discounts early, with deals on its entire lineup of devices, including smartphones, tablets, laptops, and wearables. While not all of these early Black Friday offers are true discounts, you can find ways to save money on some devices through these promotions. Here's what Samsung's offering ahead of the official Black Friday discounts.

Best early Black Friday deals on Samsung smartphones

Samsung is offering some decent discounts on both its flagship smartphones and its midrange and budget lines. However, as part of its early Black Friday sale, the company is also offering increased trade-in credits towards these devices. While all of the devices here have trade-in credit options, only some have optional discounts for early Black Friday. Here's what you can expect:

Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra: Save $350 without trade-in (up to $720 with trade-in)

Samsung's premier flagship, the S26 Ultra, is getting a price cut ahead of Black Friday. You can save up to $350 off Samsung's MSRP without trading in another device, or up to $720 if you bring something to trade in. That brings the cost down from $1,399.99 (256GB) to $1,049.99.

  • Galaxy S26 Ultra: Up to $720 trade-in credit ($250 off without trade-in)

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: Up to $800 trade-in credit (or $350 without trade-in)

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the company's new "passport-style" foldable. This isn't Samsung's premier foldable—that title belongs to the Z Fold 8 Ultra—but the Z Fold 8 offers a similar experience in a smaller footprint and price tag. Ahead of Black Friday, you can take $350 off the Z Fold 8 without trade-in, or get up to $800 when trading in another device.

  • Galaxy Z Fold 8: Up to $800 trade-in credit (or $350 off without trade-in)

Here are the other deals Samsung is offering this year:

  • Galaxy S26 FE: Up to $400 trade-in credit ($150 off without trade-in)

  • Galaxy S26: Up to $340 trade-in credit ($150 off without trade-in)

  • Galaxy S26+: Up to $440 trade-in credit ($250 off without trade-in)

  • Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra: Up to $800 trade-in credit (or $350 without trade-in)

  • Galaxy Z Flip 8: Up to $400 trade-in credit (or $200 off without trade-in)

  • Galaxy A27 5G: Up to $120 trade-in credit ($100 off without trade-in)

  • Galaxy A37 5G: Up to $205 trade-in credit (or $100 without trade-in)

  • Galaxy A57 5G: Up to $205 trade-in credit (or $100 without trade-in)

Best Early Black Friday Samsung Smartwatch Deals

Samsung's wearable deals are much like its smartphone deals: mostly trade-in offers, but some traditional discounts if you don't have a trade-in as well.

Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2: Save $100 without trade-in (up to $250 with trade-in)

Samsung's Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is the company's latest model aimed at athletes and power users. Right now, the company will take $100 off the watch without trade-in, or up to $250 off depending on the device you choose to exchange.

  • Galaxy Watch Ultra 2: $599.99 down from $699.99 (without trade-in)

Samsung Galaxy Watch 9: Save $50 without trade-in (up to $250 with trade-in)

Samsung's latest flagship smartwatch is (sort of) on sale for Black Friday. Like the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, you can take $50 off the watch without a trade-in, or up to $250 when trading in with another device:

  • Galaxy Watch 9: $329 down from $379 (without trade-in)

Samsung also has deals available for the following watches and wearables:

  • Galaxy Watch 8 Classic: Up to $150 trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Watch 8: Up to $150 trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Watch 7: Up to $100 trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Ring: Up to $150 trade-in credit (out of stock as of this article)

  • Galaxy XR: Up to $1,030 off (plus three months of YouTube TV at $1 per month)

Best Early Black Friday deals on Samsung tablets

For some of its tablets this early Black Friday, Samsung is advertising that it will take off a certain amount in "total savings." That's a wiggily way of saying that to get the best deal, you'll need to stack multiple offers at once: certain trade-in values, per-device discounts, as well as discounts from the Samsung Offer Program.

Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra: Up to $1,095 in total savings

That "total savings" deal applies to Samsung's Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. This tablet typically starts at $1,399.99, but with the right trade-in, you can take off $550. Samsung says you can take another $100 off with code "PAYPAL100," and stack another discount at checkout, which is as high as 15% for certain products. According to Samsung, all of those combined will bring your Tab S12 Ultra down to $304—of course, if your trade-in isn't valued at $550, the tablet's total will be higher.

  • Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra: Up to $1,095 in "total savings" ($550 trade-in credit)

Samsung is running promotions on these tablets as well:

  • Galaxy Tab S10 Lite: Up to $75 in trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Tab S10 FE: Up to $110 in trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Tab S10+: Up to $205 in trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra: Up to $305 in trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Tab S12+: Up to $995 in "total savings" ($550 trade-in credit)

  • Galaxy Tab A11+: Up to $75 trade-in credit

  • Galaxy Tab A11+ Kids Edition: Up to $75 trade-in credit

Best Early Black Friday deals on Samsung computers and accessories

Samsung has early Black Friday deals on both laptops (specifically Galaxy Book 6 devices) and external monitors, particularly ones meant for gaming.

Samsung Odyssey OLED G9 (49-inch): Save $720 (plus a $50 upgrade credit)

Samsung's 49-inch OLED G9 gaming monitor is currently $720 off, bringing the price from $2,039.98 to $1,179.99. Plus, you can take another $50 with Samsung's "upgrade credit," bringing the price down to $1,129.99. Samsung says it'll throw in a 24-inch "Essential" S3 monitor as well.

  • Odyssey OLED G9 (49-inch): $859.99 off, plus $50 upgrade credit

Samsung Galaxy Book 6: Up to $500 without trade-in

Samsung has a confusing deal with its Book 6 laptop. The company says it'll offer up to $335 (or more) in trade-in credits, but it'll take off $500 if you don't have a trade-in. I'm not sure what the incentive for trading in a device would be, but if you don't, you can add another $165 to the savings. Samsung says you can also take $100 off with "PAYPAL100," and stack another 15% discount on top of that:

  • Galaxy Book 6: Up to $500 trade-in credit ($335 trade-in credit); $100 off with code; 15% off at purchase

Other Samsung computer deals include:

  • Galaxy Book 6 Edge: Up to $335 trade-in credit

  • MovingStyle Essential Smart Monitor (43-inch): $200 off, plus $150 upgrade credit

  • Odyssey OLED G8 (27-inch): $300 off, plus $50 upgrade credit

Best Early Black Friday deals on Samsung TVs

Samsung doesn't have as many TV deals as it does for its other devices, but there are some good options here—particularly for the company's more expensive offerings:

Samsung Micro RGB R95H: Up to $1,500 off

Right now, Samsung is taking up to $1,500 off its Micro RGB R95H TVs. That brings the price of the 85-inch model from $6,499.99 to $4,999.99.

  • Micro RGB R95H: Up to $1,500 off

Samsung OLED S95H: Up to $1,500 off

Similarly, the company is taking up to $1,500 off its S95H line of OLED TVs. That means the 83-inch model has the same price drop: From $6,499.99 to $4,999.99.

  • OLED S95H: Up to $1,500 off

Samsung Neo QLED QN80H: Up to $1,200 off

Samsung is taking up to $1,200 off the company's NEO QLED QN80H TVs. The 85-inch model drops from $2,999.99 to $1,799.99.

  • Neo QLED QN80H: Up to $1,200

Samsung Mini LED M80H: Up to $500 off

Finally, Samsung is cutting its Mini LED M80H line by up to $500 for early Black Friday. That brings the price of its 85-inch model from $1,599.99 to $1,099.99.

  • Mini LED M80H: Up to $500 off

Early Black Friday Samsung deals FAQs

Are Samsung's Black Friday deals worth it?

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

When is the best time of the year to save the most?

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

Does Samsung have Black Friday deals?

Yes! Samsung is running a number of Black Friday deals already, on devices including smartphones, tablets, computers, and TVs.

Are Samsung’s trade-in credits worth it?

They can be. The company is offering up to $800 off the Galaxy Z Fold 8 if you bring a device to trade in. Meanwhile, you get more money off the Galaxy Book 6 by not trading in a device.

Which Samsung devices have the biggest Black Friday discounts?

The company's TVs, by far. You can save up to $1,500 on the Samsung OLED S95H and Samsung Micro RGB R95H lines.

issues.title: Humor Writing 101: Making Our Sentences Funnier (with Elissa Bassist)
issues.summary: In season 5 episode 11 of "Writer's Digest Presents," senior editor Michael Woodson and author Elissa Bassist discuss how to make our writing funnier. The post Humor Writing 101: Making Our Sentences Funnier (with Elissa Bassist) appeared first on Writer's Digest .
issues.author: The Editors of Writer’s Digest
issues.content_html:
Humor writing is challenging for one simple reason: Humor is subjective. What makes one person laugh may make another person cringe. Genre itself defines humor differently. So, how do we go about infusing humor into our stories?

(Book Cover Design 101: How To Make Your Story Stand Out)

In season 5 episode 11 of “Writer’s Digest Presents,” senior editor Michael Woodson and author Elissa Bassist (INSIDE JOKES: A Comedy and Creativity Guide for All Writers) discuss how to make our writing funnier—how to commit to the bit, how to study what makes you laugh, how to turn a simple sentence into a joke, and more.

About Elissa Bassist

Elissa Bassist is the author of the memoir Hysterical, a semi-finalist for The Thurber Prize for American Humor. She has worked in media and publishing since 2007, as an editor, a managing editor, a TV and film writer’s assistant, a producer, a performer, a speaker, and a barista. Her writing has appeared in over 30 publications and anthologies, and she’s taught for over 20 writing programs. Her second book is INSIDE JOKES: A Comedy and Creativity Guide for All Writers. Elissa lives in Brooklyn and is probably her therapist’s favorite.

issues.title: Alice Openshaw: On the Differences Between Being a Reader and a Writer
issues.summary: In this interview, author Alice Openshaw discusses the “what if” questions that led to her debut mystery novel, On the Killer’s Trail. The post Alice Openshaw: On the Differences Between Being a Reader and a Writer appeared first on Writer's Digest .
issues.author: Robert Lee Brewer
issues.content_html:
Alice Openshaw has been a fan of mysteries since the age of 10, when she discovered Perry Mason books at her tiny town’s public library. She holds a BA in psychology from Middlebury College in Vermont and an MLS from Vanderbilt University. She lived in rural Maine for 30 years, where she worked as a librarian and adult literacy teacher, and raised three children and an assortment of animals on a small farm. She now lives near Cape Cod, Massachusetts, with her husband and her tuxedo cat, Frankie. Follow her on Facebook and Instagram.

In this interview, Alice discusses the “what if” questions that led to her debut mystery novel, On the Killer’s Trail, her hope for readers, and more.

Name: Alice Openshaw
Literary agent: Gina Panettieri, Talcott Notch Literary Agency
Book title:On the Killer’s Trail
Publisher: Crooked Lane Books
Release date: November 17, 2026
Genre/category: Mystery
Elevator pitch: A young police sergeant in rural Maine investigates the murder of a victim whose life seems eerily similar to her own.

Bookshop | Amazon
[WD uses affiliate links.]

What prompted you to write this book?

I have always been a reader and a fan of mysteries. I was living in Maine where we raised a few animals on a small farm on the edge of the woods. The barn was a very peaceful place, but one had a sense of the wilderness just outside the door, especially at night when it was pitch dark. I felt safe, but the mystery reader in me asked the “what if” question. What if an “ordinary” woman was murdered when she went out to tend to her animals at night? Why would that happen? What was going on in her life? Who did it? That was how the story began.

How long did it take to go from idea to publication? And did the idea change during the process?

I asked that initial “what if” question over 15 years ago. For years, the story existed only as an exercise of my imagination, with no thought of it becoming a book. I cultivated it in my mind the way someone else might plan a dream vacation or imagine a house renovation. I never wrote any of it down. In November 2021, a year after we moved from the farm to our current home, I heard a news story about National Novel Writing Month. The goal was to blast out a first draft in one month. I had never written anything before. I wrote a rough first draft in six weeks. From that point, it was almost exactly four years of learning, revising, querying, more learning, more revising, and more querying until I signed the contract with Crooked Lane Books. And another year until publication. The basic story has remained the same although there have been a lot of minor changes along the way.

Were there any surprises or learning moments in the publishing process for this title?

The entire publishing process has been a series of learning moments! As a librarian, an adult education english teacher, and an avid reader, I had a lot of experience with books, but always as a consumer. I had never heard of querying. I didn’t know the difference between a developmental editor and a line editor. I knew some writers had agents, but I didn’t know anything about what the book business entailed. Marketing and promotion does not come naturally to me. I am still learning, and I am so grateful for all of the support I have had.

Were there any surprises in the writing process for this book?

My first draft had no arc. There’s a certain freedom in not knowing what you are doing. I just wrote. With each revision, I added detail and depth to the characters and the story. After a few revisions, I still didn’t know if I had anything. I started querying literary agents to get some feedback and because that was what you were “supposed” to do at that stage of the process. I got a full request overnight on my first query. It was exciting and encouraging, but ultimately it wasn’t helpful because the manuscript still needed a lot of work and I didn’t know it. Beta readers, a good critique group, and a developmental editor helped me home in on the parts I needed to work on.

What do you hope readers will get out of your book?

I love fiction. As a reader, even with mysteries, I don’t try to figure out the ending ahead of time. I like to go along for the ride. When I get to the destination, if the solution is too obvious or too contrived or obscure, I’m disappointed. Otherwise, I’m satisfied. I hope readers will go along for the ride with me on On the Killer’s Trail and enjoy both the journey and the destination. If they take away something meaningful from the underlying message of the book, so much the better.

If you could share one piece of advice with other writers, what would it be?

This is my first attempt at writing and my first published work, so it feels presumptuous to offer advice. Stephen King, Maine’s most famous writer, has said, “If you don’t have time to read, you don’t have time to write.” I would echo that thought. If you read good literature in a variety of genres, your own work will be true to yourself and won’t imitate another writer because you will have a deep and rich well of inspiration to draw on. The flip side of that is that you also need to seek out and heed competent critique of your work.

The post Alice Openshaw: On the Differences Between Being a Reader and a Writer appeared first on Writer's Digest.

*****

Poetic forms are the backbone of a poet’s writing. They are the building blocks for length, rhyme scheme, subject matter, and so much more. In The Complete Guide of Poetic Forms, Writer’s Digest’s resident poetry expert and former poet laureate of the blogosphere Robert Lee Brewer showcases more than 100 poetic forms to serve as both an informative resource and inspiration for new writing.

Click to continue.

*****

Here’s my attempt at a New and/or Old Poem:

“Old News”

Every new poem is built upon an old poem
whispering through the leaves of grass and
trees. Each branch grasps at air and sunlight
wanting only to exist one ring at a time.

Even the oldest words breathe heavy with life
the first time they are read by an open mind
and heart. Each thought grasps at what
can’t be pinned down by logic or reason.

Every poem (new and old) spirals through
the spaces between your thoughts and mine
as if there’s a purpose more than just
wanting (like always) to merely exist.
