issues.title: Kale Pesto Pasta
issues.summary: A delicious and really quick way to get more good-for-you kale into your life – Kale Pesto Pasta! Tasty garlic, lemon and parmesan flavour, it’s faster to make than basil pesto and stays bright green for days – all high appeal matters! Kale Pesto Pasta I don’t know if you’re pro or anti kale, but ... Get the Recipe The post Kale Pesto Pasta appeared first on RecipeTin Eats .
issues.author: Nagi
issues.content_html:
A delicious and really quick way to get more good-for-you kale into your life – Kale Pesto Pasta! Tasty garlic, lemon and parmesan flavour, it’s faster to make than basil pesto and stays bright green for days – all high appeal matters!

Kale Pesto Pasta

I don’t know if you’re pro or anti kale, but whichever camp you’re in, this is a shockingly delicious and quick way to turn kale into a meal. You’ll feel especially smug if you’ve got a sad limp bunch that’s been in the fridge for weeks (really, the shelf life of kale is impressive) because you’ve just turned something destined for the bin into something you’ll actually be excited to eat!

It’s lemony and garlicky with a good hit of parmesan (which, let’s face it, can make anything delicious), and the kale just tastes fresh rather than the background of grassiness that some people don’t like about kale.

And it’s quick! You’ll get the kale pesto made in the time the pasta takes to cook. And you don’t have to worry about the pesto turning brown and it stays green for days (I’m glaring at YOU, basil pesto!)

Ingredients in Kale Pesto Pasta

Here’s what you need to make kale pesto pasta. The lemon really lifts it, taking the “grassy” edge off the kale. So don’t skip it! 🙂

For the kale pesto

  • Kale – Use regular curly kale, or cavolo nero / lacinto kale (also known as Tuscan kale or dinosaur kale). You will need four long stems around 30cm/12″ long (ie measure of the leafy bushy part, not the naked stem).

    Other leafy greens – Any leafy greens will in theory work here, like baby spinach, English spinach, silverbeet (chard), collard greens. I wouldn’t use frozen though as they are too wet to blitz.

  • Parmesan – It always tastes better if you freshly grate, but for convenience, I use store bought (the sandy type is best, though even the thin batons will be fine as it gets all blitzed up).

    Substitute – Anchovies! Just like Caesar Salad Dressing, this will go a long way to add depth of flavour to this without tasting fishy. Blitz it up with everything else, starting with a modest amount, taste, then adding more as needed.

  • Walnuts – My nut of choice, just because I feel the earthiness goes well with kale which is also a bit earthy tasting (in a good way). Cashews or almonds would be my first choice for substitutes, or sunflower seeds for a non-nut option. Pine nuts will give this a basil-pesto flavour edge, but use half the amount because it’s got a stronger flavour.

  • Extra virgin olive oil – There’s no need to use your good stuff for this pesto, this pesto has lots of other flavours going on that overpower it (lemon, garlic, parmesan). Just a regular extra virgin olive oil is fine here.

  • Lemon – This really brings lovely brightness to the pesto and cuts through the earthiness of kale. I used to just use lemon juice but then I added lemon zest as well and I never looked back! I like it because it adds real lemon flavour into this, not just sour juice.

  • Garlic – Just one small clove. Not too large because it remains raw, and when it’s blitzed up a little bit goes far.

  • Chilli flakes (red pepper flakes) – This adds a hum of warmth into this pesto which gives it a bit of attitude! It doesn’t make it spicy, but you definitely notice the warm buzz. Feel free to reduce if you’re concerned, or for not spicy at all just leave it out and substitute with a good grind of black pepper.

  • Salt – Important, if you don’t use enough it will taste bland. I use it in both the pesto and in the pasta cooking water which seasons the pasta as it cooks.

THE PASTA

I used Casarecce N.88 pasta, picture below, a short twisted pasta shapes with pesto-catching grooves. This is a good easy recipe to experiment with different pasta shapes – no performance pressure! 🙂

How to make Kale Pesto Pasta

Get the pasta boiling first. Then by the time it’s ready, you should be just about done with the pesto!

  1. Torn kale leaves – Grip the stem of a kale leaf then enclose your fist around the leafy part and run your hand up it to rip the leaves off. Then tear into bite size pieces with your hands.

  1. Toast walnuts – Toast the walnuts in a small skillet over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, tossing every now and then, until the walnuts have golden spots and it smells nutty. No need to use oil for toasting nuts.

    Note – There are many recipes on this website where I don’t insist on toasting nuts beforehand. For this recipe, I really recommend it to bring out the flavour, so the pesto doesn’t taste too kale-y.

  2. Pesto ingredients – Put the kale, walnuts (hot, straight off the stove is fine – unlike basil, kale is hardy and won’t turn black on contact with hot nuts!) and remaining pesto ingredients into a large bowl.

  1. Blitz – Then blitz using a stick blender for a good 20 to 30 seconds, moving it around as you go, to puree it well into a pesto texture. Kale is pretty hardy stuff, so you will need to blitz assertively!

    I find using a stick blender works best to blitz up the kale into a semi-pureed texture. A food processor doesn’t work quite as well, the kale bits end up larger no matter how long you process and how many times you scrape down the sides. But it works well enough, if you don’t have a stick blender. A NutriBullet and blender aren’t suitable, the pesto is too thick.

  2. Kale pesto! Here’s a close up of the texture once blitzed.

  1. Reserve pasta cooking water – Cook pasta per packet directions. Just before draining, scoop out about 1 cup of pasta cooking water and set aside, then drain the pasta.

  2. Making the pasta – Pour the drained pasta back into the now-empty pot and add the pesto straight onto the hot pasta. Unlike basil pesto, you don’t have to worry about kale pesto going black on contact with heat! It stays green!

  1. Add pasta water – Then pour over 1/3 cup of the pasta cooking water. Keep the rest in case you need it.

  2. Toss well – Then toss the pasta well, until it’s all coated in the kale pesto. Use extra pasta cooking water if needed to thin the sauce. Then that’s it! Divide between bowls and enjoy!

And it stays green!

This is lovely served warm, freshly made, when the pasta is hot and slick and the warmth really opens up the flavour of the basil and lemon. But it’s also terrific eaten as a cold pasta salad, straight from the fridge.

I have also made pesto pasta salad using this kale pesto, spread it on toast with ricotta, and smeared it on pan fried fish. Basically, whatever you do with basil pesto, you can do with kale pesto, with the added bonus that this stays green for days without having to do anything to stop it from turning brown.

Anyone else around here tried kale pesto before? Love to know thoughts! – Nagix

Watch how to make it

Print

Kale Pesto Pasta

Recipe video above. This bright green kale pesto pasta is a little bit lemony, a little bit garlicky, a little bit parmesany and a whole lot of yum! All these flavours disguise the "grassiness" some people don't like about kale, just leaving a pleasant freshness. I also like that unlike basil pesto, kale pesto doesn't go brown when tossed with hot pasta, there's no fiddly leaf picking (just grab the stem and rip the leaves off!) and it stays green for days! I just think it's a really delicious way to incorporate virtuous kale into a meal. Workflow: Get the pasta cooking then start on the kale pesto. You should be able to get it done by the time the pasta is ready to drain. Course Mains, Pasta Cuisine Western Keyword kale pasta, kale pesto, kale pesto pasta, kale recipe Prep Time 5 minutes minutes Cook Time 11 minutes minutes Servings 4 – 5 people Calories 702 cal Author Nagi

Ingredients

Kale pesto:

  • 4 cups tightly packed (100g) kale leaves , torn by hand, about 4 stems (curly kale or Cavolo nero/lacinto) – Note 1
  • 1/2 cup tightly packed (50g) finely grated parmesan , store bought sandy-type from fridge is fine here, else grate your own – Note 2
  • 1 garlic clove , minced using garlic press
  • 1/2 cup (50g) walnuts – substitute cashews or almonds, or halve the quantity for pine nuts
  • 2 tsp lemon zest
  • 3 tbsp lemon juice
  • 1/2 cup (125 ml) extra virgin olive oil
  • 3/4 tsp cooking salt / kosher salt
  • 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes , for slight warmth – feel free to reduce, or omit (substitute with black pepper)

For pasta:

  • 500g / 1 lb pasta of choice – long or short (pictured: Casarecce N.88)
  • 2 tsp cooking salt / kosher salt , for pasta cooking water
  • 1/3 cup reserved pasta cooking water , for pasta tossing
  • Parmesan , for serving

Instructions

ABBREVIATED RECIPE:

  • Toast walnuts, pour into bowl with all pesto ingredients, blitz until finely puréed. Toss with hot pasta and with 1/3 cup pasta cooking water.

FULL RECIPE:

  • Cook pasta – Bring a large pot of water to the boil with the 2 teaspoons of salt. Add the pasta and cook for the time per the packet directions.
  • Reserve water – Just before draining, scoop out 1 cup of pasta cooking water. Then drain the pasta and return into the pasta cooking pot.

Make pesto (while pasta is cooking):

  • Toast walnuts – Heat a small pan over medium high heat (no oil). Add the walnuts and toast for 3 minutes, tossing every now and then, until it has light brown spots and it smells nutty.
  • Blitz pesto – Immediately pour the walnuts into a large bowl (no need to cool, can blitz while hot). Add remaining pesto ingredients. Blitz using a stick blender until the kale is as finely blitzed as you can, about 20 – 30 seconds. It won't turn into a smoothie (kale is hardy!). (Note 3 on food processor)
  • Toss with pasta – Pour over the hot pasta and add 1/3 cup of the reserved pasta cooking water. Toss well until evenly coated, using extra pasta cooking water as needed to loosen, then serve immediately garnished with extra parmesan. It's especially nice hot (brings out the garlic and parmesan flavour) though also lovely served as a cold pasta salad.

Notes

1. Kale – You’ll need 4 curly kale stems, about 30cm/12″ long (measuring leafy part only, not naked stem). To measure the kale, push the kale leaves into a measuring cup quite firmly. Or use scales – easier! The recipe is quite forgiving – so if you use too much kale you’ll know as the pesto will be too thick and dry – just add extra oil. If too little, too loose and oily, just add more kale leaves (or baby spinach, if you’re out of kale). To remove kale leaves, grip the stem, close your fist loosely around the leaves and slide your hand up to rip the leaves off. Then use your hands to tear into pieces. Other leafy greens – Any leafy greens will in theory work here, like baby spinach, English spinach, silverbeet (chard), collard greens. I wouldn’t use frozen though as they are too wet to blitz. 2. Parmesan substitute (non-dairy) – Anchovies! Terrific flavour booster, like used in Caesar Dressing. Start with a modest amount, blitz, taste, then add more if desired. 3. Blitzing tool – I find the stick blender most effective, you can move it around, there’s no need to scrape down the sides, and it really purees up the hardy kale well. If using a food processor, you’ll need to scrape down the sides quite a few times but it still won’t puree it quite as well as a stick blender can. Leftovers will keep for 2 days, beyond this I find the fresh flavours start to fade. The pesto can also be frozen for up to 3 months in an airtight container (I wouldn’t freeze on the pasta, just the pesto by itself). Nutrition per serving, assuming 5 servings.

Life of Jaffle

It was less than five months ago when puppy Jaffle didn’t know any better and would munch through giant kale leaves enthusiastically like they were steak…

These days, he knows better – there are so many tastier food options out there in the world…..!!

And from somewhere up in the Big Sky Kitchen, Dozer is nodding his approval…. 🥰

issues.author: Nagi
issues.content_html:
Crinkle Cookies have many names – Earthquake Cookies, Snow Capped Biscuits, Chocolate Crackle Bickies – but they’re instantly recognisable! They taste like a fudgy, chewy brownie inside a crisp meringue shell. Holiday cookie favourite!

Crinkle Cookies

I’m just going to put this right upfront to clearly set the expectation of these Crinkle Cookies – this is not your typical recipe. Most use a cookie dough made with oil and only use cocoa powder for chocolate flavour.

My Crinkle Cookies are made using what is essentially a brownie batter disguised as a cookie, full of all the goodness that is butter and melted chocolate. I add extra flour to turn it into a cookie, baking powder to make it poof up into thick domes and create impressive cracks, and reduce the butter so the cookie isn’t too oily which would absorb the all-important white icing sugar coating.

The result is a Crinkle Cookie that has a very fudgy brownie-like texture with a really chocolatey flavour, in a way you can never achieve with just cocoa powder alone. Yes it’s decadent! But if there’s ever a time for indulgence, it’s the holidays – and Crinkle Cookies are a classic holiday cookie favourite!

Ingredients in Chocolate Crinkle Cookies

Here’s what you need to make these extra chocolatey Crinkle Cookies. Essentially everything you need for fudgy brownies, plus icing sugar for coating!

For the cookie dough

  • Dark chocolate (US: semi-sweet chocolate) – Don’t be tempted to fancy up these cookies with a higher % cocoa chocolate like 70% cocoa / bittersweet chocolate as it will mess with the fudgy texture. A costly lesson I learned last year when I tried to make a more luxurious version for Christmas gifting and ended up ruining the whole batch instead!

    You can use melts (wafers/discs), chips or chop up a block. Just be sure to use chocolate from the baking aisle, not from the confectionary aisle which is not designed for cooking.

  • Cocoa powder – Use regular unsweetened cocoa powder. As with the chocolate, don’t be tempted to upgrade by using dutch processed cocoa powder which has a more intense chocolate flavour – it is more absorbent and will make the cookie less fudgy inside.

  • White and brown sugar for the cookie dough – All other things being equal, brown sugar makes cookies more chewy and white makes them crispier. For Crinkle Cookies, I want them fudgy-chewy with a crispy shell, so I use both! But it would not be the end of the world to use only one or the other. For the white sugar for the cookie dough, you can use either caster sugar (superfine sugar) or regular white sugar (granulated sugar).

  • Butter – Unsalted butter which we melt, so no need to bring to room temperature.

  • Flour – Just plain / all-purpose flour. Don’t use self raising flour as it has the wrong amount of baking powder built in.

  • Baking powder – This is what makes the cookies poof up into lovely little domes! Make sure yours is still alive if it’s been hiding in the corner of your pantry for months. Also, don’t substitute with baking soda (bi-carbonate) as it behaves differently – it will make the cookies spread more than it rises, plus it’s stronger.

  • Eggs – Use “large eggs” from cartons labelled as such which are determined by industry standards. They are eggs which are 50 – 55g/2oz each, in shell. You can use eggs slightly smaller but don’t use larger eggs as it might make the dough too wet to roll balls. If you don’t have eggs the right size, crack eggs into a bowl, lightly whisk, then measure out 1/3 cup and use for this recipe.

  • Vanilla extract – For flavour. Note – vanilla extract is real vanilla, whereas vanilla essence is artificial so the vanilla flavour isn’t as good. In recipes that rely heavily on good vanilla flavour I really recommend using vanilla extract, but for this one, you can get away with vanilla essence (which is cheaper).

  • Salt – Just a pinch brings out flavours in the cookie.

for the snowy white coating

The cookie dough balls are rolled in sugar first before rolling in icing sugar. Brilliant tip from the folks at Cooks’ Illustrated that serves three purposes:

  1. Makes the outside of the cookie crisper by drawing moisture to the surface;

  2. This also creates more impressive cracks; and

  3. Keeps the icing sugar white rather than patchy or translucent. It does this by creating a barrier for the icing sugar that helps prevent it from absorbing moisture and dissolving or sweating. Pet peeve with Crinkle Cookies!

  • Sugar – Use regular white sugar / granulated sugar, not caster sugar (superfine sugar), which are finer grains and will melt too quickly on the surface of the cookie.

  • Icing sugar (called powdered sugar in the US) – The snowy white powder on the cookies! There is no need to sift it for ball coating purposes, unless yours has hardened in boulders, then you might want to break it up a bit. 🙂

    Note: Australia – use soft icing sugar not pure icing sugar, if presented with the choice. Soft icing sugar contains a little starch to prevent clumping. If you’re outside Australia, you needn’t worry about the distinction as the default icing sugar for mainstream brands should contain the starch. Yes, I am that nerd who intently studies the ingredient label of grocery items in every country she visits – and for those she hasn’t yet visited, she googles madly.

How to make Chocolate Crinkle Cookies

Make sure you pack the icing sugar really thickly on the cookie dough balls. Just when you think you’ve coated them enough, shower it with more then press it on firmly! The goal is to coat them so thickly you practically cannot see any brown cookie dough through the icing sugar. This way, you can ensure your cookies come out with lovely white surfaces rather than translucent patchy surfaces that look like melted muddy snow……

1. Make the cookie dough

The cookie dough is quite loose when it’s first mixed, but it only takes 30 minutes to firm up enough to roll into balls. You don’t need the dough to be rock hard, just firm enough to handle so you can roll soft balls.

  1. Mix the Dry ingredients in a bowl and set aside (flour, cocoa powder, baking powder and salt).

  2. Melt the chocolate in a large heatproof bowl using the microwave using 20 second increments on high, mixing in between (I use a chopstick – less surface area for the chocolate to get stuck to!). Else, set the bowl over a pot with barely simmering water (don’t let the water touch the bowl). Let the melted chocolate cool for 5 minutes before mixing in the other ingredients.

  1. Whisk wet ingredients – To the chocolate, add the eggs, both sugars, vanilla and melted butter. Whisk well to combine really well.

  2. Make cookie dough – Add the Dry ingredients then use a wooden spoon to mix until you no longer see flour. The batter will be like a thick dollop-y cake batter, have faith! It will firm up quickly. 🙂

  1. Refrigerate 30 minutes – Put the bowl in the fridge for 30 minutes to firm into a cookie dough so it’s roll-able. If you didn’t let the chocolate cool enough, or if your fridge is really packed or runs a bit warm, it might take longer, but the dough will firm up enough because the melted chocolate will eventually cool down and set.

    ⚠️ Only refrigerate the dough for as long as required to scoop and roll balls. Don’t try to keep the dough for later to bake as it doesn’t work – the cookie doesn’t spread/crack as it is supposed to, and if it’s a hot humid day then the dough can get sweaty which absorbs the icing sugar. If I figure out a way to keep the dough to bake later, I’ll come back and update.

  2. Firmed up dough – After 30 minutes in the fridge, what was a dollop-y batter should have firmed up into a soft cookie dough. It will still be soft but be just firm enough so you can scoop and roll it into balls. The balls will be a bit soft, but manageable. (If the dough is too sticky to roll balls, pop it in the fridge for a bit longer).

2. roll, coat and bake

Only coat the balls just before baking, otherwise the icing sugar will absorb moisture from the dough and disappear, taking that lovely white coating with it!

  1. Roll – Scoop out 1 1/2 tablespoons of dough (size 40 cookie scoop) and roll into balls. You should get 20–22 balls.

  2. Light sugar coating – Roll a ball lightly in the white sugar.

  1. THICK icing sugar coating! Then coat the ball in icing sugar, packing it on thickly until the ball is completely covered with white powder. Aim for full coverage so you can’t see any brown cookie dough! If you only do a light dusting, it will sweat off in the oven so instead of the lovely snow-capped surfaces, you’ll end up with patchy brown cookies that look like muddy snow has melted!

    IMPORTANT: Only coat as many balls as you’re baking straight away. Don’t leave icing sugar-coated balls sitting around waiting to be baked, as the icing sugar will absorb moisture from the dough and the lovely white coating will disappear!

  2. Baking trays – Line two baking trays with baking paper / parchment paper. Place the coated balls on the trays at least 7.5cm / 3″ apart, not just to leave room for spreading (they don’t spread much, only double in width) but also for good heat circulation to let the edges crisp up nicely. I put 6 balls on each tray. I could fit more – 8 comfortably, but I still need to do a second bake for the remaining cookies so I just prefer to do less on each tray for more even cooking.

    Keep uncoated cookie dough balls in the fridge while you bake the first batch.

  1. Bake the cookies for 13 minutes at 180°C/350°F (160°C fan-forced). The balls will melt slightly and bake into puffy domes with the “earthquake” cracks. Do not switch the trays or rotate during the bake time as this may deflate the domes, they are very delicate while poofing up and prone to collapsing.

    To check if they cookies are done, touch the surface very gently – it should have a thin crusty surface but be jiggly underneath. It will feel so underdone you will be concerned – but please, have faith and trust the process, this is what makes it fudgy!

  2. Cool the cookies on the tray for 5 minutes then use a spatula to transfer them to a rack. Avoid touching the icing sugar as it will come off easily! Let them cool for at least another 5 minutes to set before diving in – the edges and base will set and become crispy, and the inside will firm up so it becomes fudge-like.

Unpopular opinion: they’re even better cold

I know most people like Crinkle Cookies when they are still warm, but I personally prefer them when they are fully cool because they’re even chewier and fudgier. But this requires a full (painful) 30 minutes of waiting time, which of course you know I don’t have the patience for. Instead, I justify the need to try it at various stages of the cooling process “for recipe testing purposes”.

It’s a tough job, but someone has to do it. 🤷🏻‍♀️

Then after all that “recipe testing”, the few you have left will keep for a whole 5 days. 🎉 As long as it’s not super hot and humid where you are, the snowy white icing on the cookies should last for 3 – 4 days before it starts to fade, thanks to the double sugar coating. Bear in mind if you stack them then you’ll mess it up a bit as the icing sugar gets brushed off and falls into the cracks.

Happy baking! – Nagi x

Crinkle Cookies FAQ

The cracks are slightly larger but the flavour, texture and shape of the cookies are virtually identical. JB says he can taste the faintest fine grittiness in the texture that is inherent with using gluten-free flour, however, I didn’t notice it.

Note: These were tested with White Wings Gluten-Free flour, a brand that is carried by large grocery stores here in Australia. Gluten-free flour blends vary a lot between brands, so I can only vouch for White Wings. However, the fact that it worked so well gives me confidence other good gluten-free flour blends should work too.

Keeps 5 days in an airtight container in the pantry. As long as it’s not super hot and humid where you are, the snowy white icing on the cookies should last for 3 – 4 days before it starts to fade, thanks to the double sugar coating.

I haven’t figured out if it’s possible to make the dough ahead and bake later. The versions I’ve tried so far haven’t worked great, they taste fined but the cookies didn’t spread/crack as they should. Will come back and update if we can figure it out!

Watch how to make it

Print

Chocolate Crinkle Cookies

Recipe video above. One of my favourite holiday cookies – everybody loves those dramatic chocolate cracks against the snowy white coating! They taste like a fudgy, chewy brownie inside a crisp meringue shell. My recipe is based on my brownie batter so they're extra fudgy and chocolatey because it uses both melted chocolate and cocoa powder. Ordinarily, only cocoa powder is used. Meanwhile, the outside is crisp with impressive cracks, and that all-important snowy white coating that stays white thanks to a double-sugar coating – rolling the balls in sugar first to create a barrier, then icing sugar. Trick I picked up from the clever folks over at Cooks' Illustrated!Gluten-free – Recipe works great with gluten-free flour! See FAQ for more information. Course Cookies Cuisine Western Keyword chocolate crackle cookies, chocolate crinkle cookies, crinkle biscuits, crinkle cookie, earthquake cookies, snow cap cookies Prep Time 30 minutes minutes Cook Time 30 minutes minutes Dough fridge and cookie cooling time 45 minutes minutes Total Time 1 hour hour 45 minutes minutes Servings 22 cookies, 6.5cm / 2.5″ wide, 2.25cm / 0.9″ high Calories 132 cal Author Nagi

Ingredients

  • 200g/ 6.5oz dark chocolate chips or discs/melts (US: semi-sweet chocolate) – Note 1
  • 60g (4 tbsp) unsalted butter , melted and cooled
  • 2 large eggs , at room temperature (50 – 55g/2oz each, no larger)
  • 1/4 cup white sugar / granulated sugar (or caster sugar / superfine sugar)
  • 1/4 cup (tightly packed) brown sugar
  • 1 tsp vanilla extract
  • 1/4 cup unsweetened cocoa , sifted (not Dutch processed) – Note 1
  • 1 cup plain flour / all-purpose flour
  • 1 1/2 tsp baking powder (make sure yours is still alive), don’t substitute with baking soda
  • 1/8 tsp cooking salt / kosher salt

Dusting:

  • 1/4 cup white sugar / granulated sugar (not caster sugar / superfine, it’s too fine)
  • 3/4 cup icing sugar / powdered sugar , no need to sift
Cups – Metric

Instructions

ABBREVIATED RECIPE:

  • Melt chocolate, cool 5 min. Add Wet ingredients, whisk well. Stir in Dry ingredients with wooden spoon. Fridge 30 min. Roll 20 – 22 x 1.5 tbsp balls, roll in sugar then pack on icing sugar thickly – only do what fits on the trays. Bake 13 min 180°C/350°F (160°C fan).

FULL RECIPE:

Make cookie dough:

  • Mix dry ingredients – Whisk the cocoa powder, flour, baking powder and salt together in a medium bowl. Set aside.
  • Melt chocolate – Place the chocolate in a large heatproof bowl. Microwave in 20-second increments, stirring between each, until melted and smooth. Leave to cool for 5 minutes.
  • Make cookie dough – Add the butter, eggs, both sugars and vanilla to the melted chocolate. Whisk until thoroughly combined. Add the dry ingredients and mix with a wooden spoon until incorporated. The dough should be very thick but too soft to roll into balls. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm up, don't leave it in so long the dough gets hard. (Note 2 for skipping this step.)

Coating and baking:

  • Preheat oven to 180°C/350°F (160°C fan-forced). Line 2 baking trays with baking paper/parchment paper.
  • Prepare coating – Place the sugar in one shallow bowl and the icing sugar in another. Wider bowls make coating easier.
  • Roll balls – Take the dough out of the fridge. It should be firm enough to roll into soft balls (if not, refrigerate a little longer). Scoop out 1 1/2 tablespoons of dough (size 40 cookie scoop) and roll into balls. You should get 20–22 balls.
  • Coat – Roll a ball lightly in the sugar, then coat in the icing sugar, packing it on thickly until the ball is completely covered. Aim for full coverage so you can't see cookie dough! Place on a prepared tray. Repeat with enough balls to fill both trays, spacing them 7.5cm/3" apart. (I do 6 per tray for the first batch, then 4 – 5 per tray for the second. Feel free to fit more if you have larger trays and oven.) Keep the remaining uncoated balls in the fridge until needed (don't coat until just before baking, it will sweat off).
  • Bake for 13 minutes. The cookies will puff up into domes and be very soft. Don't open the oven or rotate the trays during baking – this can cause the cookies to collapse. The cookies are ready when they have a light crust on the outside but they will still be jiggly inside.
  • Cool – Leave the cookies on the trays for 5 minutes to set a bit (the outside goes crispier and the inside will set like fudge). Then carefully transfer to cooling racks using a spatula, cool for another 5 minutes (avoid touching the icing sugar coating with your fingers). Coat and bake remaining dough balls. Most people enjoy these a bit warm. But I like them fully cool because they become chewier and fudgier!

Notes

1. Chocolate and cocoa powder – Don’t substitute the dark chocolate (semi-sweet chocolate) with a higher cocoa chocolate (like 70% cocoa or bittersweet chocolate) and don’t use dutch processed instead of regular cocoa powder. This will mess with the cookie dough thickness – it will make it drier and firmer, so the cookies may not spread. 2. Refrigeration time – Only refrigerate the dough for as long as needed to scoop and roll balls, if you leave it in for longer than 1 hour, the flour can absorb too much moisture and the cookie may not spread and crack properly. Skip the refrigeration time by adding an extra 1/4 cup flour to the cookie dough which makes it firmer so you can roll it straight away. The cookie will spread slightly less, be a little thicker and looks slightly more cakey inside but it is still fabulously fudgy inside when you eat it. (It’s just even fudgier if you stick with 1 cup flour + 30 min fridge :)! ) Storage – Keeps 5 days in an airtight container in the pantry. As long as it’s not super hot and humid where you are, the snowy white icing on the cookies should last for 3 – 4 days before it starts to fade, thanks to the double sugar coating. Making ahead – I haven’t figured out if it’s possible to make the dough ahead and bake later. The versions I’ve tried so far haven’t worked great, they taste fined but the cookies didn’t spread/crack as they should. Will come back and update if we can figure it out! Nutrition per cookie.

Nutrition

Add bread + olive oil = instant app. Sprinkle on any meats or veg to instantly elevate. GIFT IT! Costs a pittance to make – and it’s “gourmet”! JB’s Dukkah recipe Dukkah ... Get the Recipe The post Dukkah appeared first on RecipeTin Eats .
issues.author: Nagi
issues.content_html:
This is JB‘s Dukkah, and it may well be the most useful recipe you find this year, especially with the upcoming holiday season! Add bread + olive oil = instant app. Sprinkle on any meats or veg to instantly elevate. GIFT IT! Costs a pittance to make – and it’s “gourmet”!

JB’s Dukkah recipe

Dukkah is an Egyptian nut, seed and spice blend that is popular throughout the Middle East and now enjoyed all around the world, often carried in gourmet shops with price tags to match!

JB’s been making it for as long as I’ve known him, we always seem to have a little jar stashed away somewhere. It’s one of those universally handy things like chilli crisp and sriracha, that once you start using, you’ll never look back. A topping and finish that adds crunch, flavour and a little Middle Eastern flair to everything from roasted vegetables to meat, fish and even eggs.

But my absolute favourite way to eat it is the traditional way – with bread and olive oil for dipping. Just put out a bowl of dukkah with bread pieces and olive oil, then you just dip a piece of bread in olive oil then the dukkah (it totally sticks), then pop it straight in your mouth. That’s right, there’s no need to go to all that effort to make a dip, just pour dukkah into a bowl and watch everyone dive in. How good is that!!

Ingredients in Dukkah

Here’s what goes in dukkah. It is JB’s recipe, one he picked up during his years working in restaurant kitchens using the classic combination of ingredients typically found in Egyptian dukkah.

  • Hazelnuts – Traditionally the most common nut in dukkah. Use skinless roasted hazelnuts (skinless hazelnuts are roasted). If you only have skin-on ones, it’s best to remove the skin as it is quite bitter – I’ve popped directions in the recipe card for how to do this (roast then rub with a tea towel).

    Best substitute – I think blanched almonds are the best substitute, but then replace the blanched almonds in this recipe with another nut, either walnuts or more pistachios (so you end up with a combination of 3 nuts). Cashews would also be lovely!

  • Blanched almonds and pistachios – These are the other two nuts that JB uses, both of which are commonly used in traditional dukkah. I like how pistachios adds little specks of green in the dukkah! But feel free to swap them for walnuts which is also a popular choice, or use only one of them. (Note: blanched almonds are skinless, for the small amount we use, I wouldn’t go out of my way just to get this, you can use regular skin-on almonds).

  • Sesame seeds – Another key ingredient that adds toasty sesame flavour into the mix.

  • Fennel seeds – Another spice commonly used in traditional Egyptian dukkah. They add a subtle sweetness and warm, slightly aniseed flavour that gives dukkah that “gourmet” edge!

  • Spices – Coriander and cumin are the classic spices that give dukkah its distinctive warm, earthy flavour, while cayenne adds just a little background heat. Not enough to make it spicy, just enough to give it a little warm hum! Feel free to reduce or omit the cayenne pepper.

How to make Dukkah

The defining characteristics of traditional Egyptian dukkah is its coarse, crumbly texture and toasty, nutty flavour. So make sure you don’t grind it into a fine powder or paste, and don’t skip the nut roasting!

  1. Roast nuts first – Spread the nuts on a tray and bake for 5 minutes at 180°C/350°F (160°C fan-forced). By “nuts”, I mean the hazelnuts, almonds and pistachios.

  2. Add the seeds – Then add the sesame seeds and fennel seeds to the tray and shake to spread everything out. Then bake for 3 minutes.

  1. Fully cool on the tray for 15 minutes.

  2. Coarsely blitz – Pour the nuts and spices into a mini food processor. Then blitz until the nuts are coarsely ground. Don’t let it all turn into powder! You want a coarse, crumbly mixture with little bits of nuts for texture and crunch.

    I use a mini food processor because there’s not enough to effectively blitz in a regular large one. But if you triple the recipe (or more!), feel free to use a large one!

    Alternative to food processor – Use a mortar and pestle, or put everything in a ziplock bag and pound with the flat side of a meat mallet or rolling pin. I find my spice grinder, Nutribullet and blender doesn’t work well for Dukkah to evenly blitz so you get coarser small bits. You either end up with everything as a super fine powder or have some giant chunks.

And that’s it! Your dukkah is ready to use!

How to use dukkah

The traditional way to use dukkah is as a bread dip for a starter. Just pour the dukkah into a small bowl and some good extra virgin olive oil in another (my favourite shop-bought is Lomondo from Mudgee in NSW, carried at Harris Farms). Pile warm cubes of bread, focaccia or wedges of pita bread on the side. Dip bread into olive oil first then the dukkah (it will stick to the oil). Eat!

But it’s also incredibly useful as a topper, sprinkling and crumbing, a simple way to add extra flavour and interest to vegetables, meats, eggs and breads. Here are some ideas!

  • Dukkah bread – Brush bread with olive oil then sprinkle with dukkah and sea salt flakes, then bake. Ideal to use bread with a large surface area (eg pita bread – pictured below, Lebanese bread, focaccia)

  • Topping or finish – Sprinkle generously over foods to make a good dish gourmet, or to make simple foods instantly more exciting! Examples: Garlic prawns, roasted vegetables, glazed carrots, oven baked chicken breast, a store bought roast chicken (add olive oil as well), pan fried fish, avocado toast, scrambled eggs. It’d be spectacular sprinkled on these Sweet Potato Steaks or Maple Roasted Carrots with Whipped Tahini (instead of pine nuts).

  • Crumbing – Add to a breadcrumb mixture, like these Crumbed Baked Chicken Tenders or Schnitzel!

  • Garnish for dips – like hummus, whipped feta and labne.

  • GIFT IT! “Everybody” does sweet gifts. Stand out and do something different! 🎁

However you choose to use it, my one advice is to be generous and don’t hold back! If you’re dipping bread, press the bread in firmly to get plenty of dukkah to stick to it. If you’re sprinkling on vegetables or bread, sprinkle with abundance!

But that’s enough from me. What about you? Dukkah lovers out there, share your ways! – Nagi x

* This is a quick “OMG” dish that JB made using the Garlic Prawns recipe except using scallops instead. It was a massive hit at an event we hosted a few years back! I’ve also made it using the prawns as well and it too was a hit.

Watch how to make it

Print

Dukkah recipe

Recipe video above. This is JB's recipe for dukkah, the Egyptian nut, seed and spice blend that is endlessly useful for sprinkling to add crunch, flavour and a little Middle Eastern flair to everything from roasted vegetables to meat, fish and even eggs. But the traditional – and my favourite use – is as a bread dipper. Brilliant instant app! PS Also a fabulous gourmet food gift that's very cost effective (~$3.50 per batch) and easy to make loads. Everybody gifts chocolate. Stand out and be different! 🙂 Makes: 3/4 cup (105 grams) Course Appetiser, Dip, Spice Mix Cuisine Arabic, Egyptian, Middle Eastern Keyword dukka, dukkah, duqqa Prep Time 5 minutes minutes Cook Time 8 minutes minutes Cooling 15 minutes minutes Total Time 28 minutes minutes Servings 0.75 cups Calories 742 cal Author Nagi

Ingredients

  • 1/4 cup skinless hazelnuts , roasted (Note 1)
  • 1 1/2 tbsp blanched almonds (ie skinless almonds), substitute skin-on, or walnuts, cashews or more pistachios (Note 2)
  • 2 tbsp pistachios kernels , unsalted – substitute more almonds, or walnuts or cashews
  • 2 tbsp white sesame seeds
  • 1 1/2 tsp fennel seeds (substitute 1/2 tsp ground, I'd still toast to bring out flavour)

Spices:

  • 1/2 tsp cumin powder
  • 1/2 tsp coriander powder
  • 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper – feel free to reduce or omit
  • 1/4 heaped teaspoon cooking salt / kosher salt (halve for table salt, + 50% for flakes) – Note 3
Cups – Metric

Instructions

ABBREVIATED RECIPE

  • Toast nuts 5 min @ 180°C/350°F (160°C fan), add seeds, toast 3 min. Cool 15 min, blitz with spices until coarsely ground.

FULL RECIPE

  • Preheat oven to 180°C/350°F (160°C fan-forced).
  • Roast nuts – Spread the hazelnuts, almonds and pistachios on a tray. Bake for 5 minutes.
  • Roast seeds – Add sesame seeds and fennel seeds to the tray. Shake the tray to spread evenly. Bake for 3 minutes.
  • Coarsely blitz – Cool on the tray for 15 minutes. Pour everything into a mini food processor. (Note 4) Add the Spices. Blitz until coarsely ground – don't let it become a powder. (Or do this in a mortar and pestle, or in a ziplock bag and bash using a rolling pin or meat mallet). Note – the chunkier nut bits will rise to the surface and powder will sink, so don't be tricked into thinking it's chunkier than it is!
  • Use as a bread dipper with olive oil or sprinkling over "everything"! Use generously, not a sparse sprinkle, defeats the purpose!

USES:

  • As a bread dip (traditional) – Pour dukkah into a small shallow bowl and a good extra virgin olive oil in another (my favourite shop-bought is Lomondo from Mudgee in NSW). Pile warm cubes of bread, focaccia or wedges of pita bread on the side. Dip bread into olive oil first then the dukkah (it will stick to the oil). Eat!
  • Dukkah bread – Brush bread with olive oil then sprinkle with dukkah and sea salt flakes. Ideal to use bread with a large surface area (eg pita bread, Lebanese bread, focaccia)
  • Crumbing – Add to a breadcrumb mixture, like these Crumbed Baked Chicken Tenders or Schnitzel!
  • *Note on cooking* If using dukkah to sprinkle on things that go into the oven, be mindful of the nuts burning. Best to use for things that have a short bake time (eg on bread, ~10 min in oven) or mix it with breadcrumbs. Otherwise, use to sprinkle on the cooked food.
  • Topping or finish – Sprinkle generously over foods to make a good dish gourmet, or to make simple foods instantly more exciting! Examples: Garlic prawns, roasted vegetables, glazed carrots, oven baked chicken breast, a store bought roast chicken (add olive oil as well), pan fried fish, avocado toast, scrambled eggs. It'd be spectacular sprinkled on these Sweet Potato Steaks or Maple Roasted Carrots with Whipped Tahini (instead of pine nuts). (Remember – use generously!)
  • Garnish for dips – like hummus, whipped feta and labne.

Notes

1. Skinless hazelnuts can be purchased from regular grocery stores and come roasted. If you only have skin-on, I recommend removing the skin as it is a little bitter. To do this, roast the hazelnuts in a 180°C/350°F (160°C fan-forced) oven for 10–12 minutes until the skins start to crack. Tip onto a clean tea towel, wrap them up and rub vigorously to remove the skins. Don’t worry if some bits of skin remain! As they’re freshly roasted, there’s no need to roast them again before blitzing, just roast the other nuts and seeds. Best substitute – Blanched almonds, but then replace the 1/2 tbsp of blanched almonds with another nut, either walnuts or more pistachios. Or use cashews. 2. Almonds – Because the quantity used is so much less than the hazelnuts and the skin isn’t bitter, it’s fine to substitute with skin-on almonds, preferably roasted (if raw, give them a 3 minute head start in the oven). 3. Salt – I know a heaped 1/4 teaspoon is an odd amount but honestly, 1/2 tsp was slightly too salty and I really feel like 1/4 tsp is slightly under salted! Also, I know it doesn’t sound like a lot of salt for 3/4 cup of dukkah, but the salt gets blitzed so a little goes further than you expect. And you can always add extra salt at the end, if you want. 4. Mini food processor – There’s not enough volume to use a regular size food processor, though if you triple or quadruple the recipe, then it would be fine! Storage – Keep in an airtight jar and store in a cool pantry for 2 weeks, fridge for 2 months or freezer for 6 months (provided the nuts and spices were fresh). Nutrition for full batch.

Nutrition

Life of Jaffle

Jaffle went to stay with the golden retriever boarder while I was in Norway for the last few weeks! Every goldies’ dream to live in a house full of goldens, thundering down the hallways, wrestling on the rugs, stealing each other’s toys and behaving like they own the place. Which, based on the daily reports she sent through, they absolutely do!

Plus, the golden retriever boarder owns Jaffle’s mum, Clem. So not only was he having a party with his friends, he was also with his mum! And it turns out, Jaffle is a total mummy’s boy which I think will surprised no one. 😂 Apparently he just wanted to be by her side wherever she was, at the beach, at the park, at home!

But of the many (many!) photos and videos sent with the daily Jaffle Reports, this was hands down my favourite – just look at that smile!❤️

issues.author: Nagi
issues.content_html:
This is how to get your Chinese BBQ Pork fix – fast! It’s pork mince fried up using char siu sauce rather than marinating large pieces of pork. Sweet and savoury with a hint of five spice powder, it tastes just like the glaze on Chinese BBQ pork. Serve over rice for a quick dinner!

Chinese BBQ Pork Bowls

Recipes come into existence on this website in all sorts of ways. Sometimes they’re carefully planned, developed and tested to death with a specific goal in mind (like last Friday’s bagels). And sometimes they are impromptu recipes that came out of necessity, like today’s recipe, which was born only because I had a packet of pork mince in the fridge yesterday that needed using on that day and a desire to do something new with it than reaching for my quick ‘n easy faithfuls (Vietnamese Pork Bowls, Bun Cha (Vietnamese Meatballs) and Sausage Patties).

A quick rummage through the pantry, a sudden inspiration to use the marinade for Chinese BBQ Pork to fry up mince instead of marinating a pork roast, and here we are. A new recipe I thought tasted so good (and so quick to make), I had to share it!

(I really did film, photograph, edit and write this all up today. JB tested the recipe too, and we actually ended up making it 6 times in total, tweaking the sauce a bit until we were both happy with it. Proof it’s a seriously quick recipe!! 🙂 )

Ingredients in Chinese BBQ Pork Bowls

Here’s what you need to make this:

  • Pork mince (ground pork) – Use any fat % pork you want, though the higher the fat, the juicier your meat. 🙂 This recipe should also work nicely with chicken and turkey meat, but the sauce is probably a little lighter than ideal for beef and lamb (which are “meatier” tasting). Bear in mind though that chicken and turkey are leaner so the meat will be be a little drier.

  • Garlic and onion – Essential flavour base for this otherwise simple recipe, please don’t skip these.

  • Hoisin (dark not orange) – Proper hoisin sauce is a dark brown colour, almost as brown as oyster sauce. I use Lee Kum Kee and Panda brands. Hoisin sauce that is a more pale orange colour lacks proper flavour – I’m thinking specifically of Ayam Hoisin sauce here in Sydney. It tastes almost like a plum sauce, it’s very odd.

  • Chinese Five Spice Powder – A blend you can find at any grocery store these days, made up of (gasp shock horror!) five spices! This is the signature spicing flavour of Chinese BBQ Pork.

  • Dark soy sauce – This colours the pork a dark brown colour as well as adding salt and soy flavour. It can be substituted with all purpose soy or sauce, but double the quantity and note that the pork colour won’t be as dark brown as pictured, and the pork will have a touch less flavour than it should. If you could add a slosh of Mirin or Chinese cooking wine to compensate, you’d make me happy. 🙂

  • White pepper – White rather than black pepper is typically the default pepper for Chinese cooking, but it’s not a big deal in this recipe, just substitute with black if you don’t have it.

  • Red food colouring (OPTIONAL!!!) – This is to give the pork a faint red hue like you get with Chinese BBQ Pork! But it’s absolutely optional. I just added it for a bit of fun!

How to make Chinese BBQ Pork Bowls

Make sure to caramelise the pork well! It really makes a difference here.

  1. Sauce – Mix the ingredients together in a small bowl.

  2. Sauté – Heat the oil in a non-stick pan over high heat. Sauté the onion and garlic until the onion is tinged golden on the edges, about 1 1/2 to 2 minutes.

  1. Cook pork – Add the pork and cook, breaking it up as you go, until you no longer see pink.

  2. Sauce – Pour in the sauce.

  1. Caramelise! Then cook the pork, still on high heat, for a good 2 to 3 minutes until the sauce is absorbed by the pork and the pork caramelises. The more the pork caramelises, the better the flavour!

  2. Serve over rice and sprinkle with green onion or sesame seeds.

Because the pork is quite boldly flavoured, I like to just add fresh slices of cucumber and tomato or shredded carrot on the side. Quick, simple, and refreshing against the strong flavour of the pork.

Steamed greens like broccoli, beans or snow peas would also go great – anything really. If you want a quick Asian dressing to add a bit of flavour to the greens, try this Asian Sesame Dressing.

Oh! And I forgot to take a photo, but another way you could serve this is in lettuce wrap form. Add rice to fill it out, or for a lower carb-option, it would be terrific with some Vietnamese pickled carrots and daikon (radish).

Hope you enjoy! – Nagi x

Watch how to make it

Print

Quick Chinese BBQ Pork Bowls

Recipe video above. This is a quick dinner bowl made using the marinade from Chinese BBQ Pork (Char Siu) to fry up pork mince rather than marinating large pieces of pork. It tastes just like the glaze on Chinese BBQ Pork – sweet and savoury with a hint of Chinese Five Spice flavour! I even use a little drop of red food colouring, to give it a little authentic Char Sui colour – but this is 100% optional. 🙂 Serve it over rice and add some crunchy veggies on the side. Or make lettuce wraps! Course Mains Cuisine Chinese Keyword Ground pork recipe, pork bowl, Pork mince recipe Servings 4 Calories 413 cal Author Nagi

Ingredients

  • 1 tbsp oil
  • 1/2 onion , chopped
  • 2 garlic cloves , finely minced
  • 500g/ 1 lb pork mince / ground pork (or chicken or turkey)

Sauce:

  • 1 tbsp (tightly packed) brown sugar (or 1 1/2 tbsp honey)
  • 3 tbsp hoisin sauce (avoid orange hoisin eg. Ayam, Note 1)
  • 1 tbsp dark soy sauce (Note 2)
  • 3/4 tsp Chinese five spice powder
  • Pinch white pepper , or black pepper
  • 1/8 tsp red food colouring , optional (for touch of Chinese BBQ Pork colour!)

Serving:

  • White rice
  • Green onion , finely sliced, and/or white sesame seeds
  • Fresh veggies for the side – cucumber slices , tomato, grated carrot, steamed broccoli

Instructions

ABBREVIATED RECIPE:

  • Sauté onion and garlic, cook pork, add sauce, cook until caramelised. Serve over rice!

FULL RECIPE:

  • Sauce – Mix the Sauce ingredients in a small bowl.
  • Sauté – Heat the oil over high heat in a large non-stick pan. Add the onion and garlic, and cook for 1 1/2 minutes until the onion edge are tinged with gold.
  • Cook pork – Add the pork and cook, breaking it up as you go, until you no longer see pink. Add the Sauce and cook aggressively on high heat for a good 2 to 3 minutes until the sauce evaporates and the pork mince caramelises. The stronger the heat, the better the caramelisation, the tastier your pork!
  • Serve over rice with fresh veg of choice, sprinkled with green onion or sesame seeds.

Notes

1. Hoisin sauce – Make sure to use a dark brown coloured hoisin sauce (ie the colour of oyster sauce). Avoid the orange ones (eg. Ayam), the flavour is not proper hoisin flavour, it’s weaker and more plum-like. Substitute with oyster sauce and add an extra 1/4 teaspoon five spice powder (the flavour is fairly similar actually!). 2. Soy Sauce – This recipe calls for DARK soy sauce, which has more soy flavour than light and all purpose soy sauce, and makes the food a deeper brown colour. Can substitute with all purpose soy or sauce, but double the quantity and note that the pork colour won’t be as dark brown as pictured. The pork will have a touch less flavour than it should (as dark soy has more flavour than light soy) so if you could add 1 tablespoon of Mirin or Chinese cooking wine to the Sauce to compensate, you’d make me happy. 🙂 Leftovers – Cooked meat will keep for 3 to 4 days in the fridge, or freezer for 3 months. Nutrition per serving, assuming 4 servings, pork only (ie excluding rice and vegetables).

Pork mince is the softest out of all ground meats. No wonder it’s a favourite with Asian cooking!

Life of Jaffle

Wise people told me that after losing your soul dog, you would doubt if you could ever love another as much but you had to have faith, that one day you would wake up and realise your heart had made room.

For me that moment was an hour before I left for the airport for a 3 week holiday to Norway, when the separation anxiety set in. This naughty, mischievous boy has well and truly stolen my heart.

(Oh what, you didn’t know I was away for the last three weeks! 😉 I worked very hard to keep recipes coming while I was away so you wouldn’t know!! And to be honest, it is hard for me to stay away completely so I was still answering questions. I really try to switch off, but I can’t! Might have to send me to Everest or somewhere with ZERO reception for that to happen!).
