issues.author: Kieren Johns
issues.content_html:
Direct dynastic succession was a rare thing in the Roman Empire. Biology, bad fortune, and court intrigue ensured that control of the Empire rarely passed to a hereditary heir, but rather to the best available option. Augustus tried and failed to find a Julian heir, but was left with his Claudian stepson Tiberius. In AD 79, Vespasian was the first Roman emperor to be succeeded by his biological son, Titus; a feat that would not be repeated for a century. In the 2nd century AD, the Antonine emperors used adoption to nominate their successors. This functioned for decades, and power passed peacefully from one emperor to the next in what became known as the Roman Empire’s “Golden Age.” Unfortunately, in AD 180, Rome’s Golden Age came to an abrupt end when Marcus Aurelius chose to be succeeded by his biological son, Commodus.

Ancient Rome’s Golden Age: The Adoptive Antonines

In AD 96, the new emperor, Nerva, had a problem. Chosen by the Senate as an interim solution, he had recently replaced Domitian, the last of the Flavian emperors. While the assassinated autocrat had been unpopular with the Senate, he was beloved by the people and the army. Consequently, the Praetorians, the premier military force of Rome, were threatening revolt. To settle this unrest, the elderly Nerva invited a young general, Trajan, to be his heir and adopted him as his legal son. It proved to be a political masterstroke.

Trajan, who had been commanding legions in Germania, succeeded in AD 98. He was recognized in antiquity as the optimus princeps, the “best of emperors.” It was a reputation built on several factors. There were his stunning military victories, notably the conquest of Dacia. There were the incredible building projects in Rome: his eponymous Forum, public thermae (baths), and a grand market complex. There was also his continuation of Nerva’s succession policy.

Trajan’s decision to adopt an heir was not the ideal approach. In true Roman fashion, he would have preferred to have a son of his own to groom for succession. Biology dictated otherwise, and he adopted his cousin Hadrian as his successor. However, some sources critical of Hadrian suggest Trajan’s wife orchestrated the adoption after the emperor’s death.

The desire for a dynasty was never lost in this approach to imperial succession, as each was legally adopted as the son of their predecessor, even if they maintained some loyalty to their existing gens. Hadrian was succeeded by Antoninus Pius, who was in turn succeeded by Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, the latter of whom died before his partner and therefore is often overlooked.

Collectively, the Antonine emperors oversaw the period of Roman history which is often characterized as a “Golden Age,” a period of peace and stability also sometimes called the Pax Romana.

Warning Signs: War in the Age of Marcus Aurelius

The notion of the Pax Romana has proven to be particularly enduring. This is partly thanks to the characterization of this period as the happiest in history, an assessment made by Edward Gibbon in the 18th century, in his “Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.” The extent of “peace” in the Pax Romana is, however, up for debate. For the Dacians conquered by Trajan, for instance, it was unlikely to have been a particularly happy period. Fundamentally, the characterization of this period as one of peace refers to the internal conditions of the Empire, namely the peaceful transition of power from one adopted emperor to the next, not freedom from external threat.

While the empire’s internal politics maintained a high degree of peace, over the course of the 2nd century the empire found itself embroiled in wars. Trajan’s reign was marked by the conquests of Dacia and an unfinished war in Parthia. Although Hadrian retreated to the Empire’s former boundaries, his reign endured the brutal Bar Kokhbah revolt in Judea. Antoninus Pius’ reign was marked by a degree of stasis, and the emperor famously never even left Italy!

Conflict returned in the reign of Marcus Aurelius. First, there was the protracted Parthian War in the AD 160s. Although the Romans were ultimately successful, the Empire paid a heavy price. A decade of war naturally cost many lives, including that of the co-emperor, Lucius Verus. However, Verus did not die in battle. Instead, he probably perished as a result of the so-called “Antonine Plague.” This pestilence, probably smallpox, devastated the Empire.

To compound the strife, the Empire was soon at war with the Germanic tribes on the Northern frontiers. These Marcomannic Wars were fought by Marcus Aurelius, more commonly viewed as a philosopher than a warrior. The emperor’s victories in Germania were commemorated on the eponymous Column of Marcus Aurelius, a monument erected in central Rome by his son, and successor, Commodus.

A Philosopher’s Failing: Commodus’ Accession

Marcus Aurelius was not alone on the German frontier. He was accompanied by his young son, Commodus. Unlike his predecessors, Marcus was an extraordinarily fecund emperor. With his wife Faustina, he sired numerous children. Unfortunately, a great number of the imperial couple’s offspring died in infancy. The only male child who survived was Commodus.

From a very early age, Marcus took steps to ensure that his plan for dynastic succession was crystal clear. Commodus was presented to the soldiers and elevated to the status of Caesar (the junior partner to Augustus at the age of just five in AD 166). Around the Empire, his likeness was presented to the imperial populace. Commodus, who was on the frontlines with his father, was hailed imperator at the age of 15 in AD 175, and then became consul in January of AD 176, the youngest ever. Later that year he received the title Augustus, making him his father’s (junior) co-emperor.

From an early age, however, it seems that Commodus was perhaps not cut from the same cloth as his father. An extraordinary claim in the Historia Augustarelates that the 12-year-old Commodus ordered a slave to be thrown into the furnace as punishment for the crime of running his bath too cold. The slave was saved when a colleague chucked an old sheepskin onto the fire instead; the pungent smell was enough to convince Commodus that his orders had been followed. The whole story is only recorded in the Historia Augusta, which probably means it is an invention, but it was the type of behavior attributed to the young prince.

Emperor in the Arena: Commodus’ Reign

Commodus took sole power in AD 180, when his father died at Vindobona (Vienna) on the Germanic frontier. A speech in Herodian’sHistory, which is almost certainly an invention by the historian, makes clear that the people of the Empire recognized that Commodus was something wholly novel at this time: an heir born and raised to be emperor, meaning that he was porphyrogennetos, or “purple born.”

Unfortunately, the new emperor seemingly inherited few of his father’s virtues. Almost immediately, Commodus paid off the Germanic tribes to bring an end to the war. Returning to Rome, he rid himself of the advisors who had been picked by his father and instead fell under the influence of courtiers and sycophants. Tensions with the Senate escalated, and Commodus soon found himself threatened by several coups, including one orchestrated by his sister Lucilla.

Commodus survived, but the consequences were violent as paranoia set in. Leading senators were hunted down. On the imperial borders, dissatisfaction escalated, and the troops began to rebel, including in Britain. Seemingly oblivious to it all, Commodus instead began to masquerade in the arena as a gladiator, giving himself over to spectacle and entertainment, rather than rulership.

Commodus’ Assassination

Scholars have argued that Commodus’ portrayal as a gladiator was, in a way, a response to a problem that arose from his dynastic status. Because the emperor had been groomed to rule, he had never had an established career through which he could develop a sense of status. In other words, he was not a soldier of repute or a career politician. In other words, the gladiator display was a novel articulation of status by the new emperor; an innovative paradigm of representation.

The same could be said for Commodus’ other infamous act: his self-presentation as Hercules. The famous portrait of the emperor, covered by the skin of the Nemean lion and brandishing the demi-god’s iconic club, is one of the most striking portraits to have survived from antiquity.

While there may well have been an ideological motivation for Commodus’ masquerading as a gladiator and a demi-god, it is also apparent from the literary sources that the emperor alienated his subjects to a staggering degree. Aside from his megalomania, he was charged with being cruel, indolent, excessive, and ineffective, most notably by Cassius Dio. The historian, a contemporary of Commodus and a senator, barely hides his dislike in his narrative.

The inevitable end for Commodus came on New Year’s Eve, AD 192. Already drunk, having gorged himself, the emperor retired to his private bath. Unbeknownst to him, a conspiracy against his life was unfolding. Orchestrated by senators, poison was slipped into his wine. Unfortunately, the inebriated emperor had already imbibed too much; Commodus vomited up the poisoned wine. He was desperately weakened by now, however, and easy prey for the conspirators who had collaborators within the palace. Narcissus, a wrestler and Commodus’ trainer, was dispatched into the bath chamber, and there he strangled the emperor.

With Commodus’ death, the Antonine dynasty came to an end. There was, the sources record, jubilation in the streets of Rome, as the death of the tyrannical Commodus was widely celebrated. His statues were pulled down, and his name scratched out of inscriptions in episodes of memory sanctions enacted across the Empire as the news spread. He was the first emperor to be murdered since Domitian, almost a century earlier. The Empire’s Golden Age was definitively over.

The Age of Iron and Rust: The Year of the Five Emperors

For a counterweight to Gibbon’s characterization of a period of greatest happiness, we can turn to Cassius Dio. Although his history is “universal,” detailing the history of Rome from its foundation, its primary merit is for the passages of contemporary history: Dio’s personal experience of the emperors from Marcus Aurelius onward. The senatorial historian is under no illusions that Rome’s Golden Age came to an end with Commodus. Famously, he described the accession of Commodus after Marcus Aurelius’ death as the moment the Empire transformed from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust.

Removing Commodus did little to restore order. When the Empire awoke on New Year’s Day AD 193, imperial subjects found themselves under the command of a new princeps: the elderly statesman, Pertinax. With an esteemed political and military career, it was hoped that Pertinax, who must surely have been involved in the conspiracy against Commodus, could restore some of the Empire’s golden sheen. His attempts were futile. Trying to curb the influence of the Praetorians cost Pertinax his life: the guards murdered him in March, bringing an end to a reign that lasted barely 90 days.

What followed was a period of unrivaled political chaos. The year AD 193 would be remembered as the “Year of Five Emperors” as, along with Pertinax, five rivals around the Empire were acclaimed imperator. There was even the degrading sight of two men bidding against each other for the acclaim of the Praetorians, as the Empire became a lot in an auction. The ultimate victor in this desperate struggle for supremacy was Septimius Severus, a general from Lepcis Magna (modern Libya).

Ironically, his reign was marked by his attempts to present his dynasty as the continuation of Rome’s lost Golden Age. To the chagrin and mirth of the senators, he claimed to have been adopted by Marcus Aurelius and had the damnation of his “brother,” Commodus, reversed. He also renamed his seven-year-old son Lucius Septimius Bassianus, later nicknamed Caracalla, as Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. But Septimius Severus’ reign was one characterized by conflict that no amount of Antonine pretending could mask. The luster of Rome’s Golden Age could not be restored.

issues.title: How Did a French Postman Build the Palais Idéal by Hand?
issues.summary: In 1879, a postman in rural Hauterives in France stumbled across a stone that caught his attention while he was doing his rounds. It ignited a 33-year-long passion. Ferdinand Cheval was his name, and working alone, he spent more than three decades building a palace. Despite having no architectural training, his work has […]
issues.author: Greg Beyer
issues.content_html:
In 1879, a postman in rural Hauterives in France stumbled across a stone that caught his attention while he was doing his rounds. It ignited a 33-year-long passion.

Ferdinand Cheval was his name, and working alone, he spent more than three decades building a palace. Despite having no architectural training, his work has become a monument to fantasy and imagination, exemplifying the spirit of one man’s creativity and a passion for DIY.

Who Was Ferdinand Cheval Before He Built the Palais Idéal?

Ferdinand Cheval was born in 1836 into a poor farming community in Charmes-sur-l’Herbasse in Southeastern France. He left school at the age of 13 and originally planned to become a baker’s apprentice, but became a mail carrier instead. During his life, he suffered significant loss, outliving both of his wives (he remarried after his first wife died) and all three of his children.

He expressed that he had had a dream in his younger days where he was building a palace or a cave, and around 15 years later, an incident reminded him of this dream. He was walking fast and stumbled upon a rock of such strange shape that he picked it up and took it home. The next day, he returned to the spot and found more stones with the same features of sandstone shaped by water. He said to himself, “Since Nature is willing to do the sculpture, I will do the masonry and the architecture.”

And so the 43-year-old man spent the next three decades fulfilling that desire, building the most famous example of naive architecture in the world.

How Did a Rural Postman Build a Palace by Hand?

For a single human being, building a palace by hand is, quite literally, a monumental task. Ferdinand collected rocks on his 20-mile mail route, first using his pockets, then a bag, and eventually a wheelbarrow, as his task became grander.

He often worked at night by the light of a lamp, creating a wire frame of his palace and then covering it with wet cement and lime into which he pressed his rocks and stones. It was a slow process of hard labor, mixing architecture and sculpture, but the palace began to take shape, turning into a gargantuan structure as the years passed on.

What Features Make the Palais Idéal Such a Visual Masterpiece?

Ferdinand’s mail route took around two days to complete, and he spent a lot of time alone, sleeping in barns along the way. His thoughts were entertained by imaginary visions influenced by the imagery on postcards he delivered.

He incorporated fantastical elements into his structure, and drew from architecture from all over the world, turning his palace into a surreal landscape of magic with winding staircases, grottoes, turrets and labyrinthine corridors. Decorative façades draw on features from famous buildings such as the Royal Pavilion in Brighton and the Sagrada Familia, as well as aesthetic styles from Christian, Hindu and Egyptian architecture, among many others.

The palace is also a monument to nature, with the north façade resembling a forest. It even has two waterfalls, which Cheval named the Source of Life and the Source of Wisdom.

Despite the influence from so many sources, the overall structure remains visually coherent with a distinct style of its own, attributed to Ferdinand Cheval’s methods and brilliant mind. Throughout the palace are inscribed the words of Cheval, which he carved as a narration. Here, he describes his work as the “Dream of a peasant” and “The Pantheon of an obscure hero.”

What Happened to Ferdinand Cheval and His Palais Idéal?

Cheval wanted to be buried in his palace, but for legal reasons, his request was denied. So he spent another eight years building himself a mausoleum, which he finished one year before his death in 1924 at the age of 88.

His work was widely recognized for its cultural and artistic value, especially by Pablo Picasso, who had great admiration for Cheval. The Palais idéal du facteur Cheval was declared a national monument in 1969, and today it is a place that commands deep respect and draws tourists from around the world.

issues.title: 10 Magnificent Ancient Masterpieces Lost to History
issues.summary: In the surviving pages of ancient history, many authors mention famous artworks that inspired contemporaries and changed the course of Western art. Sadly, most of these artistic treasures have been lost to history, destroyed by fires and earthquakes, stolen by foreign powers and melted down, or just eaten away by slow natural decay. Here […]
issues.author: Jessica Suess
issues.content_html:
In the surviving pages of ancient history, many authors mention famous artworks that inspired contemporaries and changed the course of Western art. Sadly, most of these artistic treasures have been lost to history, destroyed by fires and earthquakes, stolen by foreign powers and melted down, or just eaten away by slow natural decay. Here are ten of the most celebrated ancient artworks that have sadly been lost, from a 4,500-year-old richly decorated Egyptian sarcophagus to elaborate murals buried by the following generation, only to be rediscovered in the Renaissance and decay all over again.

1. The Sunken Royal Sarcophagus of Pharaoh Menkaure

Pharaoh Menkaure built the third and smallest tomb at Giza, which served as his final resting place following his death in c. 2504 BC. Before this time, the sarcophagi of the pharaohs were usually unadorned stone boxes. Menkaure had a more elaborate coffin, setting a new precedent that would culminate in the stunning golden sarcophagi known from the Valley of the Kings over a millennium later.

Carved from a massive three-ton block of dark basalt, the exterior of the sarcophagus was carved to look like a palace façade, featuring recessed paneling, niched walls, and symbolic false doors that functioned as spiritual portals that allowed the pharaoh’s ka to pass in and out of his sarcophagus.

Menkaure’s sarcophagus was found inside his pyramid when his burial chamber was opened, using gunpowder, in 1837, roughly 4,300 years after it was placed there. It was empty and lidless, but still a spectacular find. Work immediately began to remove the sarcophagus from the tomb and transport it to the British Museum.

In September 1838, it was placed on the British merchant ship Beatrice to travel from Alexandria to Malta and then on to Liverpool in England. But as the ship left Malta, it encountered a severe storm and sank to the bottom of the Mediterranean. Neither the ship nor the sarcophagus has ever been located. But basalt is highly resistant to seawater erosion, so it may still be lying intact at the bottom of the sea.

2. Phidias’ Chryselephantine Statue of Zeus at Olympia

The famous master Greek sculptor Phidias was commissioned to create the statue of the god Zeus for his temple at Olympia around 435 BC. He crafted a chryselephantine piece, made of wood and embellished with ivory and gold. It stood 40 feet tall, so that his head almost touched the roof of the temple, giving an imposing presence. The geographer Strabo noted that if Zeus were to stand, he would take the roof off the temple.

The statue was so impressive that ancient Greek travelers numbered it among the Wonders of the Ancient World. The statue also served as the focal point for the Olympic Games. To preserve the statue for centuries, Phidias had a shallow pool of olive oil installed at the base of the statue. The oil was rubbed onto the statue daily to preserve the ivory and make it shine. Phidias established the image of Zeus as a bearded god.

Today, the statue is lost without a trace, and there are multiple theories about what happened to it. One is that when the Olympic Games were banned by the Roman Emperor Theodosius I in the late 4th century AD, the statue was transported to Constantinople and placed in the Palace of Lausus. It was then destroyed when the palace burned down in AD 475. Another theory is that it was destroyed at Olympia when Theodosius II ordered the temple burned in AD 426.

3. Phidias’ Gold and Ivory Statue of Athena Parthenos

Phidias was also commissioned to create the statue of Athena Parthenos to stand on the Parthenon on the reconstructed Athenian Acropolis in c. 447-438 BC. Pericles commissioned the work as a symbol of renewal after the Acropolis was destroyed by the Persians.

This was another chryselephantine statue that may have been as tall as the one of Zeus at Olympia. The wooden frame was reportedly covered with ivory for her skin and 1,000 kilograms of gold for her robes and armor. In her right hand, the goddess reportedly held a statue of Nike, the goddess of victory; her aegis bore an image of the head of Medusa; while her shield depicted the Amazonomachy, during which the Athenians defeated the Amazons. The pedestal of her statue featured a relief of the creation of Pandora.

The statue, made of wood, ivory, and gold rather than marble, disintegrated over time. It was reportedly first stripped of its gold by the Athenian tyrant Lachares in 296 BC, but was later restored. It was then badly damaged in the Parthenon fire of AD 267. Finally, the statue was likely removed in the 5th century AD when the Parthenon was converted into a Church dedicated to the Virgin Mary. It may have been transported to Constantinople, but then did not survive the sack of the city during the Fourth Crusade.

4. Lost Masterpieces of the Classical Painter Apelles

The 4th-century BC painter Apelles of Kos was universally acclaimed as the greatest classical painter in antiquity. He served as the official court painter of Alexander the Great, capturing his achievements in works that reportedly set new standards for life-like realism, three-dimensional depth, and proportion.

His most famous work was one of Alexander holding a thunderbolt, like Zeus. Alexander was so pleased with Apelles’ work that he reportedly forbade any other painters from rendering his likeness. When he was asked to paint a portrait of the one-eyed general Antigonus Monophthalmus, he depicted him in three-quarter profile to conceal his lost eye, no doubt pleasing the sitter, and providing the first recorded use of this framing in Western art.

While the ephemeral nature of paintings without modern conservation techniques meant that they were lost in antiquity, Renaissance masters like Botticelli, Raphael, and Titian still held Apelles as the gold standard from descriptions of his paintings. They often tried to recreate his works, resulting in masterpieces such as Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus, inspired by Apelles’ Aphrodite Anadyomene.

5. Vanished Monumental Reliefs of the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus

The Mausoleum of Halicarnassus was built c. 350 BC as a monumental tomb of Mausolus, the satrap of Caria, and his sister-wife Artemisia II. Considered one of the Wonders of the Ancient World, its exterior was famously decorated with incredibly fine high relief sculptures. The structure was so famous that it coined the word mausoleum.

There were reportedly four major friezes showing the Amazonomachy, the legendary battles between the Greeks and the Amazons, the Centauromachy, the fight between the Greeks and the Centaurs, and a chariot race frieze, probably showing races held as part of Mausolus’ funeral games. The fourth scene is unknown. Pliny the Elder and Vitruvius claim that Greece’s four most famous sculptors at the time were each assigned a wall: Scopas, Leochares, Bryaxis, and Timotheus.

The friezes were notable because they moved away from the serene and idyllic sculptures of previous centuries to show motion and violence. It paved the way for more realistic Hellenistic art.

Remarkably, the mausoleum remained intact for around 1,600 years until it was rocked by severe earthquakes between the 12th and 15th centuries. These caused the roof, columns, and friezes to collapse. The rubble was then used by the Knights Hospitaller to construct Bodrum Castle. Some of the relief slabs were preserved by the mortar of the new castle, and starting in the mid-19th century, relief slabs have been removed from the castle to reveal the original artwork.

6. Alexander Bronzes by the Imperial Court Sculptor Lysippos

Lysippos of Sicyon was the official court sculptor of Alexander the Great, who traveled with an entourage of artists and historians. He created the definitive visual image of the conqueror with his bronzes of Alexander, made using the lost-wax technique. Like with Apelles and his painting, Alexander was so impressed with how Lysippos represented him that he forbade any other sculptor from casting his image in bronze.

It is said that Lysippos captured unique quirks of Alexander’s appearance, including his slight tilt of the neck towards the left shoulder, an upward-turned gaze to the heavens, parted lips, and swept-back locks. He also abandoned the standard 1:7 body ratio in favor of a 1:8 ratio, making Alexander a longer, leaner, and more imposing figure. Plutarch noted that, beyond physical traits, Lysippos captured his divine ambition.

Several specific Alexander bronzes by Lysippos are known, including Alexander Lanceophoros, showing Alexander with his hand on a spear, gazing skyward, and the Granicus Cavalry Monument, a colossal group of 25 bronze equestrian statues of the Macedonian Companion Cavalry.

Sadly, not a single one of his bronzes survives. When Rome conquered Macedon in 148 BC, the Roman general Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonius seized the whole Granicus group and shipped it back to Rome. Similar things probably happened to his other works. When the Roman Empire’s economy took a downturn, they were probably melted down for the bronze.

7. How a Massive Bronze Colossus of Rhodes Collapsed Into the Harbor

The Colossus of Rhodes was an enormous 108-foot statue of the god Helios erected in the city of Rhodes between 292 and 280 BC to commemorate the successful defense of the city against a siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes. Designed by Chares of Lindos, a student of Lysippos, it was quickly named among the Wonders of the Ancient World. It was funded entirely by selling the siege equipment left behind by Demetrius and his army.

The statue was cast in hollow bronze and erected in tiers from the ground up, using a massive dirt ramp to scale upwards. Inside, the statue had a skeleton of iron beams and stone masonry pillars to provide the necessary structural support for the bronze plates that were riveted together. It became the blueprint for colossal statues to come.

The statue stood for just 54 years, as it was toppled by an earthquake in 226 BC, buckling at the knees and breaking up into massive fragments. Ptolemy III of Egypt offered to finance reconstruction, but the Rhodians, following the advice of the Oracle of Delphi, decided to let the fragments lie undisturbed. They were still impressive, and travelers made their way to Rhodes just to see the fragments. They were only sold for scrap after Arab forces took Rhodes in AD 653.

While modern drawings of the lost masterpiece often show it straddling the harbor, with ships sailing between its legs, the statue almost certainly stood on a pedestal on one side of the city’s harbor, looking out over the sea.

8. The Radiant Statue of Nero That Renamed the Colosseum

While the emperor Nero lived more than two centuries after the destruction of the Colossus of Rhodes, when he decided to erect a massive bronze statue of himself in Rome on land made vacant by the Great Fire of Rome in AD 64, he based it on the Colossus of Rhodes.

Standing 100 to 120 feet tall, which is about the size of the Statue of Liberty, it was designed by the sculptor Zenodorus. It was also hollow bronze, but with more advanced Roman engineering. Rather than showing Helios, it showed Nero himself as a god holding a globe and a ship’s rudder.

After Nero’s suicide and the fall of the Julio-Claudians, the new Flavian emperor Vespasian had the statue altered to represent the god Sol Invictus, adding a radiant sun crown. Later, under Hadrian in AD 128, it was moved to a new position alongside the Flavian Amphitheater. Centuries later, during the Middle Ages, the proximity of this colossal statue led to the amphitheater being widely known as the Colosseum.

The statue disappears from the historical record sometime between the 5th and 8th centuries AD, probably due to earthquakes that struck the area. The remains were probably melted down to make coins, weapons, and other tools. While the statue is gone, the concrete and brick masonry pedestal, which was originally clad in marble, still stood beside the Colosseum until Mussolini ordered it demolished in 1936.

9. Buried Murals of the Domus Aurea That Inspired Renaissance Masters

At the same time as Nero built his colossal statue, Nero also built a new palace for himself on land cleared by the fire. It was built on such a grand scale that it was known as the Domus Aurea, or Golden House.

One of its most decadent features was its interior design, with murals mostly painted by the master, Famulus. Pliny the Elder described the artist as solemn and dignified, even wearing a toga while painting. He also called the Domus Aurea the “prison of his art,” as he spent almost his entire career painting its murals.

The murals defined what is known as the Fourth Style of Roman wall painting. It was characterized by delicate candelabras, floating mythological figures, and vibrant backgrounds of white, red, and gold leaf. In this way, rather than creating solid wall images, the murals made the wall surfaces look like airy vistas.

The palace was abandoned shortly after Nero’s fall from grace, and the emperor Trajan stripped it of its precious metals and marbles, knocked down the vaulted ceilings, and filled in the rooms with soil. He then built the Baths of Trajan directly on top. But burying the palace in this way protected the murals until they were rediscovered accidentally in the 1480s.

Renaissance artists such as Raphael, Pinturicchio, and Michelangelo visited the site and copied many of the images, coining the term grotesque to describe them. Raphael recreated these ancient motifs on the walls and ceilings of the Vatican Loggias and the Villa Madama. But as soon as the original murals were exposed to the elements, a new wave of destruction began. Today the once-vibrant murals are faded ghostly outlines.

10. The Sacred Golden Menorah Captured by Roman Conquerors

The Second Temple of Jerusalem held many treasures, but one of the most important was the Golden Menorah. According to Jewish tradition, the Menorah was forged from a single solid talent of pure beaten gold. Its central shaft and six branching arms were adorned with intricately carved motifs depicting almond blossoms, calyxes, and petals, terminating in seven oil lamps. More than a light fixture, the Menorah represented the divine presence resting upon Israel, burning continuously as a perpetual witness to the covenant.

The Romans, led by the future emperor Titus, captured and destroyed the Second Temple of Jerusalem in AD 70, following revolts across the province. The Menorah was among the treasures taken by the Romans and paraded in the triumph celebrating the victory. The Menorah featured prominently on the Arch of Titus, which celebrated both the victory and the subsequent posthumous apotheosis of Titus.

Around AD 75, the emperor Vespasian constructed a Temple of Peace in the Roman Forum that also acted as an imperial museum, showing spoils from across the Empire. According to the contemporary Jewish historian Josephus, the Menorah was displayed there. But in AD 192, a devastating fire spread through the Forum and may have destroyed the Menorah along with the temple.

Some sources suggest that the Menorah survived and was later carried off by King Genseric of the Vandals in AD 455. Then, when the Byzantine general Belisarius reconquered North Africa from the Vandals in AD 534, he reportedly recaptured the treasures of Jerusalem and took them back to Constantinople. The 6th-century historian Procopius of Caesarea recorded that the emperor Justinian received a warning detailing that holding the treasures of the temple carried a curse, so Justinian ordered the treasures returned to Jerusalem, where they were placed in the Nea Church of the Theotokos. From there, the Menorah was probably destroyed when the Sasanian Persians sacked Jerusalem in AD 614, or when Muslim forces captured the city in AD 637.

issues.title: How Armies Turned Geography Into Their Greatest Weapon
issues.summary: Wars and battles are not won by armies and their commanders alone. A key aspect of the art of war involves identifying how natural features such as mountains, hills, rivers, and forests can be used to improve the odds of military victory, particularly when facing a numerically superior enemy. Some of the most famous […]
issues.author: Jimmy Chen
issues.content_html:
Wars and battles are not won by armies and their commanders alone. A key aspect of the art of war involves identifying how natural features such as mountains, hills, rivers, and forests can be used to improve the odds of military victory, particularly when facing a numerically superior enemy. Some of the most famous military engagements in history were determined by geography, whether on a strategic, operational, or tactical level. While armies and weapons have changed considerably over thousands of years, terrain remains a major factor in modern warfare.

Water: A Barrier and a Lifeline

Water is a necessity of human survival. In a military context, water is a double-edged sword. Depending on circumstances, rivers and seas can either serve as vital lifelines for reinforcements and supplies, or death traps that restrict the movements of both advancing and retreating armies.

Alexander the Great is best known for his battlefield victories that enabled the conquest of the Persian Empire. While Alexander defeated large Persian armies with ease, he faced one of his greatest challenges in 332 BC with the Siege of Tyre. The heavily fortified Phoenician island city was out of range of Alexander’s siege engines.

When Alexander attempted to build a causeway to approach the island by land, the Tyrian fleet easily disrupted his efforts. It was only after Alexander secured the assistance of the navies of nearby Sidon and Cyprus that he could stifle the Tyrian fleet and force Tyre to surrender after a seven-month siege. The causeway that Alexander built has survived over the centuries and is now part of the fabric of modern-day Tyre, the fifth-largest city in Lebanon.

Rivers are natural defensive barriers that often determine where a major battle will take place. Typically, a commanding general will deploy his army behind a river. Any advancing enemy would be exposed to casualties crossing the river. Deploying an army in front of a river is almost always considered a mistake, since it cuts off an army’s lines of supply and retreat.

On rare occasions, a general may choose to fight in front of a river on purpose. Amidst the collapse of the Qin Empire, in late 208 BC the southern warlord Xiang Yu led around 70,000 men across the Yellow River to confront the Qin general Zhang Han. Xiang Yu ordered his men to destroy most of their supplies, leaving only three days’ worth, and to sink their boats. By purposely cutting off his line of retreat, Xiang Yu let his men know that their only path to survival was to defeat the enemy. Despite being outnumbered three-to-one, Xiang Yu duly won a famous victory that brought an end to the famous Qin state and enabled him to wield hegemonic power over China until he was defeated by Liu Bang, the founder of the Han Dynasty.

Mountain Passes and Strategic Chokepoints

The Battle of Thermopylae is one of the most famous battles in antiquity. Known literally as the “Hot Gates,” Thermopylae was a narrow pass on the main road into southern Greece with mountains on one side and the sea on the other. It was an obvious spot for King Leonidas of Sparta’s outnumbered force to fight a delaying action against King Xerxes of Persia.

The narrow confines of the pass negated the numerical advantage of the Persian army and forced them into costly frontal assaults. While the Persians eventually managed to circumvent the formidable position on the third day of battle, their casualties were much higher than those of the Greek force.

Control of strategic mountain passes could bring lasting advantages over a much longer period. More than two thousand years of Chinese imperial history began in 221 BC when Qinshihuang completed his conquest of the rival warring states to complete the unification of China. The success of the Qin owed much to its geographical advantages.

The heartland of the Qin state was the Wei River valley in Shaanxi province. This area was also known as Guanzhong or “Between the Passes,” since the valley was protected by mountains on all sides. During the 4th century BC, while the rival warring states were struggling for power in the Central Plains of China, the Qin gathered its strength in Guanzhong behind the Hangu Pass until it was ready to break out of the pass.

With its major rivals to the east, in the 310s BC Qin armies conquered the Shu and Ba kingdoms to the southwest (around present-day Sichuan and Chongqing). These fertile and wealthy regions brought vital manpower and resources for the methodical campaigns east of the Hangu Pass over four decades between the 260s and 220s.

Occupying and Exploiting High Ground

An army that occupies the high ground is widely understood to enjoy an advantage in battle. Hills and ridges enable an army to have greater visibility of approaching enemies, artillery is more effectively deployed, and it is easier for both men and horses to fight downhill than uphill.

At the Battle of Hastings in 1066, King Harold Godwinson’s Anglo-Saxons took up an imposing defensive position on Senlac Hill, forming a shield wall that held firm against repeated attacks by the Duke of Normandy. Had the Anglo-Saxons maintained their cohesion on top of the hill, the last thousand years of English history may have been very different. Instead, either by design or by chance, the retreat of the Bretons on the Norman left flank encouraged the Anglo-Saxon warriors to pour down the hill, exposing their vulnerability to Norman cavalry and sealing the fate of Anglo-Saxon England.

On an otherwise level plain, high ground does not have to be very high. In late 1805, as Napoleon prepared for an ultimate clash with the Austro-Russian coalition army in Moravia, he occupied the gently sloping Pratzen Heights southeast of Brno. In order to entice the coalition army to attack him, Napoleon purposely abandoned the high ground to the enemy, feigning weakness and leaving his right flank seemingly undefended.

The ensuing Battle of Austerlitz was Napoleon’s tactical masterpiece. As Allied columns streamed down the Pratzen Heights to attack his right on the morning of December 2, Marshal Soult’s IV Corps emerged from the mist in the valley below to take control of the heights. With the coalition army split into two, Napoleon sent reinforcements onto the Pratzen to defeat both halves in detail and gain a decisive victory.

The Engineering of Terrain

Civilizations throughout history have often enhanced the defensive capabilities of the natural terrain with human engineering. The Great Wall of China is one of the most famous manmade defensive structures in the world. Often credited to Qinshihuang and his general Meng Tian in the 210s BC, the Great Wall describes several different walls in northern China built by successive dynasties over the centuries.

Regardless of its precise location and date of construction, the builders of the Great Wall often exploited natural features such as rivers and mountain ridges. The wall was more than a defensive barrier, it was a network of fortified outposts and camps that enabled Chinese armies to project power beyond the northern frontier and deter raids from the Xiongnu or the Mongols. Beyond its military purpose, the wall also served to regulate diplomacy and trade in peacetime.

Another famous set of walls from antiquity are the Walls of Constantinople. The city of Constantinople, present-day Istanbul, is surrounded by water from three sides. The city’s founder, Emperor Constantine the Great protected the city with a circuit of walls consisting of the Sea Walls and the Constantinian Wall on land. With subsequent expansion of the city, Emperor Theodosius II constructed the Theodosian Walls in the first half of the 5th century AD. This formidable fortification consisted of two circuits of walls defended by a moat and contributed to the city’s reputation as an impregnable fortress capable of withstanding sieges indefinitely.

In addition to the Sea Walls, Constantinople would prevent enemy ships from entering the Golden Horn by deploying the Great Iron Chain across the waterway. The device proved effective on countless occasions but was famously circumvented in 1453 when Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II brought his ships over land via the Galata district to assist in the conquest of Constantinople.

Why Terrain Still Defines Modern Warfare

Although warfare has changed significantly since the days of Alexander the Great and Qinshihuang, geography and physical terrain remains an unavoidable factor of military conflict in the modern age. Despite a massive firepower advantage, American forces were unable to defeat Vietnamese guerrillas who retreated into the jungle during the Vietnam War. In more recent memory, both the Soviets and US-led forces struggled to negotiate the mountainous landscape of Afghanistan, ultimately leading to ignominious withdrawal and the collapse of friendly regimes.

Globalization in the 21st century has only increased the strategic importance of key waterways that carry vital commodities from oil and gas to fertilizer and grains. Blockades of the Strait of Hormuz or the Suez Canal, whether intentional or accidental, have the effect of increasing the prices of goods all over the world. While the nature of warfare will undoubtedly continue to evolve, successful strategists and commanders still have to take geography into consideration in future conflicts.

issues.title: Individual expression needs leadership, not restrictions
issues.summary: What happens when an educator’s individual expression becomes a management problem? Modern organizations encourage employees to express their individuality and contribute their unique perspectives to the workplace. While freedom can increase creativity, it also presents a challenge for management.
issues.author: Noel Regalado, Global Program & People Operations Leader
issues.content_html:
What happens when an educator’s individual expression becomes a management problem? Modern organizations encourage employees to express their individuality and contribute their unique perspectives to the workplace. While freedom can increase creativity, it also presents a challenge for management. Without clearly defined professional standards, individual decisions may conflict with the organization and the community they serve. Educational leaders must establish clear professional guidelines balancing employee autonomy with organizational standards.

The growth in technological accessibility has enabled individuals to explore different
identities, beliefs, and communities more freely than in previous years. According to the International Telecommunication Union, global internet usage increased from 60% of the world’s population in 2020 to 74% in 2025. Growth in connectivity enables people to connect with others sharing similar experiences beyond their immediate local community, giving them greater confidence to express parts of themselves otherwise kept private. As individuals bring their experiences and forms of self-expression into the workplace, establishing professional standards promoting employee autonomy has become a challenge.

My own professional experience of managing educational programs across 15 countries and 3 continents convinced me of this growing challenge across all communities. In some businesses, a very open culture has created confusion and debate within the students’ families. When a student is exposed to a new belief or custom, they go back home to present what they learned with excitement and curiosity. Unfortunately, in their attempt to share newly acquired ideas with their families, some students are met with resistance and result in conflict due to differences in cultural, religious, or personal beliefs.

Recently, I found myself having to resolve a dispute due to the lack of organizational guidelines. A teacher had displayed a pride flag in the classroom, sparking curiosity among students and raising questions from some families. Although the flag was not part of the planned lesson, its presence became a topic of discussion beyond the classroom. Being so open to individualism had shined light on the absence of clear organizational guidelines.

When organizations fail to establish clear professional expectations, the consequences extend beyond individual disagreements. Consequently, employees become uncertain about decisions they can make independently, and families question the organization’s standards. Over time, uncertainty can weaken employee confidence, strain relationships with families, and distract leadership from its primary responsibility: deliver quality educational experiences. Clear standards are not simply rules for employees to follow, they are essential tools for effective organizational management.

In other countries, I have witnessed how the opposite extreme can be equally damaging, when restrictive organizational standards undermine teacher creativity and diversity. For example, while living in Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, I had the opportunity to go into the schools and meet the employees, parents and students. As an outdoor education program manager, I experienced firsthand how restrictive policies limited educators’ professional freedom. Being a heavily tattooed person, I was precisely instructed on what to wear and how to express myself. Taking away several creative skills developed throughout my career, and made it a challenge to connect with students. This sentiment was familiar to other educators who expressed concern about the inability to use their creative skills, due to restrictions placed by the educational program.

Limited individual expression can discourage educators from developing creative lesson plans, catering instruction for students with learning disabilities, and creating environments where students can succeed. There is value in educators’ freedom to express themselves and discover efficient methods for their students. However, such freedom is best exercised when clear professional expectations are bestowed by the community they serve along with standards to protect the students’ and teachers’ individuality.

Developing standards is not solely up to management. The best practice for establishing standards is to combine these elements: student satisfaction, parent feedback, and education professionals’ observations and recommendations. By listening to collective voices, educational organizations can honor the creativity of the teacher, respect the community they serve, and nurture the curiosity of the student. Management can establish quality control standards guiding teachers’ individual expression and professional judgement. The duty of leadership is not to silence individuality but to empower it with proper direction.

issues.title: Can your district recover? A cybersecurity checklist
issues.summary: The opening weeks of school are among the most operationally complex of the year. New students and staff need accounts, devices come back online, applications return to daily use, and vendors reconnect to systems.
issues.author: Katherine Hennessey, Everpure
issues.content_html:
The opening weeks of school are among the most operationally complex of the year. New students and staff need accounts, devices come back online, applications return to daily use, and vendors reconnect to systems. Large volumes of student and operational data start moving again at once. That activity can create gaps attackers may try to exploit.

The recent cyberattack against Springfield Public Schools in Massachusetts shows how disruptive an incident can be at the start of the school year. The attack affected systems needed for essential school operations and ultimately led to a breach involving student and staff data. Schools were closed for four days, and the district has since approved a shorter winter break to make up the lost instructional time.

The incident shows why back-to-school readiness must include preparing for disruption. October is also Cybersecurity Awareness Month, which offers an opportunity for districts to review which functions and data are most critical, where key dependencies exist, and how they will keep schools operating when systems go offline.

Decide what has to keep working

When a disruption occurs, not every application needs to come back at the same time. Start with what must remain available to keep schools operating safely: emergency contacts, attendance records, transportation information, student health data, payroll, or critical communications. From there, IT teams can map the data and systems that support them across on-premises infrastructure, cloud platforms, and vendor-managed environments.

Schools should also determine how staff will reach essential information while primary systems are offline. Protected copies of key records, alternate access procedures, and offline contact information can help bridge the gap between disruption and recovery.

Treat the start of the year as an access reset

Role changes every fall can leave behind stale accounts or permissions that no longer match a person’s responsibilities.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends that K-12 organizations prioritize multi-factor authentication (MFA), particularly for accounts with access to sensitive systems. Districts can pair that safeguard with a review of privileged accounts, outdated credentials, and permissions to make sure access still reflects current roles. Fewer unnecessary pathways into critical systems means fewer opportunities for an attacker.

Check outside dependencies

A district may take all manner of recommended measures to secure its own environments and still face disruption when a third-party provider is compromised or unavailable.

As schools rely on more technology to support instruction and operations, districts should have a clear picture of which outside services support critical functions, what data those providers hold, and what options exist if a service goes offline.

Planning should account for outages that last several hours as well as those that stretch into days. For each critical service, determine whether the underlying data can be accessed elsewhere or whether an alternate process can keep the function running while service is restored.

Protect the path to recovery

Backups and snapshots remain central to cyber resilience, but having copies of data is only part of the equation. Districts need confidence that those copies are protected and can be restored quickly.

That requires knowing how often recovery points are created, how quickly teams can restore them, and whether an attacker who reaches the primary environment could also reach the systems or credentials used to manage recovery data. Separating recovery copies from production systems and limiting who can alter or delete them can reduce the chance that one compromise affects both live data and the district’s recovery options.

Consistent protection policies and clear visibility across storage environments can also help IT teams locate the right recovery point faster when time matters.

Test the operation, not just the backup

CISA recommends that K-12 organizations exercise incident response plans and test backups. Districts can take that a step further by testing whether restored systems actually allow staff to resume the work those systems support.

Testing a full operational process can expose gaps that a backup test alone may miss. It can also help leaders set recovery expectations based on what teams have demonstrated they can do.

The value of having a recovery plan in place becomes clear when districts face an actual disruption. When a widespread software outage affected Spring Branch Independent School District in Texas in July 2024, the district turned to its existing backups after initial recovery efforts failed. Its IT teams restored core systems within four hours and completed recovery within six hours. The incident also gave the district an opportunity to put its response plan into practice and identify ways to improve future recovery efforts.

Put cyber resilience on the back-to-school checklist

Comprehensive back-to-school planning helps ensure that staff, devices, and applications are ready for the year ahead. Cyber resilience and recovery planning belong in that same review. Districts should verify who has access to systems, understand their vendor dependencies, identify the functions that need to keep running, protect the data behind them, and test whether those functions can continue during an outage.

The goal is to reduce the uncertainty a cyber incident creates. Districts that understand what they depend on and how they will operate through disruption are better positioned to limit downtime and keep academic and administrative operations moving.

issues.title: Modernizing voice communications at district scale
issues.summary: In my role as Supervisor of Telephone and Data Wiring for Prince George’s County Public Schools (PGCPS), my team and I oversee E-Rate funding along with internet, dark fiber, cellular, and communication services across the district.
issues.author: Robin Evans, Prince George’s County Public Schools
issues.content_html:
In my role as supervisor of Telephone and Data Wiring for Prince George’s County Public Schools (PGCPS), my team and I oversee E-Rate funding along with internet, dark fiber, cellular, and communication services across the district. Supporting a school system that serves more than 130,000 students, over 20,000 employees, and spans roughly 500 square miles requires balancing operational reliability, budget stewardship, and long-term technology planning every day.

Communication systems are one of the most critical, yet often overlooked, components of a district’s infrastructure. Voice platforms support emergency response, daily operations, family engagement, and districtwide coordination. When those systems fail, even briefly, the impact is immediate.

A Phone Isn’t Just a Phone

In education, a phone is a lifeline that connects front offices with families, enables coordination with first responders, and ensures accurate location information during emergency calls. Because they are expected to work without fail, they are easy to take for granted.

That reality shaped how we approached modernizing our voice environment. We understood that any disruption, even temporary, could have real consequences for the communities we serve.

Why We Chose to Modernize

Several years ago, our district migrated from traditional telephony to a VoIP platform. Over time, however, it became clear that we needed a more modern solution that could better support the operational and technical needs of our district. We were looking for more than a replacement system. We wanted a platform that could improve visibility, simplify administration, enhance functionality, and reduce costs while providing reliable long-term support.

Selecting the Right Partner

For a district our size, responsive support is essential. My team is small, with just a few people supporting a communication system that serves the entire district. While we bring strong operational experience and work closely with our internal engineering teams, access to external expertise is critical. We ultimately chose UDT Voice because we needed a partner that understood our goals, prioritized customer service, and could respond quickly when support was needed. That partnership proved especially important throughout the migration process.

Improving Functionality and Visibility

Because we had prior experience managing a VoIP system, we approached this migration with a much clearer understanding of what mattered operationally. We evaluated not only cost, but also usability, scalability, administrative efficiency, and feature improvements.

One major improvement was consolidation. Under our previous platform, we had to manage multiple administrative portals due to the size of the district. With the new platform, we now operate through a single portal, significantly improving efficiency and simplifying day-to-day management.

The platform also provides greater visibility into system performance. We can now remotely identify registered phones, monitor line status, detect devices placed in “Do Not Disturb,” and troubleshoot issues far more efficiently than before.

Equally important were the emergency communication features. For example, when a 911 call is placed from a school building, automated notification emails immediately identify the location, allowing us to coordinate more quickly with local authorities when needed.

Reducing Costs While Improving Service

Budget considerations also played a significant role in our decision-making process. Like many districts, we continue to face financial pressures while expected to do more with limited resources. Our transition allowed us to reduce operational costs while simultaneously improving service and functionality. Those savings can be reinvested into additional technology initiatives that support our staff and students.

Planning and Executing the Migration

Large-scale VoIP migrations can understandably make districts cautious. We viewed the project as an opportunity not just to replace technology, but to improve our overall environment. We understood the challenges we had encountered during our first VoIP transition and used those lessons to build a more strategic migration plan.

Communication was central to the plan. Each school functions as its own community and building leaders are focused on protecting students and staff. They need clear, timely updates on what is changing, when work will occur, who will be onsite, and what to expect.

Before every site cutover, we emailed each school a migration schedule, expected changes, voicemail updates, and user instructions. We also distributed getting-started guides for staff ahead of each transition. To minimize disruption, we collaborated closely with our partner to maintain familiar phone layouts and workflows wherever possible. The more intuitive the experience feels for users, the smoother the transition becomes in practice.

Our migration strategy was deliberate and staged to minimize disruption. At each site, we initially migrated a single phone connected to the main line while keeping the remaining phones on the legacy platform. This allowed incoming calls to continue uninterrupted while we validated performance through testing. Once successful, we transitioned the remaining phones.

Scheduling was another critical factor. We carefully planned around holidays, testing windows, and instructional priorities to minimize operational impact. We also organized deployments regionally to reduce “windshield” time and leveraged call forwarding on critical numbers ahead of port dates to avoid unnecessary pressure during cutovers. Additionally, our vendor partner completed extensive preparation behind the scene to expedite the migration process.

As a result, we successfully migrated 260 sites in under five months — despite a two-week winter break, Thanksgiving week, and eight snow days during the project timeline!

Lessons for Other Districts

For districts considering a voice migration, several lessons stand out:

  • Choose a partner that understands K–12 environments and prioritizes responsiveness
  • Communicate early and often with school leaders and staff
  • Plan carefully around the academic calendar and remain flexible
  • Treat migration as an opportunity to improve, not replicate, your current system
  • Prioritize familiarity for users to support adoption and reduce disruption

I am incredibly proud of what our team accomplished throughout this transition. I am grateful to Dr. Andrew Zuckerman, PGCPS Chief Information Officer, and Senthil Parameswaran, PGCPS Director of Technology Operations, for their confidence in our team and support throughout this modernization effort.

We approached this transition with a clear understanding of what was at stake and a
commitment to building a more reliable, responsive and sustainable communications
foundation for the future.

issues.title: The clock is ticking for states to get ready for the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit
issues.summary: The federal Education Freedom Tax Credit (EFTC) takes effect on January 1, 2027, and the potential funding source for families could put $26 billion into their hands.
issues.author: ESchool News Staff
issues.content_html:
The federal Education Freedom Tax Credit (EFTC) takes effect on January 1, 2027, and the potential funding source for families could put $26 billion into their hands. With less than three months to the start of the new year, there is growing concern that states might not be ready with their perfected lists of Scholarship Granting Organizations (SGOs) that need to be submitted to the IRS by February 15, 2027.

States that miss the deadline might be preventing other organizations in the state from qualifying as an SGO for 2027.

A new source of education funding

The EFTC creates a federal tax credit for taxpayers who contribute to approved nonprofit SGOs. Individual taxpayers can receive a dollar-for-dollar tax credit of up to $1,700, while married couples filing jointly can receive up to $3,400. SGOs, in turn, award scholarships that families can use for qualified educational expenses, potentially including tuition, tutoring, instructional materials, and other educational support services.

The program isn’t limited to families whose children attend private schools. Students who are eligible to attend public schools may benefit provided their family’s income does not exceed 300% of area median income. According to the Treasury Department, 96% of children in states that have opted in could qualify.

Before families can access these scholarships, states and SGOs must establish the infrastructure to administer them.

Opting in doesn’t mean being ready

A state may have opted in to the EFTC, but that doesn’t mean its program is ready and operational. For states to be EFTC-ready, there are several dependent steps, with states ultimately responsible for certifying SGOs before submitting their perfected lists to the IRS.

Existing SGOs may already have the organizational structure, tax-exempt status, and scholarship administration processes in place. However, they still need to submit documentation proving they meet federal EFTC requirements.

New SGOs, however, must establish governance, obtain their tax-exempt status, and develop scholarship administration procedures before seeking state approval.

LearningSpring is a school choice management platform that helps states, schools, families, SGOs, and providers run their EFTC programs. “The U.S. Treasury Department has stated that states face a significant paperwork burden in compiling and submitting their perfected SGO lists. This is only the tip of the paperwork iceberg,” said Cecilia Retelle Zywicki, co-founder and CEO of LearningSpring.

This paperwork bottleneck “is one reason why having a compliance infrastructure partner like LearningSpring is so essential,” she added.

The paperwork is only the beginning

As new SGOs apply, change status, or lose approval, states will need to maintain accurate records and ensure that participating organizations continue to meet program requirements. States also have responsibilities for taking reasonable steps to prevent fraud and abuse. With potentially multiple SGOs operating in a single state, preventing duplicate scholarship awards and maintaining accountability will require careful coordination.

This creates a challenge beyond meeting the initial deadline. States must establish programs that can operate safely and efficiently over time. Some may choose to develop their own administrative infrastructure. Others may work with third-party partners like LearningSpring that already have systems for SGO onboarding, compliance, oversight, and program management.

Helping families benefit means investing in operations now

With the potential for putting $26 billion into the hands of parents to choose the educational supports their child needs, the EFTC has enormous potential for students in public, private, or charter schools as well as for those who are homeschooled.

Outsourcing the administrative load is one option for helping states meet federal deadlines and make scholarships available to families at the start of the year. “With LearningSpring, states don’t need to create new infrastructure to participate in the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit (EFTC) program,” added Retelle Zywicki.

issues.title: The Revelator Gallery: November 2026 Exhibit
issues.summary: Creative artists and photographers celebrate the changing seasons around the globe. The post The Revelator Gallery: November 2026 Exhibit appeared first on The Revelator .
issues.author: Colleen M. Crary, Ph.D.
issues.content_html:
The art and photography in this month’s Gallery reflect the voices of people who want to capture the magnificent, and often curious, “wow” moments when we see something in nature that delights and surprises us. Many of the animals and plants they share speak to cultural traditions that have ancient meanings or are symbolic of heritage. These artistic visions have the power to inspire viewers to take action to preserve nature’s mystery and magic.

“I dried some yellow molly ( Paeonia daurica subsp. mlokosewitschii) golden flowers on a plate that I had purchased that was a very beautiful dark grey color. The match of colors was my inspiration. The bird is a crow. I use elements from Petrykivka Ukrainian folk technique of painting.”

“Please support City of Goodness, an international charity that provides comprehensive care for children, mothers, older women and animals in Ukraine.”

“Upstate New York sports lots of planted sunflowers in late summer. These remained longer than most, lasting into the peak of autumn’s color.”

“Over the summer, a doe would often hide her twin fawns in our intentionally overgrown yard. The fawns were unseeable when lying down, but would occasionally stretch their legs, and here I caught them grooming each other.”

See more of Jim’s work at longing4nature.com. “I am a retired physicist who, after a career with the government in Washington D.C., returned like some Odysseus to Ithaca, New York — hometown to my wife and site of a rewarding post-graduate stint at Cornell scores of years ago. Actually, I’ve retired twice, the second time from running an all-volunteer nonprofit watershed group in southern Maryland. This website is a retirement project aimed to salve a creative itch.”

“I recently began exploring wildlife photography because I enjoy discovering the small details and moments in nature that are easy to overlook. These photographs reflect that interest and my appreciation for the wildlife around me.”

Anupam Ditta, Wildlife Photographer & Writer
Kolkata, India
Portfolio: https://anupamdutta.in/
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/duttanupam/

“These birds of paradise look like “floraraptors,” because of the perfect backlight and low camera angle (yes, I was on my belly), emerging from a Jurassic jungle (even though flowering plants did not appear until the Cretaceous period). I used a simple point & shoot camera in an Orange County, California, garden.”

Artist Barri Hitchen is inspired by the unique beauty of The Somerset Levels, a vast, low-lying coastal plain and wetland area in Somerset, England. He is especially interested in the visually and spiritually rich waterways and wetlands. Born in Hampstead, London, Barri is a Fauvist painter in the naive tradition, working in mixed-media, using blocks of color. A graduate of the Fitzwymarc School, and the University of Essex-East 15 Acting School, he is also an actor/director and makes independent short films.

“We were thrilled to see this during our holiday in Scotland, out in the back of our lodge near Ben Nevis.”

“Hedgehogs come into our garden every night between March-October. They’re not easy to photograph because it’s usually dark when they arrive, so when I do see one, I try to get a good photo if I can. I love to see them snuffling around the garden — they’re very docile and tend to freeze rather than run away, so they’re fun to be around.”

Claire comments, “Not often you see birds this big in England or Scotland, so have to take a photo!”

Note: Claire and Chris Sandys are the producers of The Silent Why Podcast, where loss and grief are explored and discussed, asking the question: Can hope be found in every type of loss?

The Revelator Gallery Archives

Each monthly exhibit is archived here in chronological order with links and listed under each new exhibit, so your work can be seen and enjoyed moving forward. And don’t be shy about submitting more work so we can spotlight uplifting artists and photographers each month who are inspired by wildlife and nature. October 2026 Exhibit: https://therevelator.org/gallery-oct2026/September 2026 Exhibit:https://therevelator.org/environmental-gallery-sept2026/August 2026 Exhibit: https://therevelator.org/environmental-gallery/Guidelines to get your masterpiece into the Revelator Gallery:
    • Original photos and art from you
    • No AI-generated or enhanced images
    • Images can be horizontal, square, or vertical
    • We accept only .jpgs and .png files
    • THERE’S NO LIMIT on how many submissions you send.
    • One image and description per email. No Exceptions.
    • No people in the images, just wildlife and landscapes (animals, plants and trees, insects, sea life…)

Send your submissions to ccrary@biologicaldiversity.org with the following information:

    • Your name
    • Title of image (if applicable)
    • Species of wildlife (if known)
    • The location (where it was created)
    • A brief description of what inspired you to capture or create this image
    • Medium: Photography (many types, be specific), painting, drawing, pottery, sculpture, textiles/fabric art, mixed media, glass, etc.
    • Let us know if you want us to include a specific copyright notice “©”

All submissions are considered intended for publication; submission does not guarantee publication. Monthly galleries will be distributed to our partner publications under a Creative Commons license, but you retain the copyright on your individual images. There’s no prize or payment, just bragging rights.
