issues.title: Wildlife and Nature Books for Gift-Giving
issues.summary: Gifting someone a book can open a door into other people’s experiences and perceptions of wildlife and nature. The post Wildlife and Nature Books for Gift-Giving appeared first on The Revelator .
issues.author: Colleen M. Crary, Ph.D.
issues.content_html:
There’s nothing more satisfying than curling up with a good book. Turn off the machines and tune out the social media and noise so you can relax with the beautiful insights of others.

Here are several new books — along with some exciting volumes from the past couple of years that we haven’t covered before — about biological diversity, veganism, art, and more that offer insight into the minds of other nature and wildlife guardians.

We’ve adapted the books’ official descriptions below, and the link in each title goes to the publisher’s page. You can also find any of these titles through your local bookseller and library.

The Hidden Nations of Animals: A Grand Tour of Earth’s Wild Civilizations

by Ryan Huling, illustrated by Oliver Uberti

From far-flung forest settlements in Canada’s “beaver belt” to disputed territories of clashing Argentine ant armies, this around-the-world odyssey takes us to places most people don’t even know exist. Along the way we meet renowned ecologists, anthropologists, geographers, and historians whose work has uncovered vast sub-Saharan tunnel complexes, booming animal metropolises nestled within the urban sprawl of the American Southwest, and ancient Silk Road-style migration routes that traverse the Eurasian Steppe.

When humans settle in an area, it is deemed, by definition, populated. By contrast, the millions of other species we share this planet with have long been viewed as fleeting ephemera, living brief and transitory lives in “uninhabited” wilderness. Over the course of a year, Huling investigates how technology is rapidly changing that perception by deepening humanity’s understanding of our fellow animals and their unique relationships with the land, air, and sea. His immersive account fuses with vivid full-color maps and hand-drawn sketches by award-winning cartographer Oliver Uberti, revealing a radically reimagined version of our world and illuminating its true contours for the first time.

Wild Lives: The World’s Most Extraordinary Wildlife

by Gregory Green, photography by Art Wolfe

Wild Lives presents a celebration of the beauty, ferocity, and revival of Earth’s endangered wildlife through the lens of legendary photographer Art Wolfe. This is a celebration of the extraordinary diversity of species that inhabit the planet. Some are common, some rare, and many are conservation success stories, species that have been brought back from the edge of extinction but are now flourishing. These recoveries are an uplifting testament to the resilience of life when it’s given a chance. From amphibians and reptiles to mammals and birds, Wild Lives portrays an earthly aesthetic millions of years in the making. Wolfe has photographed more than 500 species in 60 countries, and the never-before-seen work in Wild Lives forms the most comprehensive, globe-spanning book of photography he has ever published. Accompanying Wolfe’s photos are essays by renowned conservationist, Gregory Green. Focusing on the why of wildlife conservation and recovery, Green discusses the redistribution of animals and their habitats dating all the way back to the Ice Age. Together, Wolfe and Green have crafted a monograph that will not only shed new light on the creatures that surround us, but on humanity as a species as well.

The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness

by Cal Flyn

From the black sand beaches of Iceland to river crossings deep in the Amazon jungle to the barren beauty of Antarctica, wildernesses make up some of the world’s more alluring natural landscapes. But what is a wilderness, really? It’s a powerful, ancient concept, lying at the intersection of landscape, philosophy, and ecology. And for thousands of years, people have sought out uncontrolled, unknown, or uncharted nature in search of religious epiphany, self-actualization, and an escape from modern life. More recently these “pristine” places have been seen as the subject of a last effort to repair a planet imperiled by humans. Cal Flyn traverses the most forbidding, untamed and inhospitable wild lands, and she finds that such truly untouched lands don’t exist: Nearly every wilderness has been or is actively inhabited by humans. Here we meet ascetics in search of theophany in the desert, lonely shepherds running off wolves under the stars, missionaries preaching from shacks deep in the jungle, wise lamas meditating under lofty mountain peaks. The Savage Landscape takes us into these breathtaking wilds — deep into dark forests, to the tops of mountains, and into the hearts of deserts — asking provocative questions about the nature of wilderness, its preservation, and its meaning.

Tree Lore: Magic, Myth, and Wisdom From Root to Bough

by Dawn Nelson, illustrated by Julia Asenbaum

Explore the vast and wondrous legends behind 35 of the world’s tree species and enjoy a new approach to nature-based spirituality. In this nature connection and spiritual wellness guide, Dawn Nelson offers a new way of connecting with trees — and in turn the landscape and nature around us — through stories, lore, and sacred symbolism. Tales drawn from around the world reveal how these iconic trees have become so significant in human culture. Featuring Native American stories about the famous California redwoods, Norse myths about the mighty oak tree, Incan tales about palo santo, and Middle Eastern folklore about frankincense, Tree Lore covers many continents and cultures. Stunning illustrations capture each tree’s unique properties, and an affirmation following each tree’s story encourages readers to pause and consider its message and can be used as a daily meditation tool to find strength in the trees and their ancient wisdom.

Green Architecture

by Philip Jodidio

The most exciting new buildings today are almost all environmentally aware, sustainable, and conceived to consume less energy than ever before. Discover the best examples of green projects from the Architecture Now! series in this handy Bibliotheca Universalis edition. Celebrated architects like Frank Gehry and Norman Foster are presented alongside young up-and-coming creators from all over the world. Filled with plans, renderings of proposed projects, and stunning architectural photography, this is nothing short of an encyclopedia of eco-design. From a water treatment facility to an art museum, luxurious holiday homes to commercial structures, these buildings all make a bold environmental statement. Being “green” means being aware of the responsibility in the construction and use of modern buildings; some solutions are as old as the history of architecture, while others are born of cutting-edge technologies. Explore these approaches and many more in this groundbreaking collection showcasing 100 of the world’s most innovative eco-friendly buildings.

Slow Looking: The Art of Nature

by Olivia Meehan, Alice Vincent, Lizzie Marx, Miya Tokumitsu, and Harriet Baker

An astounding visual compendium of artworks that illuminates the deep connection between artistic expression and the natural world, leading to a heightened individual experience of both art and nature. Slow Looking: The Art of Nature is a unique celebration of the relationship between art and nature across millennia. This inspirational collection of artworks allows readers to make connections between the nature that surrounds them and the vision of a dazzling wide range of artists. Art historian Olivia Meehan has mixed paintings, drawings, sculpture, textiles, and decorative arts from across the globe in thought-provoking juxtapositions, inviting us to find something new in a familiar landscape and experiment in observing nature’s wonders.

Exploring the various intersections between artistic techniques and thematical elements across land, water, and sky, the pages reveal the deep­rooted connections between human beings and our natural world: the form and colors of a Georgia O’Keeffe painting of a shell echo a carved fossil from 500,000–300,000 BCE; Van Gogh’s olive trees (1889) are juxtaposed with ancient Egyptian carved limestone dated between 1353 and 1323 BCE; and while water lilies captivated Claude Monet, their allure also traveled to mid­18th-century India in Hunhar II’s watercolor work. Following nature’s patterns, Slow Looking: The Art of Nature takes readers on a journey from fields, mountains, forests, and glaciers to lakes, ponds, waterfalls, and rivers and on to sunrises, rainbows, comets, clouds, constellations, and so much more. This guided observation of nature offers a whole new way of contemplating the world.

Mastering the Art of Plant-Based Cooking: Vegan Recipes, Tips, and Techniques

by Joe Yonan

A James Beard Award winner, this cookbook is rich with new ideas for vegan cuisine. It features more than 300 mouthwatering recipes for flavorful staples, weeknight meals, and celebratory feasts. Voted by NPR and Bon Appetit, this is the first book to treat vegan food as its own cuisine, worthy of mastery. Joe Yonan has spent years reporting on and making plant-based foods. With his finger on the pulse of this ever-growing cuisine, he has collected recipes and essays from prominent food writers in the plant-based sphere, creating a book that shows the true abundance of vegan food around the world, offering something for everyone. The book opens with an in-depth pantry section, showing how to create homemade versions of foundational ingredients like milks, butters, stocks, dressings, and spice mixes. The following chapters build on these elements, with recipes for meals throughout the day.

With numerous variations on base recipes, an extensive dessert section, hundreds of vegan meals, and stunning photography, Mastering the Art of Plant-Based Cooking will become a mainstay in your kitchen, delivering new ideas for years to come.

The 29-Minute Vegan: Real Food, Real Vibes, Anytime

by Isa Chandra Moskowitz

Bestselling vegan author Isa Chandra Moskowitz shows readers how to get a plant-based meal on the table in just under 30 minutes. If you avoid cooking plant-based meals at home because it might be a lot of work and time, Moskowitz is here to say: Nope. She features more than 100 crazy-easy, super-fast, satisfying vegan meals perfect for the pacing of our busy lives. Moskowitz’s unique flavor profiles, frank humor, and punk style offer guidance on all aspects of vegan cooking. Her recipes appeal to both lifelong vegans and aspiring vegans who crave the flavors, aromas, and textures of meat. Whether you’re hungry for a comforting Massaman curry, need your Taco Tuesday fix, or just crave a super-fast green curry tofu noodle salad, Moskowitz will have you set up faster than ordering in.

Books for young readers, including titles that can be paired with several of the selections above or to share with their favorite grown-ups.

The Buzz on Wild Bees: The Little-Known Pollinators That Keep Our Planet Humming

by Kira Vermond, illustrated by June Steube

Ages 7-10 (grades 2 to 5)

Ask kids about bees, and most will think of honeybees or bumblebees. This book expands the world of bees to the young, exploring wild, solitary bees like mason bees, mining bees, leafcutter bees, cuckoo bees, and even oil-collecting bees. Wild solitary bees make up about 95% of the world’s bee population. Solitary bees have no hive or queen to protect, so they never swarm and most don’t even sting (but if they do, it just feels like a pinprick). This book explains why we need these super pollinators for the health of our planet. Using a clear, concise language that keeps it light and engaging with plenty of silly word play, The Buzz on Wild Bees describes their life cycles, habitats, and behaviors — some of which are weirder than others. For example, sweat bees use their long tongues to lick salty sweat off animals, including humans, because pollen and nectar don’t contain enough salt. Teaching the supreme importance of wild solitary bees to all life on Earth educates the young in greater appreciation for bees, such as how 1 in 3 mouthfuls of food we eat depends on the pollinating powers of all bees, not just honeybees. Children and young people will learn about the challenges bees face, and the things we can do to bee part of the solution and help save all the bees! Includes a glossary, bibliography and full-color endpapers displaying all the amazing-looking bees included in the book.

Climate Is Just the Start

by Mikaela Loach

Ages 8-12

A young people’s guide to tackling the climate crisis from a prominent activist working on the front lines. Mikaela Loach’s approach is one of hope and optimism, inspiring kids to feel truly empowered to change the world. Kids hear about the climate crisis every day from their parents, teachers, social media, and the news — there’s no escaping it. So it’s easy for young people to feel a sense of “doom and gloom” and powerlessness. Loach offers her urgent and inspiring message for kids who want to stop the climate crisis and build a better world. Mikaela explains the climate crisis and its broader social implications through personal stories about her activism journey. She writes about friends from around the world who are experiencing the worst of it today and about what they’re doing to fight back. She delivers a message of not only hope, but of excitement for the opportunity to create a sustainable future for Earth and better lives for people in the process.

Detective Dogs: How Working Dogs Sniff Out Invasive Species

by Alison Pearce Stevens

Ages 8-12

A lively introduction to some of North America’s most troublesome invasive species — and to the industrious dogs and handlers working to stop their spread. Meet Fenton and Frost; Fagen and Dia; Hilo, Diesel, and Seuss. These intrepid environmental detectives are on the front lines of the fight to stop the spread of invasive species — and all of them are dogs! Pervasive and often difficult to locate, invasive species and the economic and environmental harm they cause have posed a continued challenge to scientists worldwide who dedicate their time to ecosystem conservation. Now environmental scientists are harnessing the amazing olfactory abilities of working dogs to meet this challenge head-on. This engaging and accessible narrative showcases three ongoing conservation projects that use working dogs to tackle serious invaders in the United States and Canada. Readers will learn more about the threats posed by these species and about the way scientists and handlers work with dogs to locate and eliminate them.

Ocean Anatomy: The Curious Parts & Pieces of the World Under the Sea

by Julia Rothman with John Niekrasz

Ages 6-adult

Take a deep drive into the wonders of the sea with Julia Rothman’s bestselling illustrated ocean guide. Follow her inquisitive mind and perceptive eye along shorelines, across the open ocean, and below the waves for an artistic exploration of the watery universe. Through her drawings, discover how the world’s oceans formed, why the sea is salty, and the forces behind oceanic phenomena such as rogue waves. Colorful anatomical profiles of sea creatures from crustacean to cetacean, surveys of seafaring vessels and lighthouses, and the impact of plastic and warming water temperatures are just part of this compendium of curiosities that will entertain and educate readers of all ages.

Weird and Wonderful Nature: Tales of More Than 100 Unique Animals, Plants, and Phenomena

by Ben Hoare

Ages 7-11 and beyond

Enjoy more than 100 extraordinary stories of unusual species, behaviors, and objects, such as why do Mexican jumping beans jump? How do sea cucumbers defend themselves? What causes the northern lights? This book is filled with facts about the most surprising and curious plants, animals, rocks, and phenomena in nature and teaches about the weird and wonderful side of the natural world. This book includes facts from a range of topics, from animals to plants and rocks to natural phenomena, that are guaranteed to wow adults and children alike, and large photographs and illustrations that show each species or item in incredible detail. Ben Hoare’s friendly, informative explanations are paired with photographs and charming illustrations to make sure every page captivates the imagination, while a glossary and index help you navigate the chapters.

You can find hundreds more environmental book recommendations in the “Revelator Reads” archives to help you choose additional books to gift your friends and family for holidays, birthdays, or just because you think the world of them.

And let us know what you’re reading: Drop us an email at ccrary@biologicaldiversity.org.

issues.title: After the Blue Wave: X Out Musk
issues.summary: The world’s richest man is an enemy of democracy and the environment. Let’s stop using his products and get the government to give him and his companies the boot. The post After the Blue Wave: X Out Musk appeared first on The Revelator .
issues.author: John R. Platt
issues.content_html:
The world’s richest man is also one of its most destructive and anti-democratic. Elon Musk invested almost half a billion dollars toward electing extreme right-wing candidates this past year — more than the right wing’s convenient boogeyman, George Soros, has donated to political causes in his entire life. The fact that most of Musk’s candidates lost this time doesn’t make him any less dangerous. After all, he helped get Trump reelected in 2024.

Between that presidential election and the 2026 midterms, Musk strip-mined the government for our data; eliminated USAID (a loss that has already killed tens of thousands of people); inserted himself into the Russian invasion of Ukraine by turning off Starlink (and killing more people); polluted communities with his data centers and space launches; and threatened everyone who tried or promised to stand up to him.

He’s not going to stop, but people with a conscience can stop supporting him by divesting from the Elon Musk ecosystem.

That means no X, Tesla (both vehicles and EV chargers), Starlink, SpaceX, xAI, etc. Don’t buy his products, don’t use them, don’t invest in them. Walk away.

Individuals can only accomplish so much with this tactic, but Musk’s fortune is directly tied to government contracts and tax subsidies, so the critical next step would see the United States government similarly divesting from these companies, systems, and programs. We should call our newly elected Blue Wave representatives and encourage them to cancel those contracts, develop alternatives, or even take over semi-essential programs like Starlink’s Starshield.

After that, let’s encourage an environmental comeuppance for Musk. He’s gotten away with shocking amounts of pollution related to his space launches and data centers. It’s time to institute massive fines, criminal punishments, and forced cleanups. Again, our new reps can help with that.

That’s just one way to re-regulate Musk, who has gotten preferential treatment from the FAA, EPA, National Labor Relations Board, and other agencies. Can our new legislators reenergize those federal authorities? Under normal conditions it would be just too expensive for Musk to run his many businesses the way he does. Let’s level the field.

While we’re at it, is it time for congressional oversight? Hearings and subpoenas should aim to dig out corruption and possible crimes. We’re already hearing senators promise action in this direction; let’s voice our support.

And, of course, we can encourage our new Congress and Senate to tax the hell out of Musk and other billionaires. They’ve gotten a free ride far too long. That will be hard to accomplish while Trump remains in office with veto power, but maybe we can at least rehire some IRS agents to audit these ultrawealthy tech bros.

Meanwhile opportunities also exist outside the federal government following the Blue Wave. Musk moved his companies to Texas in anticipation of a favorable regulatory and tax environment. On the campaign trail, newly elected Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa and attorney general Nathan Johnson both promised to stand up to or investigate Musk and his empire. Let’s get that moving once they take office in January.

Looking further ahead, there’s one more important area incoming federal legislators can address: campaign-finance reform. Let’s get obscene amounts of money and undue corporate/billionaire influence out of our elections. Again, this feels next to impossible with Trump still in office, but anticorruption was a winning message in 2026, so maybe it’ll help in 2028 and beyond.

Time is of the essence. Musk is reportedly planning on expanding into mobile telecommunications, which would give him more power and reach. He’s building more data centers. His pollution is ongoing (if not worsening). And he’s no doubt eyeballing candidates for 2028. Let’s not waste an opportunity to right-size this right-wing extremist’s business empire — and help people and the planet alike. By tackling this technocrat trillionaire we can put billionaires like Peter Thiel, Marc Andreessen, Charles Koch, and others in their place, too.

issues.content_html: Between roughly 1450 and 1648, Europeans both changed their view of the world and their place in it. Humanists in the Italian city-states revived the study of classical literature and philosophy while patrons such as the Medici and the popes commissioned art and architecture. The printing press carried these ideas northwards, where Erasmus and Thomas More applied humanist learning to religious and social reform. At the same time, monarchs in Spain and England built centralized states. Portuguese and Spanish navigators opened sea routes to Asia and the Americas, starting the Columbian Exchange and the transatlantic slave trade, and imported a vast amount of American silver that shifted Europe's economic centre from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

issues.title: Thanksgiving Turkey
issues.summary: From thawing to carving, this juicy Thanksgiving Turkey recipe walks you through the whole bird, with an optional dry brine for extra-crispy skin. The post Thanksgiving Turkey appeared first on Budget Bytes .
issues.author: Jess Rice
issues.content_html:
Roasting a whole turkey can be intimidating, but it really doesn’t have to be! That’s why I’ve put together this thoroughly tested (and tested, and tested again!) step-by-step guide to getting juicy, flavorful meat and beautifully golden, crispy skin without the guesswork. I’ll walk you through everything from safely thawing and prepping your Thanksgiving Turkey (including an optional dry brine) to roasting and carving, with plenty of helpful tips along the way. I’ve even included a printable Thanksgiving Day timetable you can stick on your fridge, so you can spend less time worrying about the turkey and more time enjoying the holiday!

A Method You Can Count On

There is NO WAY I’d publish a recipe this important without making sure you have everything you need to get it right on the big day. I’ve worked through all the little details, from the seasoning to the roasting method, so you can feel confident making a turkey your whole family will love. Grandma likes dark meat? This method yields the juiciest, most flavorful thighs and drumsticks. Auntie Linda only eats white meat? The breast stays tender and juicy thanks to the garlicky herb butter tucked under the skin. And if your brothers and Dad love crispy skin, I can help you there! The optional dry brine and thin coating of seasoned oil give this roasted turkey a beautifully golden, crispy finish that the whole family will beg for.

But if there’s one thing I’ve learned through all my testing, it’s just how important a good meat thermometer is. The size of your turkey and even the pan you roast it in can affect the cooking time, so I always recommend checking the internal temperature rather than relying on the clock alone. Be sure to read my top tips and comprehensive FAQ section, too. I’ve covered everything you might need (including rescuing a turkey that’s still frozen on Thanksgiving morning!)

Recipe Success Tips

There’s a lot riding on this one bird, so naturally, there’s a lot of tips and guidance I need to cover, too. I recommend reading through this whole guide once (if not twice!) before getting started, including these tips and the FAQ section at the end.

  1. Season under AND over the skin. I tuck a garlicky herb compound butter (made from butter, garlic, dried herbs, and paprika) under the skin to keep the breast meat juicy and flavorful, then brush a micro-thin sheen of seasoned oil over the outside for beautifully crispy skin. Gently massage the butter through the skin to distribute it evenly, and dab the oil over the buttered areas, so you don’t accidentally move the butter out of place.
  2. Dry brine if you have the time. You don’t have to, but it makes a massive difference! Unlike a wet brine that waterlogs the skin, a dry brine uses salt to chemically restructure the meat proteins so they trap and hold onto their own natural juices while roasting. Plus, letting it sit uncovered in the fridge pulls surface moisture away, which is the absolute secret to getting that addictively crispy skin. Short on time? Just skip Steps 4 and 5 in my recipe below. The compound butter will still give your turkey plenty of flavor (promise!)
  3. Use a meat thermometer. Roasting times vary depending on your turkey’s size and the pan you use, so I’ve included weight-based guidelines in the recipe card below to help you plan ahead. I highly recommend an electronic probe thermometer so you can monitor the temperature without opening the oven.
  4. DON’T baste your turkey! Every time you open the oven door to baste, you let out heat, extending the cooking time. Pouring pan juices over the skin also adds moisture, which ruins all the effort you put into getting that skin bone-dry and shatteringly crisp. Trust the compound butter under the skin to do its job. If the breast or drumsticks start getting too dark before the turkey reaches temperature, tent them loosely with aluminum foil so they can finish cooking without overbrowning.
  5. Pull the turkey at 157-160°F and let carryover heat finish the cooking. Avoid touching bone with your thermometer, as this can skew the reading. As the turkey rests, the internal temperature continues rising, bringing it to a safe 165°F. Before carving, I always double-check three places with an instant-read thermometer: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh, and the innermost part of the wing. All three must reach at least 165°F before serving. If not, let it rest a little longer and check again.
  6. Save those pan juices, too! Don’t throw away the flavorful juices and drippings left in your roasting pan, either. Save them to make a delicious homemade turkey gravy.
  7. Short on time? Break down your turkey first. Cutting your turkey into individual pieces before roasting can help it cook much faster than leaving it whole. If you’re pressed for time on Thanksgiving Day, check out Melissa’s video on breaking down a whole chicken (also below!) for a helpful demonstration. You can use the same basic technique for turkey, but remember that cooking times will vary depending on the size of the pieces.

Budget-Saving Tips for Feeding a Smaller Crowd

A whole turkey is actually one of the most economical ways to feed your family this Thanksgiving. I recently spotted frozen whole turkeys at Walmart for just $0.84 per pound, which is an incredible deal. If you have the time and freezer space, all that extra meat can be put to good use in soups, sandwiches, casseroles, and more over the following days (I’ve shared some leftover ideas below!).

However, if you’re only feeding a few people, don’t want a fridge full of leftovers, or simply want to skip roasting a whole bird, you can still enjoy those same delicious holiday flavors with our roasted turkey breast or swap to turkey drumsticks instead.

You can use the exact same aromatics, butter-under-the-skin technique, and dry-spice profile as my whole turkey recipe below, just adapted for dark meat turkey drumsticks!

Check out our baked chicken drumsticks recipe for the full step-by-step technique, then make these easy adjustments for turkey:

  • Spices and fats: Keep the ingredients identical! Use the same compound butter tucked under the skin and the seasoning oil blend (canola oil, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and ground mustard) brushed over the exterior.
  • Temperature and time: Because turkey drumsticks are significantly larger than chicken legs, roast them at 350°F for roughly 1 hour-1 hour 15 minutes, flipping them halfway through.
  • Target temperature: Use your digital thermometer and pull them when the thickest part hits 165°F (or ideally 175°F so all that collagen in the dark meat melts into tender, succulent meat).

How many turkey legs do I need?

  • 1 turkey leg per adult (or 1 leg per big eater).
  • 1 turkey leg per 2 young children (or smaller appetites).

What to Serve with Roasted Turkey

Roasted turkey might be the main event, but it’s nothing without all the classic Thanksgiving fixings. Creamy mashed potatoes and plenty of turkey gravy are a must, especially for serving alongside the leaner white meat. Cranberry sauce (or my cranberry relish for something a little fresher) helps balance all those rich flavors, while sausage stuffing brings plenty of herbs and comforting holiday flavor to the plate. I’d also add a side of green beans, for something easy and colorful, and a classic sweet potato casserole for a little sweetness. Of course, there’s always room for more family favorites!

To make Thanksgiving Day easier, I like to make the cranberry sauce ahead of time and get any sides (like stuffing and sweet potato casserole) prepped in advance. The green beans and gravy can be made while the turkey rests. For more affordable holiday dishes and help planning your menu, check out my recent holiday guide.

Got Leftovers?

Once you’ve removed the meat from the bones, refrigerate any leftovers in shallow, airtight containers within 2 hours. It’ll keep in the fridge for 3-4 days, or you can freeze it in portions for up to 3 months. Reheat leftovers in the microwave, skillet, or oven until they reach 165°F.

However, leftover turkey is also delicious cold! My family loves a good turkey sandwich with leftover cranberry sauce and stuffing, or you can tuck it between toasted bread with a little mayo and whatever salad ingredients you’ve got on hand. It’s also perfect for making meals over the next few days. Use it to make a turkey pot pie, swap it for shredded chicken in your favorite recipes, or make a big pot of turkey noodle soup (recipe coming soon!).

Print Add to Collection Go to Collections

Thanksgiving Turkey Recipe

From thawing to carving, this juicy Thanksgiving Turkey recipe walks you through the whole bird, with an optional dry brine for extra-crispy skin. Course Main Course Cuisine American Total Cost $14.07 recipe / $1.76 serving Prep Time 1 day day Cook Time 3 hours hours 15 minutes minutes Resting Time 30 minutes minutes Total Time 1 day day 3 hours hours 45 minutes minutes Servings 8 servings Calories 739 kcal Author Jess Rice

Equipment

  • Electronic Probe Thermometer
  • Large Baking Sheet with Rack
  • Gloves

Ingredients

  • 12-14 lbs. whole turkey with giblets, (mine was 13.72lbs) $11.52*

Optional Dry Brine

  • 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s Kosher Salt see important salt notes below!! $0.05**

Compound Butter (Under the Skin)

  • 2 sticks unsalted butter room temperature, (1 cup) $1.48
  • 4 garlic cloves pressed or finely minced, (about 1 Tbsp) $0.24
  • ½ tsp ground black pepper $0.09
  • 1½ tsp dried rosemary $0.18
  • 1 tsp dried thyme $0.12
  • ½ tsp rubbed sage $0.07
  • ½ tsp paprika $0.02

Seasoning Oil (On Top of the Turkey)

  • 1½ Tbsp canola oil $0.06***
  • ½ tsp ground black pepper $0.09
  • 1 tsp garlic powder $0.05
  • 1 tsp onion powder $0.05
  • ½ tsp paprika $0.02
  • ¼ tsp ground mustard powder $0.03

Instructions

  • Safely Thaw (3 to 4 Days Ahead): Make sure to start defrosting your whole turkey in the refrigerator, unopened, on a rimmed tray at least 3 to 4 full days before the day you plan to eat it. Start thawing on Sunday or Monday morning if you plan to dry-brine on Wednesday.
  • Unwrap & Trim: Once thawed, unwrap the turkey and remove the neck and giblets from the cavities. Using kitchen shears, trim away the excess neck skin and tail fat. Pour out any pooled juices from the cavity.
  • Pat Bone-Dry: Thoroughly dab the entire turkey inside and out with clean paper towels until completely dry. You should also dab underneath the skin of the turkey dry; the space between the breast meat and the skin. Transfer the bird to a wire rack set inside your large baking sheet or roasting pan. Tuck the turkey’s wings behind it’s back in preparation for when it goes in the oven (this keeps the wings from burning!).
  • (If you're planning to dry brine your turkey, read on. If you are skipping the dry brine, go to Step 6!) Apply the Dry Brine: Measure out 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp of Morton’s Kosher Salt (using Morton's ensures accurate salinity). Rub ½ tsp inside the cavity, ½ tsp under the breast skin directly onto the meat, and the remaining salt evenly over the exterior skin.
  • Air-Chill Uncovered (optional, if dry brining): Make sure the skin is covering the breast meat again and place the bird back in your refrigerator uncovered for 12-24 hours (overnight is ideal). This dehydrates the outer skin so it bakes up nice and crisp.
  • Mix Compound Butter: Combine the room temperature/softened unsalted butter, pressed garlic, black pepper, rosemary, thyme, sage, and paprika in a bowl using a fork until mostly smooth.
  • Mix Seasoning Oil: In a small cup, stir together the canola oil, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and ground mustard to create your "seasoning salt" exterior paste.
  • Apply Compound Butter Under the Skin: Take the turkey out 30 minutes before roasting to take the chill off. Gently slide your fingers under the breast and thigh skin to loosen pockets. Divide your compound butter in half, pushing half deep under the left breast/thigh and half under the right. Then, massage gently through the skin with clean, dry hands from the outside (on top of the skin) to distribute.
  • Brush Exterior with Oil: Using a pastry brush, gently apply a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil mixture all over the outside skin (drumsticks, wings, and exterior). Dab gently over the buttered areas so you don't displace the butter.
  • Insert the probe thermometer into the thickest part of the turkey breast that will be facing the oven door. This way, the cable will be closest to the door and the screen showing you the temperature can neatly rest on a countertop. I highly recommend you use a probe thermometer to avoid a dry turkey breast!
  • Roast to Perfection: Roast your unstuffed bird at 350°F for roughly 2-2 ½ hours for a sheet pan with wire rack, or 2½-3 hours if using a high-sided roasting pan. Pull the bird when an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the breast reads 157°F-160°F. The breast will hit 165°F via carryover heat while resting on the counter, rather than needing to hit 165°F inside the oven. Let the turkey rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes before carving to let internal juices settle as carryover heat finishes bringing it to temperature.

See how we calculate recipe costs here.

Notes

* Buying your turkey. Walmart had the lowest price I found, so that’s where I bought my frozen turkey. Frozen is usually the cheapest option, just make sure to plan ahead and give it time to thaw in the fridge. If there’s a turkey farm near you and it fits your budget, buying directly is a nice way to support a local farmer, too! To ensure your turkey cooks to juicy perfection without undercooking larger birds or drying out smaller ones, here’s how the total cook time scales based on the 13-15 minute per pound guideline (unstuffed, roasted at 350°F):
  • For a 12 lb Turkey: 2 hours 45 minutes to 3 hours
    (begin temping the turkey at the 2 hour mark to avoid overcooking)
  • For a 13 lb Turkey: 3 hours to 3 hours 15 minutes
    (begin temping the turkey at the 2 hour 15 minute mark to avoid overcooking)
  • For a 14 lb Turkey: 3 hours 15 minutes to 3 hours 30 minutes
    (begin temping the turkey at the 2 hour, 30 minute hour mark to avoid overcooking)
Always rely on an instant-read meat thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the breast reading 157°F-160°F rather than strictly relying on the clock! I highly recommend you purchase a probe thermometer, which will be placed before the bird goes in the oven. This just about guarantees a perfectly cooked turkey! When temping your turkey, check three key spots: Use a meat thermometer to confirm your turkey has reached at least 165°F in all 3 of these places after it has rested, before carving:
  1. Thickest part of the breast (I leave the probe thermometer in as it rests so I can see when it hits 165°F)
  2. Innermost part of the thigh
  3. Innermost part of the wing
Avoid touching bone, fat, or gristle, or you will likely get a false read (touching bone accidentally typically reads higher, making you think it’s done before the turkey actually is!) **To ensure your turkey is seasoned across that 12-14 lb range without over-salting the smaller birds or under-salting the larger ones, here is how the Morton’s Kosher Salt scales based on the ½ tsp per pound of turkey guideline:
  • For a 12 lb Turkey: 2 Tablespoons (6 tsp total)
  • For a 13 lb Turkey: 2 Tbsp + ½ tsp (6.5 tsp total)
  • For a 14 lb Turkey: 2 Tbsp + 1 tsp (7 tsp total)
If you are strictly watching your salt intake, you can scale this back to ¼ tsp per pound and you will still see decent dry brining results. I only have table salt; what do I do? Cut your volume measure in half! Table salt has tiny, ultra-fine crystals that pack tightly together, making it twice as dense as Morton’s and nearly three times as dense as Diamond Crystal. For a 12-14 lb turkey, following the ½ tsp/lb rate: use 3 to 3.5 teaspoons total of table salt. If you’re watching your salt intake, go for a ¼ tsp/lb rate: 1.5 to 1.75 teaspoons total of table salt. ***Any neutral, high smoke-point oil will do, such as vegetable, peanut, or avocado oil. I experienced the best results using canola oil. Plus, it’s easy on the wallet! Equipment Needed: E lectronic Probe Thermometer, a l arge baking sheet with a rack that fits inside, and g loves (trust me). The listed prep and cook times are based on my 13.72 lb turkey with the optional dry brining for 24 hours. Roasting times will vary depending on the size of your turkey, your oven, and the roasting pan used. You’ll also need to allow 3-4 days for thawing a frozen turkey in the refrigerator. Please note that the nutrition information below is an estimate and includes the full amount of butter. Some of that butter melts into the pan drippings as the turkey roasts, so the calories and fat per serving may be lower if you serve the turkey without the drippings.

Nutrition

Serving: 1 serving | Calories: 739 kcal | Carbohydrates: 1 g | Protein: 103 g | Fat: 34 g | Sodium: 977 mg | Fiber: 0.2 g

how to make Thanksgiving Turkey step-by-step photos

Gather your turkey ingredients: This recipe is designed for a 12-14 lb whole turkey. Mine weighed 13.72 lbs. If you’re planning to dry brine your turkey, you’ll also need 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s kosher salt. Allow 3-4 days for your turkey to thaw in the refrigerator. Keep it unopened on a rimmed tray to catch any drips. If you’re dry brining, count back from the day you plan to brine.

Gather your compound butter ingredients: You’ll need 2 sticks (1 cup) unsalted butter, 4 cloves garlic (pressed or finely minced, about 1 Tbsp), ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1½ tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, and ½ tsp paprika. Make sure your butter is softened to room temperature so it’s easy to combine with the seasonings and spread underneath the turkey skin.

Gather your seasoning oil ingredients: You’ll need 1½ Tbsp canola oil, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, ½ tsp paprika, and ¼ tsp ground mustard. This mixture goes on the outside of the turkey to help create the best crispy skin.

Unwrap, trim, and pat dry: Once your turkey is completely thawed, remove the neck and giblets from the cavities. Use kitchen shears to trim away any excess neck skin and tail fat, then pour out any pooled juices. Pat the turkey thoroughly dry inside and out with clean paper towels. Place it breast-side up on a wire rack set inside a large rimmed baking sheet or roasting pan.

This is what the neck and giblets bag looks like. You can throw them away, or save them for stock (see the ‘Don’t Waste a Thing!’ section below).

Tuck the wings underneath: Fold the turkey’s wings back behind its body so the tips are tucked underneath. This helps protect them from burning while the turkey roasts.

Gently loosen the skin: Carefully slide your fingers underneath the skin covering the breasts and thighs, separating it from the meat to create pockets. Work slowly so you don’t tear the skin. This creates space for the optional dry brine and the compound butter we’ll add later.

Dry underneath the skin, too: Gently lift the loosened breast skin and use clean paper towels to dab away any moisture between the skin and the meat. The drier you can get the skin, the better it’ll crisp up in the oven.

(OPTIONAL) Apply the dry brine: Measure out 1 Tbsp + 1 tsp Morton’s kosher salt. Rub ½ tsp inside the cavity, ½ tsp directly onto the breast meat underneath the skin, and distribute the remaining salt evenly over the exterior skin. Make sure the salt is spread across the turkey rather than concentrated in one area. If you’re skipping the dry brine, go straight to making the compound butter.

Refrigerate uncovered for 12-24 hours (optional): Pull the skin back over the breast meat and return the turkey to the refrigerator on its wire rack, uncovered. Overnight is ideal! The photo above is my turkey after dry brining for 24 hours. Notice how much drier the skin looks after resting in the fridge? That’s exactly what we’re after. The salt helps season the meat while the uncovered refrigeration draws moisture away from the surface, giving you extra-crispy skin once roasted.

Make the compound butter: In a bowl, combine 2 sticks (1 cup) softened unsalted butter, 4 pressed or finely minced garlic cloves (about 1 Tbsp), ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1½ tsp dried rosemary, 1 tsp dried thyme, ½ tsp rubbed sage, and ½ tsp paprika. Mash everything together with a fork until mostly smooth, and the herbs and seasonings are distributed throughout the butter.

Mix the seasoning oil: In a small cup or bowl, stir together 1½ Tbsp canola oil, ½ tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp onion powder, ½ tsp paprika, and ¼ tsp ground mustard. Stir until the spices are evenly mixed into the oil to create a thin, speckled seasoning paste.

Add the butter underneath the breast skin: Take your turkey out of the refrigerator 30 minutes before roasting to take the chill off. Divide the compound butter into two equal portions, one for each side of the turkey. Gently push the softened butter deep underneath the loosened breast skin, directly onto the meat, working some of each portion toward the thighs.

Work the butter underneath the thigh skin: Continue distributing the compound butter into the pockets underneath the thigh skin on both sides. This helps season the dark meat as well as the breast, so you’re not keeping all that delicious garlicky, herbaceous flavor in one area.

Massage the butter into place. With clean, dry hands (or you can wear gloves, if preferred), gently massage the turkey from the outside, pressing through the skin to distribute the butter underneath. Aim for an even coating across the breast and thigh meat without tearing the skin.

Brush with the seasoning oil: Using a pastry brush, apply a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil mixture all over the turkey’s exterior, including the drumsticks and wings. Dab gently over the buttered areas rather than brushing aggressively so you don’t displace the butter underneath the skin. You want a thin, even coating, not a thick layer of oil.

Insert your thermometer and roast: Preheat your oven to 350°F. Insert an electronic probe thermometer into the thickest part of the breast facing the oven door, keeping the probe away from the bone. Positioning it this way keeps the cable close to the door and the temperature display conveniently on your countertop. Roast the unstuffed turkey at 350°F for roughly 2-2½ hours on a baking sheet with a wire rack, or 2½-3 hours in a high-sided roasting pan.

Remove the turkey when the thickest part of the breast reads 157-160°F. The temperature will continue rising during the resting period. I highly recommend using a probe thermometer rather than relying on cooking time alone!

Save those pan juices for gravy: Once roasted, don’t throw away all those flavorful juices left in the roasting pan. Carefully collect them after removing the turkey from the oven and save them for homemade gravy. Follow our turkey gravy recipe to turn those drippings into a rich, savory gravy to serve alongside your Thanksgiving dinner.

Rest and check the temperature: Let your turkey rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes before carving. During this time, carryover heat continues cooking the turkey and the juices settle back into the meat. Before serving, use an instant-read thermometer to double-check three places: the thickest part of the breast, the innermost part of the thigh, and the innermost part of the wing. All three must reach at least 165°F, without the thermometer touching bone. Once your turkey has reached a safe temperature and finished resting, it’s ready to serve…

Now Carve Your Roasted Turkey

  • Remove the drumsticks. Bend each drumstick away from the body and gently separate it, one at a time. (Photos 1 and 2)
  • Separate the thighs. Pop the hip joints, then carefully use a knife to separate both thighs from the body. (Photos 3 and 4)
  • Remove the wings. Pull away both wings, using a knife to separate them at the joints. You can also cut them into drumettes if you prefer. (Photos 5 and 6)
  • Carve the first breast. Find the breastbone and make your first cut about 1 cm to one side. Follow the curve of the ribs as you gently pull the breast away. (Photos 7 and 8)
  • Repeat on the other side. Cut along the other side of the breastbone, then follow the rib cage and cut underneath where the wing was attached to free the second breast. (Photos 9, 10, and 11)
  • Arrange the turkey for serving. Set both breasts on a platter with the drumsticks, thighs, and wings. Slice the breast meat just before serving. Enjoy! (Photo 12 and photo below)

Don’t Waste a Thing!

I use a whole turkey for this recipe and remove the neck and giblets before roasting. You can discard them if you like, or put them to work while the turkey’s in the oven:

  1. Use the giblets for gravy: Unwrap the giblets and put the neck, heart, and gizzard in a saucepan with 1 chopped onion, 1 carrot, and 1 celery rib. Add enough water to cover and simmer for 45 mins-1 hour. Leave out the liver for a milder broth. Strain and use the broth in place of the chicken broth to make your turkey gravy.
  2. Save the carcass for stock: For a deeper roasted flavor, lightly oil the bones and roast them on a rimmed baking sheet at 450°F for about 30 mins, until well browned. Check them early if they’re already quite dark. Chill the roasted bones, then pack them in a freezer bag and freeze for later (up to 3 months). If you skip the optional extra roast, refrigerate or freeze the bones within 2 hours of cooking. Thaw frozen bones in the fridge when you’re ready to make stock.
  3. Make the stock on the stove or in a slow cooker: Add the turkey carcass, 1 large onion, 2 carrots, 3 celery ribs, and 1-2 bay leaves if you have them to a soup pot or crockpot. Roughly chop the vegetables and add enough water to just cover everything. Simmer gently on the stove for 2-3 hours, or cook on High for at least 6 hours using the method in our slow cooker chicken broth guide. Strain the stock and use it for soups or gravy.

Roasted Turkey FAQ’s

If a question comes up halfway through prep, you can jump straight to the answer here:

My Turkey is still frozen! Help!

Don’t panic! Do the cold-water emergency thaw. Keep the turkey in its original leak-proof wrapper and submerge it breast-side down in a clean sink or tub filled completely with cold tap water. Swap the water out every 30 minutes so it stays safe and ice-cold. It takes about 30 minutes per pound, so a 12-14 lb bird will take 6 to 7 hours to thaw completely. If it’s just icy inside the cavity, run cold tap water through the center to break up internal ice chunks, then dab every inch bone-dry before seasoning!

(And hey, if you’re realizing this the night before Thanksgiving, set your alarm. For a 4:00 PM dinner, you’ll need to kick off that cold-water bath by 4:00 or 5:00 AM sharp to give it those 6-7 hours!)

My turkey is starting to look too dark on top; what can I do?

Tent it loosely with a sheet of aluminum foil! If the top of the breast or the tips of the drumsticks are getting deeply browned before the center reaches temp, shield them with a piece of foil folded into a light dome over the bird. This deflects direct heat while allowing the oven’s ambient heat to finish cooking the inside.

Should I trust the pop-up turkey button to tell me when it’s done?

No! Toss it out and use an instant-read meat thermometer! Those little plastic pop-up timers are notoriously unreliable. They operate on a meltable metal alloy set to trip at around 180°F, meaning by the time it pops, your breast meat is already overcooked, dry, and chalky. Instead, insert a digital thermometer into the thickest part of the breast (without touching bone) and pull the bird at 157°F-160°F. Carryover heat will bring it up to a safe 165°F while resting.

Standard USDA roasting charts recommend 3-3 ¾ hours at 325°F for an unstuffed 12-14 lb turkey in a traditional high-sided roasting pan. They outline why you should never roast a turkey at a temperature below 325°F here. (Hello, Danger Zone!)

At 350°F (as I use in this recipe), standard estimates are 2-2 ½ hours for a sheet pan with a wire rack, or 2 ½–3 hours if using a high-sided roasting pan. If you are cooking your bird in a roasting pan with high sides, start checking your bird at the 2½ hour mark. I can’t stress enough how much of a difference having an electronic probe thermometer inserted into the breast meat while the turkey is in the oven will help ensure your bird comes out PERFECT.

Why 2-2 ½ hours worked for us

  • Baking Sheet with Wire Rack: Cooking on a flat baking sheet with a wire rack allows hot air to circulate freely around the entire bird, cooking it significantly faster than a traditional high-walled roasting pan that traps steam and shields the sides.
  • Dry Brining & Air-Chilling: Drying out the skin and outer layer of meat speeds up heat transfer and skin crisping.
  • Targeting 157°F-160°F: Pulling the bird at 157°F-160°F (rather than waiting for 165°F in the oven) reduces total oven time by 15-25 minutes, relying on carryover cooking during the rest. This results in a super juicy, perfectly cooked turkey.

Do I have to brine my turkey?

No, you don’t have to, but it makes a massive difference. Just leave out Steps 4 and 5 if you decide not to. Skipping the brine won’t ruin your dinner, especially since you’re using our rich compound butter under the skin. But taking the time to salt the bird beforehand seasons the meat all the way to the bone and gives you that extra layer of flavor and moisture.

Wet Brine vs. Dry Brine: What’s the Difference?

  • Dry Brine: Gives you concentrated, deep turkey flavor, incredibly juicy meat, and shatteringly crisp, golden skin because the fridge air dehydrates the surface. It’s low-effort and takes up minimal fridge space.
  • Wet Brine: Plumps the meat up with extra water weight which does help it cook up juicy, but leaves the skin wet, rubbery, and soggy (making it really hard to get a good crisp). It also requires a giant bucket, gallons of water, ice, and a massive chunk of your refrigerator shelf.

Why rest before carving?

Because carving too soon empties all that hard-earned moisture onto your cutting board. During roasting, heat pushes juices into the center of the meat. Letting the bird rest uncovered for 30-45 minutes lets the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb those juices so every slice stays amazingly juicy. Plus, carryover heat gently finishes cooking the center to a safe 165°F without drying out the outer layers.

Storage & Reheating

If you haven’t already, remove the leftover turkey from the bones (see the above carving guidance), slice or chop it into smaller pieces, and refrigerate it in shallow, airtight containers within 2 hours of cooking (or 1 hour if it’s above 90°F). Keep the turkey at 40°F or below and use it within 3-4 days. Store any leftover gravy and sides separately.

Reheating

I’d warm only what you plan to serve. Add a splash of broth or water to keep the turkey from drying out, especially the lean breast meat. For several servings, cover the turkey with foil and warm it in a 325°F oven. For a few slices, use a covered skillet over medium heat or a microwave-safe dish with a vented cover. If you microwave it, turn the pieces partway through and let them stand briefly before checking the temperature in a few spots.

Whichever method you use, reheat the turkey to 165°F throughout. The skin will soften in the fridge and stay soft when reheated covered. If you want to crisp it back up, give the reheated pieces a quick sear skin-side down in a lightly oiled skillet.

Freezing

Freeze sliced or shredded roast turkey in meal-sized portions for up to 3 months for best texture. Press the air out of freezer bags, label them with the date, and freeze them flat so they thaw more evenly in the fridge. The meat can lose a little moisture as it thaws, so the breast may be slightly drier after reheating, and the skin will lose its crunch. A splash of broth helps when reheating, or you can use the thawed meat in soup or pot pie.

Thanksgiving Eve to Thanksgiving Day Schedule (For a 4:00 PM Dinner)

Here’s a play-by-play schedule to help you get your bird ready for the big day with minimal stress. Download it here, print it out, and stick it on your fridge so you know what to do and when.

Monday

Make sure your bird goes into the fridge by Sunday or Monday morning so it is 100% thawed by Wednesday morning!

If you are planning to do a 12-24 hour dry brine, make sure it’sfully thawedon Wednesday. (Still frozen the night before Thanksgiving? Refer to our emergency cold-water thaw guide above and make sure you start by 4:00 AM! Set your alarm!).

Wednesday (The Day Before Thanksgiving – Morning/Early Afternoon):

  • Prep: Unwrap the turkey, remove the neck and giblets, trim any excess neck skin, and pat every single inch dry with clean paper towels.
  • Dry Brine & Refrigerate (optional): Apply your kosher salt (a little inside, a little under the breast skin, and all over the exterior, see recipe for amounts). Place the bird on a wire rack set inside a rimmed sheet pan and put it uncovered on the bottom shelf of the fridge overnight. If you’re skipping the dry brine, leave the turkey wrapped in the fridge and do the prep on Thursday.

Thursday (Thanksgiving Day): 10:45 AM (5.25 Hours Before 4pm Dinner):

Take the turkey out of the fridge and let it sit at room temperature for at least 30 minutes to take off the chill. (Not to exceed 2 hours at room temperature! Perishable raw poultry should never sit in the temperature “Danger Zone”, 40°F to 140°F, for more than 2 total hours, as surface bacteria can multiply rapidly.)

Mix your room-temperature compound butter and your exterior seasoning oils. Set aside.

11:15 AM (4.75 Hours Before Dinner):

Preheat your oven to 350°F. Slide the compound butter under the skin of the breasts and thighs. Brush a micro-thin sheen of the seasoning oil over the outside.

11:45 AM (4.25 Hours Before Dinner):

Place the turkey on a rack in your roasting pan or sheet pan and slide it into the oven.

2:15 PM (1.75 Hours Before Dinner – Check Temp):

Check the internal temperature with your probe thermometer or digital instant-read. For a 13-14 lb bird, it should be getting close! Crucial rule: Pull the bird the moment the thickest part of the breast hits 157°F-160°F (the thighs will be around 175°F). If the top is getting too dark before the temp is reached, loosely tent a piece of foil over the breast (but not tightly touching the breast or the skin may tear when you remove the foil!)

2:45 PM (Target Pull Time):

Transfer the turkey from the oven to your cutting board once the breast hits 157°F-160°F.

2:45 PM – 3:30 PM (The Rest):

Let it rest uncovered on the counter for 30-45 minutes so the juices settle and the internal temperature rises safely to 165°F.

3:30 PM – 4:00 PM (Final Check & Carving): Use your instant-read thermometer to double-check that all three key spots (breast, thigh, and wing) have reached at least 165°F.

4:00 PM: Carve and serve your perfectly juicy, crispy-skinned turkey!

More Ways to Use Leftover Turkey

  • If I’m feeding a crowd again the next day, I’d make a tray of Turkey Sliders with cranberry sauce, melty Swiss, and buttery Hawaiian rolls.
  • Give leftovers a completely different flavor with our three-bean Turkey Chili. Sauté the vegetables first, then stir in shredded roast turkey near the end of simmering in place of the ground turkey and heat it through to 165°F.
  • When there’s a little bit of everything left, tuck the turkey, stuffing, and mashed potatoes into crescent dough for a golden Holiday Leftovers Wreath.
  • For a quick lunch for one, crisp up a Thanksgiving Leftovers Tortilla Wrap filled with turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and melty brie.

SOURCES (USDA Food Safety):

  • USDA Refrigerator Thawing Guidelines: You can read the official instructions on the USDA FSIS Turkey Basics: Safe Thawing Page, which outlines the requirement of roughly 24 hours of defrost time for every 4 to 5 pounds of turkey (requiring 3 to 4 full days for a 12–16 lb bird) kept unopened on a tray to prevent cross-contamination.
  • USDA: Let’s Talk Turkey: You can see the three ways to safely thaw frozen turkey.
  • USDA Safe Handling & Tray Protocols: Check out USDA FSIS — Your Safe Thanksgiving Guide, which confirms keeping raw poultry sealed in its original wrapper and using a rimmed dish or container to catch leaking juices during refrigerator defrosting.
  • The USDA “Danger Zone” Rule (40°F–140°F): You can read the official guidelines on the USDA FSIS “Danger Zone” Page, which explains how bacteria grow rapidly between 40°F and 140°F and why perishable foods (like raw poultry) can sit out at room temperature for up to two hours during prep.
  • The USDA 2-Hour Rule: For specific Q&A details, check the USDA AskFSIS 2-Hour Rule Entry, which confirms the strict 2-hour limit for leaving perishable foods out of refrigeration before cooking or serving.

issues.title: Sweet Potato Recipes
issues.summary: Looking for new ways to cook sweet potatoes? Try these 13 easy sweet potato recipes, including creamy soup, one-pan dinners, fries, and more! The post Sweet Potato Recipes appeared first on Budget Bytes .
issues.author: Jess Rice
issues.content_html:
You gotta love a vegetable that can sit next to a burger as fries and then turn up in pie for dessert! Sweet potatoes are so much more than a Thanksgiving side, and they earn their place in my kitchen all year long. You can roast them until caramelized, blend them into silky soup, or use them to stretch a skillet dinner a little further. I’ve gathered 13 easy sweet potato recipes that put this affordable, filling ingredient to work, with a few holiday favorites for good measure! If you’ve got regular potatoes to use up, don’t miss our potato recipes roundup for even more ideas.

Classic Sweet Potato Recipes

Some days I want to make something cozy from scratch; other days, I want dinner to involve little more than a sheet pan and some salt. These classics cover both, with creamy soup, simple baked potatoes, fries, and a few sweeter options in the mix.

1. Baked Sweet Potatoes

Baked Sweet Potatoes

Baked sweet potatoes are an easy and inexpensive way to bulk up any meal. Serve them as a side dish or as the base to your favorite meal! 4.50 from 6 votes $7.33 recipe / $1.83 serving Get the Recipe

Sometimes, butter, salt, and pepper are all a baked sweet potato needs. But I also love how easy it is to dress one up with black beans, leftover chili, or whatever needs using in the fridge. They’re filling, inexpensive, and take just five minutes of hands-on prep. Short on time? Partially cooking them in the microwave before baking can cut the oven time down considerably.

2. Sweet Potato Soup

Creamy Sweet Potato Soup

This luxurious and creamy sweet potato soup features warm spices and oven roasted sweet potatoes for maximum flavor and natural sweetness. 5 from 10 votes $5.91 recipe / $1.47 serving Get the Recipe

I’m all for a quick stovetop soup, but roasting the sweet potatoes first is worth the extra step in this creamy sweet potato soup. It brings out their natural sweetness, which pairs well with the cumin, smoked paprika, cinnamon, and a little cayenne. Everything gets blended until silky smooth and finished with a splash of heavy cream (coconut milk works too!). At around $1.47 per serving, this is some seriously affordable comfort food.

3. Roasted Sweet Potatoes

Roasted Sweet Potatoes

These easy Roasted Sweet Potatoes turn tender, naturally sweet, and deliciously caramelized in the oven. You only need 3 ingredients and about 40 minutes! 5 from 5 votes $2.63 recipe / $0.66 serving Get the Recipe

Three ingredients and a hot sheet pan. That’s all you need for these beautifully caramelized roasted sweet potatoes! I preheat the baking sheet to give the cubes a head start on browning, then roast them until the edges are golden and the centers are soft and creamy. No parboiling, no complicated seasonings, and just $0.66 per serving. They’re delicious straight from the oven, but I also like adding leftovers to salads and grain bowls.

4. Air Fryer Sweet Potato Fries

Air Fryer Sweet Potato Fries

These 3-ingredient Air Fryer Sweet Potato Fries combine natural sweetness with a spicy Creole seasoning kick for a super tasty and easy to make side dish! 5 from 7 votes $2.01 recipe / $1.00 serving Get the Recipe

I always appreciate a side dish that only needs a few ingredients and doesn’t take over the oven. These air fryer sweet potato fries are tossed with olive oil and Creole seasoning for a sweet, salty, slightly spicy flavor that goes really well with burgers and sandwiches. They’re thicker and more tender than traditional fries rather than super crispy, but that makes them especially good for dipping into a little creamy comeback sauce.

5. Twice-Baked Sweet Potatoes

Twice Baked Sweet Potatoes

Twice Baked Sweet Potatoes makes any meal extra special. They’re perfectly cooked and topped with warm & cozy toppings! 5 from 3 votes $11.11 recipe / $2.77 serving Get the Recipe

A regular baked sweet potato is delicious, but sometimes you want to dress things up a little. For these twice-baked sweet potatoes, scoop out the fluffy insides and mash them with butter, brown sugar, cinnamon, nutmeg, and vanilla before putting them back in their skins and topping with marshmallows and homemade candied pecans. My advice? Make the pecans ahead so there’s one less thing to do when you’re ready to serve.

6. Sweet Potato Hash

Sweet Potato Hash

This easy, one-skillet Sweet Potato Hash is the perfect balance of sweet and savory flavors and hearty ingredients. It's great for breakfast, lunch or dinner! 4.69 from 16 votes $6.94 recipe / $1.15 serving Get the Recipe

This sweet potato hash brings together diced sweet potatoes, savory breakfast sausage, peppers, and onions in one hearty skillet. It’s delicious with a fried egg on top, but there’s plenty here to make a satisfying breakfast or brunch on its own. You get six servings from one skillet, making this a handy recipe for feeding a crowd or getting ahead on breakfasts for the week.

Hearty and Budget-Friendly Dinners

Sweet potatoes make a very convincing case for stretching dinner, especially when they’re paired with beans, pasta, or ground meat. These three meals have enough going on to stand alone, with plenty of savory spices to balance out the potatoes’ natural sweetness.

7. Sweet Potato Ground Turkey Skillet

Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet

This easy Sweet Potato and Ground Turkey Skillet cooks turkey, sweet potato, kale, and Parmesan-coated orzo in one pan for a practical weeknight dinner! 4.63 from 8 votes $9.07 recipe / $2.27 serving Get the Recipe

Ground turkey gets a serious flavor upgrade in this sweet potato and ground turkey skillet! Thyme, sage, and smoked paprika season the turkey and vegetables, while orzo cooks right in the same pan, soaking up the flavorful broth. A handful of kale and some Parmesan finish things off, giving you four generous servings in about 40 minutes. I particularly appreciate that the pasta cooks alongside everything else (saving another pot from the washing up!)

8. Sweet Potato Black Bean Skillet

Sweet Potato Black Bean Skillet

This Sweet Potato Black Bean skillet is a fun, budget-friendly, and veggie packed meal with lots of flavor and is perfect for meal prep! 4.48 from 38 votes $7.44 recipe / $1.86 serving Get the Recipe

This sweet potato black bean skillet is a hearty, naturally vegan dinner that comes together in about 25 minutes. The sweet potatoes are browned in the skillet to bring out their natural sweetness, then combined with black beans, bell pepper, kale, tomatoes, and a smoky blend of spices. I like serving this over rice to make it even more filling, and the leftovers are ideal for meal prep!

9. Sweet Potato Chili

Chorizo Sweet Potato Chili

This Chorizo Sweet Potato Chili is the perfect mix of spicy sausage and sweet, creamy sweet potatoes. Easy, filling, and delicious! 4.85 from 40 votes $9.59 recipe / $1.60 serving Get the Recipe

There’s a very good reason this sweet potato chili doesn’t need a long list of seasonings. Mexican chorizo already brings plenty of smoky, spicy flavor to the pot! Tender sweet potatoes balance that heat, while inexpensive canned beans help turn it into six filling servings on a budget. Add your favorite chili toppings, grab some tortilla chips, and dinner is sorted. Leftovers freeze well, too.

Thanksgiving Sweet Potato Favorites

I have a soft spot for the classics at Thanksgiving, and sweet potatoes are responsible for some of the best ones. This little lineup includes a crunchy-topped casserole, a creamy homemade pie, and two delicious breads worth making room for. Better still, they all use familiar ingredients and won’t send your holiday grocery bill through the roof.

10. Sweet Potato Casserole

Sweet Potato Casserole

Classic Southern Sweet Potato Casserole made with creamy mashed sweet potatoes and a crunchy pecan streusel topping. A Thanksgiving favorite! 4.67 from 12 votes $7.47 Recipe / $0.94 Serving Get the Recipe

I’m not saying a crunchy pecan streusel is better than marshmallows, but it makes a pretty strong case! Underneath that buttery topping, this sweet potato casserole has a fluffy, lightly spiced filling made with mashed sweet potatoes, cinnamon, vanilla, and brown sugar. It makes eight servings for less than a dollar each, which is pretty impressive for a classic Thanksgiving side dish. And you only need about 40 minutes from start to finish!

11. Sweet Potato Pie

Sweet Potato Pie

If you’re looking for an affordable homemade dessert to finish your Thanksgiving meal, don’t overlook sweet potato pie. Baking the sweet potatoes first gives the creamy custard filling a deeper, slightly caramelized flavor, while cinnamon, nutmeg, and vanilla add that familiar holiday warmth. A store-bought pie crust keeps things manageable, and you can make the whole pie ahead of time to free up the oven on Thanksgiving Day.
