issues.title: Easy Homemade Cornbread
issues.summary: This Easy Homemade Cornbread is quick, easy, delicious, and it makes a great side dish for breakfast, lunch, or dinner! The post Easy Homemade Cornbread appeared first on Budget Bytes .
issues.author: Beth Moncel
issues.content_html:
Cornbread is a highly underrated side dish. You can whip up this deliciously sweet and moist Homemade Cornbread recipe with just a few pantry staples, and it makes a perfect side dish for breakfast, lunch, or dinner! Serve it slathered with butter at breakfast, crumbled into your soup or chili at lunch, or as a side with your collard greens and pork chops for dinner. It’s inexpensive, comforting, and seriously easy to make, with 8 pieces costing just $1.27 ($0.16 each)! So toss that boxed mix and let me show you how it’s done for real. 😉

“Perfect cornbread! My cornbread always turned out too dry and crumbly – no more! Moist but still with the bit of crumbly and lightness cornbread should have. Really like cooking it in a pie dish and having wedges as well. Thank you!”

Rebecca

A Humble Side with Staying Power

I originally made this cornbread back in 2015 to help stretch a pot of stew further during one of my budget challenges, and it’s been a favorite ever since. I make it completely from scratch with yellow cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, milk, an egg, and cooking oil, most of which you’ve probably already got in your cupboard or fridge! It’s as simple as whisking the wet ingredients, combining them with the dry ingredients, and baking. I don’t even use a mixer and there’s no rising time to worry about, either.

But what I love most about this classic recipe is that it’s lightly sweetened, sitting somewhere between the sweeter, almost cake-like cornbread’s and the more savory Southern-style versions. Just ¼ cup of sugar adds a little sweetness while still letting that lovely corn flavor come through. I also use regular milk instead of buttermilk (so there’s no need to buy a whole carton that you might struggle to use up!).

It’s a simple everyday side, but I love serving a slice alongside a Thanksgiving or Christmas roast, too. You can even bake it the day before, which means one less thing to worry about when you’ve got a big holiday meal to prepare!

Recipe Success Tips

  1. Use baking powder, NOT baking soda! They’re not interchangeable. This recipe uses baking powder because it contains the ingredients needed to give the cornbread a tender crumb and good rise. Baking soda used in its place can leave an unpleasant, bitter taste and won’t give the same rise or result.
  2. Mix gently for tender cornbread. I know it’s tempting to keep stirring until everything is completely smooth, but you don’t want to do that here! Overmixing can develop the gluten in the flour and make the finished bread a little rubbery. Stir until everything is moistened. A few lumps are perfectly fine.
  3. Use the baking dish you’ve got. This amount of batter fits well into an 8×8 casserole dish, 9-inch pie plate, or a 10-inch cast iron skillet (although you should preheat the skillet as the oven preheats). Glass, ceramic, and cast iron work best, but you can also use metal baking dishes.
  4. Prefer savory over sweet? You can reduce the sugar to suit your tastes. Some readers have even left it out completely with good results, although changing the sugar can affect the browning and texture slightly.
  5. Make corn muffins instead! This is a great option if you want individual servings or something easy to grab and pack for lunch. Pour the batter into an oiled muffin tin, filling each well about ¾ full. Bake at the same temperature (425°F) for 16-18 minutes, or until the tops are golden brown. I usually get about 10 corn muffins from one batch (see photo).

Three Ways to Avoid Dry Cornbread

A little crumbliness is part of cornbread’s charm, but it shouldn’t fall apart the moment you slice it. Too much flour or cornmeal, or leaving it in the oven too long, can quickly turn a moist crumb dry. Here’s how I help keep this recipe tender without losing that classic cornmeal texture:

  • The flour adds structure, and the oil keeps things tender. Cornmeal doesn’t form gluten, so I use equal cups of all-purpose flour and cornmeal to help the bread hold together. Then the oil helps keep the crumb soft, even after it cools, because unlike butter, it stays liquid at room temperature.
  • Measure your flour and cornmeal carefully. Too much of either can throw off the balance of wet and dry ingredients, leaving you with a dry and crumbly bread. I recommend weighing them with a kitchen scale for the most consistent results (140 g flour and 150 g cornmeal).
  • Don’t overbake! This recipe takes about 20 minutes at 425°F, but the exact time can vary depending on your baking dish. Look for golden-brown edges and a golden top, then insert a toothpick into the center. It should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs (see photo below). There’s no need to keep baking once it’s done, or you risk drying it out.

What to Serve with Cornbread

Cornbread is a great side dish for any thick and hearty soup, stew, or chili. I especially love serving it with a big bowl of my classic chili. I’ll usually either dip a warm slice into the sauce or crumble it straight into my bowl (my favorite way to use up day-old leftovers!). The mild sweetness works really well with smoky spices and a little heat. But really, you can serve this recipe in place of your usual dipping bread with any soup or stew you love. It’s also delicious layered into an easy cornbread salad with beans, corn, and veggies for a potluck or gathering (recipe coming soon!)

I also love a warm slice with a pat of butter melting right on top. Add a drizzle of honey (as much or as little as you like!), and you’ve got a delicious afternoon snack with a cup of coffee or a sweet side for your eggs and bacon at breakfast.

And don’t forget about the holidays! I’d happily swap the usual dinner rolls for a slice of cornbread alongside some roasted turkey breast, a batch of my homemade cranberry sauce, and all the Thanksgiving fixings. You can also take it a step further and use this recipe to make our cornbread dressing, which is loaded with savory herbs and vegetables and makes enough to feed a crowd!

Print Add to Collection Go to Collections

Easy Homemade Cornbread Recipe

This classic Homemade Cornbread is moist, lightly sweet, and made from scratch with simple pantry staples. Ready in 30 minutes for just $0.16 per serving! Course Bread, Breakfast, Brunch, Side Dish Cuisine American Total Cost $1.27 recipe / $0.16 serving Prep Time 10 minutes minutes Cook Time 20 minutes minutes Total Time 30 minutes minutes Servings 8 servings Calories 247 kcal Author Beth Moncel

Equipment

  • Mixing Bowls
  • Glass Pie Plate
  • Whisk

Ingredients

  • 1 cup yellow cornmeal $0.29*
  • 1 cup all-purpose flour $0.23**
  • ¼ cup granulated sugar $0.07
  • 2 tsp baking powder $0.08
  • ½ tsp salt $0.02
  • 1 cup milk $0.30
  • 1 large egg $0.12
  • ¼ cup cooking oil $0.16
US Customary – Metric

Instructions

  • Gather and measure all ingredients. Preheat the oven to 425ºF/220℃/200℃ fan or Gas Mark 7 and coat the inside of a 9-inch pie plate, cast iron skillet, or 8×8 casserole dish with non-stick spray (or butter for more flavor).
  • In a large bowl, stir together the cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt until evenly combined.
  • In a separate bowl, whisk together the milk, egg, and oil.
  • Pour the bowl of wet ingredients into the bowl of dry ingredients and stir just until everything is moist. Avoid over stirring. It’s okay if there are a few lumps.
  • Pour the batter into the prepared dish and bake for about 20 minutes, or until the top and edges are golden brown. Cut into 8 pieces and serve.

See how we calculate recipe costs here.

Notes

* Use yellow cornmeal, not a boxed cornbread mix or self-rising cornmeal mix. **If you’re in the UK, use plain flour. If you want to make this recipe gluten-free, I’d try your favorite cup-for-cup gluten-free flour blend. Just keep in mind I haven’t tested this substitution, and the texture can vary by brand. Make sure your cornmeal and other ingredients are also gluten-free if needed. Avoid dry and crumbly cornbread! I recommend weighing the flour (140 g) and cornmeal (150 g) for the most accurate results. Too much of either can make your cornbread dry. The oil helps keep it tender, but be careful not to overmix or overbake! A few lumps in the batter are fine, and a toothpick inserted into the center should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cornbread add-ins: Plain cornbread is delicious on its own, but adding a little something extra can be fun! Try shredded cheddar and jalapeños (my jalapeño cheddar cornbread uses 4 oz. cheddar and 2 jalapeños), or blueberries (my lemon blueberry cornbread skillet uses ½ cup frozen blueberries, but fresh work too!). Roasted corn kernels, diced green chiles, chili powder, and cooked sausage are other ideas. Just keep additions modest (about half a cup) so they don’t weigh down the batter or affect the baking time too much.

Storage & Reheating

  • Fridge: Cool completely, then store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days or refrigerate for up to 5 days. Refrigeration can make cornbread firmer and drier, so let it come to room temperature before serving.
  • Freezing: Wrap individual portions tightly and freeze in an airtight container or freezer bag for up to 3 months. Thaw at room temperature.
  • Reheating: Microwave individual slices in short intervals until warmed through, or heat in a 300°F oven for 5-10 minutes for crispier edges. Cover loosely with foil if needed to prevent drying.

Nutrition

Serving: 1 serving | Calories: 247 kcal | Carbohydrates: 34 g | Protein: 5 g | Fat: 10 g | Sodium: 273 mg | Fiber: 2 g

How to Make Cornbread from Scratch step-by-step photos

Preheat the oven and prepare your baking dish: Gather and measure your ingredients, then preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C/200°C fan/Gas Mark 7). Grease a 9-inch pie plate, 10-inch cast iron skillet, or 8×8-inch baking dish with non-stick spray (or butter for a little extra flavor). I’ve always loved using my glass pie dish, but this time we used cast iron, and any of these options will work.

Combine the dry ingredients: In a large bowl, stir together 1 cup (150 g) yellow cornmeal, 1 cup (140 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 tsp (9 g) baking powder, and ½ tsp salt. Make sure everything is well mixed so the baking powder is evenly distributed throughout.

Whisk the wet ingredients: In a separate bowl, whisk together 1 cup (240 ml) milk, 1 large egg, and ¼ cup (60 ml) cooking oil until the egg is fully broken up and everything is well combined.

Gently mix the batter: Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir just until everything is moistened and there are no dry pockets of flour. Don’t keep stirring until the batter is completely smooth. A few lumps are perfectly fine, and overmixing can make the finished bread a little rubbery.

Bake until golden brown: Pour the batter into your prepared dish and spread it evenly. Bake for about 20 minutes, or until the top and edges are golden brown.

The top may crack a little, and that’s perfectly normal! To check it’s done, insert a toothpick into the center. It should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs. Cut into 8 pieces and serve. Enjoy!

More Cornbread Recipes to Try

  • Give the classic recipe a cheesy, slightly spicy twist with my Chili Cheese Cornbread, made with cheddar, chili powder, and sweet corn kernels.
  • I love combining two comfort food favorites in my Chili Cornbread Skillet. The homemade cornbread bakes right on top of a hearty bean chili, with a layer of melted cheddar in between!
  • Mashed sweet potato, sour cream, cinnamon, and nutmeg make this Sweet Potato Cornbread extra moist, rich, and full of warm fall flavors.

issues.title: Baked Mac and Cheese
issues.summary: This creamy Baked Mac and Cheese recipe has a rich homemade cheese sauce and a golden, buttery panko topping. Easy to make and perfect for family dinners! The post Baked Mac and Cheese appeared first on Budget Bytes .
issues.author: Jennie Alley
issues.content_html:
When it comes to Baked Mac and Cheese, I want ultra-creamy macaroni and a golden, crunchy breadcrumb topping. After countless rounds of testing, I’ve finally got that combination just right in this from-scratch recipe, with a rich, flavorful cheese sauce made from sharp cheddar and Colby Jack. Simple seasonings and bouillon in the pasta water also add extra savory depth, making this the baked mac and cheese dreams are made of! At just $1.11 per serving, it’s an affordable side dish for weeknight dinners, holiday spreads, or anytime you’re craving a really good cheesy mac.

A Baked Mac and Cheese Worth Turning On the Oven For

There’s nothing more disappointing than making a beautifully creamy pot of mac and cheese, only for it to dry out in the oven. That’s exactly what I wanted to avoid with this recipe. I wanted the macaroni to stay creamy after baking, with plenty of cheesy sauce and a crunchy topping to contrast all that richness. A simple butter-and-flour roux gives the homemade sauce a little extra body, and using whole milk means there’s no need to splurge on heavy cream. I also prefer the combination of sharp cheddar for its bold flavor and Colby Jack for its smooth, creamy, gooey melt. Both are affordable and easy to find, which is always a bonus!

The topping deserves some attention, too. I love a good layer of melted cheese, but the buttery, seasoned panko adds a crunch that makes baked mac and cheese so good. I even layer a little extra cheese through the middle (because more cheese is always the right answer here!) This recipe takes a few extra steps compared to our stovetop mac and cheese, but nothing complicated, and the whole dish still comes together in less than an hour. I’ve shared all my top tips below to help you get that creamy sauce just right.

Recipe Success Tips

  1. Undercook the macaroni to avoid mushy pasta. I cook mine for just 6 minutes, about 1-2 minutes shy of al dente. The pasta will absorb liquid from the cheese sauce as it bakes, so starting with fully cooked macaroni can make the noodles too soft and the sauce less creamy. You want the pasta to still have a firm bite when you drain it. Check your package directions, as cooking times vary between brands and shapes.
  2. Grate your own cheese for the best melt. Freshly grated cheddar and Colby Jack melt more smoothly than pre-shredded cheese, which often contains anti-caking agents that can affect the sauce’s texture. Remember to set aside the cheese for layering before making the sauce!
  3. Add the warm milk gradually and let it thicken. I whisk the warm milk into the roux a little at a time, making sure it’s smooth before adding more. This helps the flour incorporate evenly without forming lumps. Then let the sauce gently simmer until it coats the back of a spoon (see photo). A properly thickened sauce clings to the macaroni instead of pooling at the bottom of the baking dish.
  4. Add the cheese off the heat. I let the sauce cool for about a minute before stirring in the cheese, one handful at a time. Too much heat can cause the cheese to separate, leaving you with a grainy or oily sauce instead of a smooth and creamy one.
  5. Don’t overbake! At 350°F, start checking around 25 minutes. You’re looking for bubbling edges and a golden breadcrumb topping. Baking too long can dry out the sauce as the pasta absorbs more moisture. If I think the topping needs more color, I’ll broil it for about a minute, watching closely. Let it rest for 5 minutes before serving so the sauce can settle and thicken.
  6. Add more flavor by seasoning in layers. I was very intentional about the seasonings in this baked mac and cheese recipe. Bouillon in the pasta water gives the macaroni extra savory flavor from the start. Then I let the seasonings simmer in the sauce for a few minutes to distribute and develop their flavors before adding the cheese. Even the buttery panko topping gets its own helping of garlic powder, smoked paprika, and black pepper! This builds flavor throughout the dish, so it’s not just the cheese doing all the heavy lifting.
Print Add to Collection Go to Collections

Baked Mac and Cheese

This creamy Baked Mac and Cheese recipe has a rich homemade cheese sauce and a golden, buttery panko topping. Easy to make and perfect for family dinners! Course Side Dish Cuisine American Total Cost $6.65 recipe / $1.11 serving Prep Time 15 minutes minutes Cook Time 35 minutes minutes Total Time 50 minutes minutes Servings 6 servings (1 cup each) Calories 621 kcal Author Jennie Alley

Equipment

  • Large Pot
  • Colander
  • 8×8 Baking Dish (2-quart)
  • Large Saucepan

Ingredients

Baked Mac and Cheese

  • 8 oz. elbow macaroni uncooked, $0.68
  • 2 quarts water $0.00
  • 1 Tbsp chicken bouillon $0.54*
  • ¼ cup salted butter $0.38
  • ¼ cup all-purpose flour $0.05
  • 3 cups whole milk warmed, $0.89
  • ½ tsp ground mustard powder $0.08
  • ½ tsp garlic powder $0.03
  • ¼ tsp smoked paprika $0.03
  • ¼ tsp black pepper freshly cracked, $0.03
  • ¾ tsp salt or to taste, $0.03
  • 8 oz. sharp cheddar freshly grated & divided, (2 cups) $1.87**
  • 4 oz Colby Jack freshly grated & divided, (1 cup) $0.94**
  • 1 Tbsp salted butter for the cooked pasta, $0.10

Breadcrumb Topping

  • 2 Tbsp butter melted, $0.19
  • ½ cup panko breadcrumbs $0.51
  • ¼ tsp garlic powder $0.02
  • ¼ tsp smoked paprika $0.03
  • ⅛ tsp black pepper freshly cracked, $0.02
  • 1 oz sharp cheddar freshly grated, (¼ cup) $0.23**
US Customary – Metric

Instructions

  • Gather all ingredients. Preheat the oven to 350°F and grease a 2-quart baking dish.
  • Shred the cheddar and Colby Jack using the large holes of a box grater. Microwave the milk for 1-2 minutes, until warm but not hot.***
  • Bring the water and bouillon to a boil in a large pot. Add the macaroni and cook for 6 minutes, or until slightly underdone. Drain in a colander, add 1 tablespoon of butter, and toss until melted. Set aside while you prepare the sauce.****
  • In a small bowl, combine the panko, melted butter, garlic powder, smoked paprika, black pepper, and grated cheddar for the topping. Mix until the breadcrumbs are evenly coated.
  • Melt ¼ cup butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for about 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture is pale blond and slightly nutty.
  • Gradually whisk in the warm milk, adding a splash at a time and whisking until smooth before each addition. Stir in the dry mustard, garlic powder, smoked paprika, black pepper, and salt.
  • Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer and cook for 2-3 minutes, whisking frequently and scraping the corners of the pan, until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
  • Remove the pan from the heat and let the sauce cool for about 1 minute. Add the cheddar and Colby Jack a handful at a time, stirring until melted before adding more. Reserve ½ cup of the combined cheese for layering in the casserole. If the sauce becomes too thick to stir easily, whisk in a splash of milk.*****
  • Fold the cooked macaroni into the cheese sauce until evenly coated.
  • Spread half of the macaroni mixture into the prepared baking dish. Sprinkle the reserved ½ cup of cheese evenly over the top.
  • Add the remaining macaroni mixture and spread it evenly. Sprinkle the breadcrumb topping over the surface without pressing it down.
  • Bake for about 25 minutes, until the edges are bubbling and the topping is golden. If the topping needs more color, broil for about 1 minute, watching closely to prevent burning. Let the mac and cheese rest for 5 minutes before serving.

See how we calculate recipe costs here.

Notes

*I like to use Better Than Bouillon chicken base to season the pasta water because it adds another layer of savory flavor to the macaroni. The amount of salt varies by brand and product, so adjust the added salt in the cheese sauce to taste. For a vegetarian version, use vegetable bouillon instead. You can also omit the bouillon entirely and simply salt the pasta water. **For the creamiest baked macaroni and cheese, shred the cheese yourself using the large holes of a box grater. Pre-shredded cheese contains starches that can keep the cheese from melting as smoothly. ***Cold milk can make a roux clump. Warm milk helps the sauce come together smoothly. ****Tossing the drained macaroni with butter helps coat the noodles and allows them to cool slightly while you prepare the cheese sauce. In testing, I found this helps the finished mac and cheese stay creamier and reduced how much sauce the pasta absorbed during baking. *****It’ll look like a lot of sauce for the pasta at first. That’s the point, since the macaroni soaks up some in the oven! Choosing the best cheese for baked mac and cheese: I love using sharp cheddar because its bold, cheesy flavor doesn’t get lost in the sauce, while Colby Jack adds a mild flavor and melts beautifully. Both are affordable and easy to find, so they’re a no-brainer for me! I wouldn’t skip the sharp cheddar, but you can use mild cheddar if you prefer a less pronounced cheese flavor. Gruyère is another delicious option, though it’s more expensive. Monterey Jack, Gouda, and fontina are also good melting cheeses if you have some on hand. Meal Prep/Make Ahead: You can shred the cheese and prepare the breadcrumb topping up to 2 days ahead. Store the cheese in an airtight container in the refrigerator and refrigerate the breadcrumb mixture separately. For the creamiest results, cook the pasta, make the cheese sauce, and assemble the casserole shortly before baking.

Nutrition

Serving: 1 cup | Calories: 621 kcal | Carbohydrates: 44 g | Protein: 25 g | Fat: 39 g | Sodium: 900 mg | Fiber: 2 g

How to Make Baked Mac and Cheese Step-by-Step Photos

Gather your ingredients for the baked mac and cheese: You’ll need 8 oz. elbow macaroni (uncooked), 2 quarts water, 1 Tbsp chicken bouillon, ¼ cup salted butter, ¼ cup all-purpose flour, 3 cups whole milk, ½ tsp ground mustard powder, ½ tsp garlic powder, ¼ tsp smoked paprika, ¼ tsp black pepper, ¾ tsp salt, 8 oz. sharp cheddar, 4 oz. Colby Jack, and 1 Tbsp butter for the cooked pasta. Preheat your oven to 350°F and grease a 2-quart baking dish.

Gather the ingredients for the breadcrumb topping: You’ll need ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 2 Tbsp melted butter, ¼ tsp garlic powder, ¼ tsp smoked paprika, ⅛ tsp black pepper, and 1 oz. freshly grated sharp cheddar.

Shred the cheeses: Use the large holes of a box grater to shred 8 oz. sharp cheddar and 4 oz. Colby Jack. Freshly grated cheese melts more smoothly into the sauce than pre-shredded varieties. Set aside ½ cup of the combined cheeses for layering in the casserole. Also keep the additional 1 oz. cheddar for the topping separate. Warm the 3 cups of whole milk in the microwave for 1-2 minutes until warm but not hot.

Boil the water with the bouillon: Add 2 quarts of water and 1 Tbsp chicken bouillon to a large pot and bring to a boil. Stir to dissolve the bouillon, then add 8 oz. elbow macaroni and cook for about 6 minutes, or until slightly underdone. The pasta should still have a firm bite, as it’ll continue to soften in the oven.

Drain and butter the macaroni: Drain the pasta in a colander, then add 1 Tbsp butter and toss until melted and evenly coated. This helps keep the macaroni from sticking together while you prepare the cheese sauce. Set aside.

Make the breadcrumb topping: Combine ½ cup panko, 1 oz. grated cheddar, ¼ tsp garlic powder, ¼ tsp smoked paprika, and ⅛ tsp black pepper in a small bowl. Pour in the 2 Tbsp melted butter and stir until the breadcrumbs are evenly coated and the mixture looks crumbly. Set aside.

Make the roux: Melt ¼ cup butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Sprinkle in ¼ cup flour and whisk constantly for about 2 minutes, until the mixture is smooth, pale blond, and smells slightly nutty. Keep it moving so the flour cooks evenly without browning too much.

Gradually add the warm milk: Pour in a small splash of the warmed milk and whisk until completely smooth before adding more. Continue until all 3 cups have been incorporated. The mixture will thicken initially, then loosen as you add the remaining milk. Adding it gradually helps prevent lumps.

Season and thicken the sauce: Whisk in ½ tsp ground mustard, ½ tsp garlic powder, ¼ tsp smoked paprika, ¼ tsp black pepper, and ¾ tsp salt (or to taste). Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer and cook for 2-3 minutes, whisking frequently and scraping the corners of the saucepan. It’s ready when it’s smooth and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. If it’s still runny, let it simmer a little longer.

Melt the cheese into the sauce: Remove the saucepan from the heat and let it cool for about 1 minute. Add the remaining shredded cheddar and Colby Jack (from the 8 oz. cheddar and 4 oz. Colby Jack, after reserving ½ cup for layering) a handful at a time, stirring until each addition has melted before adding more. The finished sauce should be smooth, creamy, and free of lumps. If it becomes too thick to stir easily, whisk in a splash of milk to loosen it.

Combine with the sauce: Add the cooked macaroni to the saucepan and gently fold everything together until the pasta is evenly coated. The mixture should look nice and saucy at this stage, as the macaroni will absorb more of the sauce while baking.

Layer the pasta: Spread half of the macaroni mixture evenly into your prepared baking dish. Sprinkle the reserved ½ cup of shredded cheese over the top. Try to make sure it’s distributed across the dish so you get extra melted cheese throughout the casserole.

Add the remaining macaroni and breadcrumb topping: Spoon the rest of the macaroni mixture over the cheese layer and spread it evenly. Scatter the prepared panko topping over the surface, covering it as evenly as possible without pressing it down. Keeping the crumbs loose helps them turn golden and crispy in the oven.

Bake until golden and bubbling: Transfer the baking dish to the preheated 350°F oven and bake for about 25 minutes, until the edges are bubbling and the breadcrumb topping is golden brown and crunchy. If the topping needs a little more color, broil for about 1 minute, watching carefully so it doesn’t burn. Let the pasta rest for 5 minutes before serving so the sauce has a chance to settle slightly. Enjoy!

What to Serve with Baked Mac and Cheese

This baked mac and cheese is right at home on a holiday dinner table alongside baked ham or roast turkey. Our baked ham cooks at 350°F, too, so you can pop the pasta into the oven toward the end of the ham’s cooking time if there’s enough room. For Thanksgiving, you could bake it while the turkey rests, allowing about 30 minutes for baking and the mac and cheese’s short rest. I love serving it straight from the baking dish so everyone can help themselves, especially at family gatherings and potlucks. This recipe makes six servings of about 1 cup each.

For a more casual dinner, try it alongside slow cooker pulled pork piled into slider buns, or serve it with meatloaf and a simple green salad. I also love the idea of adding some roasted veggies like carrots, Brussels sprouts, or oven roasted broccoli to the table to balance out all that creamy cheese. The broccoli normally roasts at 400°F, but you can cook it on a separate tray at 350°F (which is the temp needed for this macaroni recipe) if you allow extra time.

Baked Ham

$27.24 recipe / $2.47 serving

Classic Homemade Meatloaf Recipe

$10.73 recipe / $1.53 serving

Slow Cooker Pulled Pork

$9.48 recipe / $1.19 serving

Easy Oven Roasted Broccoli

$3.34 recipe / $0.84 serving

Storage & reheating

Store leftover baked mac and cheese in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3-4 days. Let it cool slightly before storing, but be sure to refrigerate it within 2 hours of baking.

Reheating

Reheat individual portions in the microwave with a splash of milk, stirring halfway through, until heated through. For larger portions, cover the baking dish with foil and reheat in a 325°F oven until warmed through. Add a little milk before reheating to help restore the creamy sauce.

Freezing

For the best texture, I recommend freezing leftover portions rather than freezing the entire casserole before baking. Let it cool completely, then portion it into airtight, freezer-safe containers and freeze for up to 2 months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and reheat with a splash of milk. The sauce may be slightly less smooth after freezing, and the breadcrumb topping will lose some crispness.

Love Mac and Cheese? Try These Recipes Next!

  • Skip the oven and have our creamy Homemade Mac and Cheese on the table in just 25 minutes!
  • When I’m feeding a crowd, I love making my Crockpot Mac and Cheese because I can keep it warm in the slow cooker and let everyone help themselves.
  • Crispy bacon, tender broccoli, and a silky cheese sauce make our Bacon Broccoli Mac and Cheese a hearty, all-in-one dinner.
  • If you’re anything like me and love a little extra flavor in your mac, try our Green Chile Mac and Cheese with Monterey Jack, green chiles, cumin, and a pinch of crushed red pepper.

issues.title: An Airline You’ve Never Heard Of Will Fly From Seoul Incheon To Los Angeles
issues.summary: Parata Air, a South Korean airline with just a handful of planes, will launch daily Incheon to Los Angeles flights on May 1, 2027, with an A330-200.
issues.author: Ben Schlappig
issues.content_html:
A very small international airline plans to add long haul, international flights to the United States as of next spring, and I feel pretty confident in saying that 99% of people have never heard of this airline (I had to look it up after seeing one of their planes at an airport several weeks back, and I know a thing or two about identifying airplanes). 😉

Parata Air makes US debut with new LAX route

As reported by AeroRoutes, as of May 1, 2027, Parata Air will launch daily nonstop flights between Seoul Incheon (ICN) and Los Angeles (LAX). The flight will operate with the following schedule:

WE301 Incheon to Los Angeles departing 12:00PM arriving 7:20AM
WE302 Los Angeles to Incheon departing 9:50AM arriving 3:20PM (+1 days)

Parata Air will operate the route with an Airbus A330-200, featuring 260 seats, including 18 business class seats and 242 economy seats. The 5,944-mile flight is blocked at 11hr40min eastbound and 13hr30min westbound.

Tickets on the flight are now on sale, and I see fares starting at around $670 one-way in economy, and around $2,500 one-way in business class. Those aren’t exactly terribly attractive fares for a newcomer that appears to have a pretty lackluster onboard product.

For those not familiar with Parata Air, the airline launched operations back in 2019, but it has a fleet of just a handful of planes, including three Airbus A330s and two Airbus A220s. This will be the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. As I hinted at in the headline, I imagine this is a fully unknown player to most people, and I had never heard of the airline until a few weeks ago.

Random thought — can anyone think of a smaller international airline (in terms of fleet size) that added long haul flights to the United States? I know that’s very specific, but I can’t think of another one… it’s possible I’m missing something, though!

The airline acquired its three A330s secondhand from different sources, with the planes having flown for Garuda Indonesia, Hainan Airlines, and Thomas Cook (though that plane doesn’t have business class).

It’s good to see more competition in this market

The Seoul Incheon to Los Angeles market is pretty well served in terms of capacity, but not so well served in terms of competition. That’s because no US carrier flies between Los Angeles and Seoul Incheon, and with Korean Air having acquired Asiana, there’s now only one South Korean flag carrier.

If you look at the market, you’ll see that Korean Air operates up to four daily flights, and Air Premia operates up to two daily flights. Now we’ll see a third airline from the country operating in the market, though with the lowest capacity, and arguably the worst product.

It’ll be interesting to see when we see some competition here on the US side. Delta might operate the route eventually, but that doesn’t actually increase competition, since the airline has a joint venture with Korean Air. American has (smartly, probably) given up on Los Angeles as a long haul hub. So that leaves United, and I could definitely see the airline eventually adding service in the market, as a competitive response against Delta and Korean Air, if nothing else.

Bottom line

As of May 2027, Parata Air will be launching a new nonstop route between Seoul Incheon and Los Angeles, representing the carrier’s first service outside of Asia. The airline will be operating daily in the market with Airbus A330s. With this, there will be three South Korean carriers flying this route, though no airlines from the United States.

What do you make of this new Parata Air service?

issues.title: Delta CEO: “Customers Are Not Choosing Airlines Based On Wi-Fi”
issues.summary: Delta CEO Ed Bastian says customers aren't choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi, while calling Viasat "pretty darn close" to Starlink. After years of hyping connectivity, that's a notable shift.
issues.author: Ben Schlappig
issues.content_html:
I’ve gotta be honest, I don’t envy the situation that Delta CEO Ed Bastian is in. Unlike most other carriers in the United States, Delta hasn’t opted for SpaceX Starlink Wi-Fi, and has instead gone with Amazon Leo.

In theory that’s fine, except Amazon Leo is years behind Starlink, and just faced a new setback, due to a rocket failure. Elon Musk has also repeatedly publicly ridiculed Bastian, regarding what Bastian reportedly said about Musk to employees.

There’s now an interesting update, as Bastian made some comments about the carrier’s Wi-Fi choice, and overall customer preferences. It sure is amazing how narratives can change, based on what’s convenient…

Bastian downplays fast Wi-Fi, after hyping it for years

This week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum 2026, Delta’s CEO was asked about the carrier’s decision not to choose Starlink, plus the public spat with Musk. Here’s what Bastian had to say about this:

“We’ve been the leader in Wi-Fi, and in free and fast Wi-Fi, and we’ve been at it for five years. I’ve got a long history with Elon on that. We’ve looked at Starlink, we actually helped them started in aviation, we gave them our planes to use during COVID, when we weren’t flying, and they tested the system out. We just couldn’t come to agreement on a business model.”

“We’ve been the leader in free, fast Wi-Fi. We are confident there will be more than one LEO product in the world other than Starlink, and I’m confident Amazon has the capability to do a great job. Customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi. We’ve been out with a great product from Viasat, which we’ve got two new satellites in the sky. It’s not Starlink caliber but it’s pretty darn close.”

What is premium, what is fast, and what is industry leading?

Look, before I get too deep into this, let me make several points that I think no one reasonable will disagree with (which is not to say some commenters won’t disagree!):

  • Starlink Wi-Fi is better than Viasat, Viasat is better than Panasonic, and then there are a whole bunch of other services
  • As a passenger who values staying connected, there is a significant difference between Starlink and Viasat, whether you’re looking to be productive or entertained
  • A vast majority of passengers don’t choose an airline exclusively based on the Wi-Fi, but rather, it’s about the overall value (factoring in price, schedule, loyalty, and product)
  • As someone who has been flying frequently since inflight Wi-Fi was introduced, the standard of what’s considered “fast” Wi-Fi has changed massively; at one point Viasat felt lightning fast, when the reference point was otherwise OnAir, or another lesser service

When Bastian formally unveiled plans for free Wi-Fi at CES 2023 in Las Vegas, he said the following:

“At work, at home and everywhere in between, connectivity is essential to daily life, and your journey on Delta should be no different. Our vision has long been to deliver an experience at 30,000 feet that feels similar to what our customers have available on the ground.”

“We didn’t just want free Wi-Fi to offer base-level service – we wanted it to be transformative for the entire onboard experience. It is imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home, and we’ve put this system through meticulous tests to make that possible.”

Any reasonable person could agree that:

  • Based on what we know as of now, there will be an extended period of time around a year from now where United will massively overtake Delta when it comes to Wi-Fi speed and quality, and that advantage will last for years; heck, Delta has only committed to introducing Amazon Leo on under half its fleet, once the service goes live in 2028, best case scenario
  • Unless your Wi-Fi router at home is broken, Viasat simply doesn’t offer comparable quality connectivity to what you have at home, which Bastian insists is imperative

Earlier this year, when announcing plans to partner with Amazon Leo for connectivity, Bastian said that “we need to stay the leader” in inflight connectivity. Obviously that won’t be the case for a long time.

As I see it, Delta’s problem here is pretty simple. Customers absolutely notice a difference between Viasat and Starlink. The issue isn’t that people will stop flying Delta altogether. The issue is that Delta has built its entire brand on being the industry leader, and on being on the forefront of technology.

There’s no denying that this sentiment among the public changes over time, because inflight Wi-Fi is easily one of the top amenities that passengers notice nowadays. Seriously, I can’t count the number of people I’ve heard from or just overheard talking about their first Starlink experience, and how blown away they were.

I guess to look at it from another angle, there’s no airline that loves talking about how premium it is more than Delta. What makes Delta premium? If we’re going to believe that Delta is premium, it’s not based on any one single thing, but rather, it’s based on the sum of the experience. And I think anyone who thinks a major Wi-Fi disadvantage lasting for years isn’t part of what contributes to consumer sentiment is lying to themselves.

Bottom line

Delta CEO Ed Bastian is now downplaying the importance of inflight Wi-Fi. He’s arguing that “customers are not choosing airlines based on Wi-Fi,” which in isolation, is probably true. But he’s also arguing that Viasat is “pretty darn close” to Starlink, which is most definitely not true, as I see it.

I wouldn’t be so critical of these statements if it weren’t for Bastian spending years hyping up how it’s “imperative all customers onboard can enjoy their favorite content just as they would at home,” while also saying “we need to stay the leader.” And for that matter, Delta has of course also long hyped how premium it is — if that’s to be believed, it’s not about any one feature, but instead, it’s about the sum of the experience.

What do you make of Bastian’s inflight connectivity comments?

issues.title: Tulum Is Losing Airlines Fast: Why The Hyped New Airport Is Failing
issues.summary: Tulum's Felipe Carrillo Puerto Airport opened in late 2023, but airlines like JetBlue, Avianca, and Copa have left, and passenger numbers are down 33.2% so far in 2026.
issues.author: Ben Schlappig
issues.content_html:
In late 2023, we saw the opening of the Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport (TQO), in Tulum, Mexico. For those not familiar, Tulum is located on the eastern coast of the Yucatan Peninsula, and for years, it was a growing tourist destination.

While it could previously be accessed via Cancun International Airport (CUN), the hope was that by opening a new international airport, visitor numbers would expand massively. Unfortunately what has actually happened is exactly the opposite, as airline after airline has pulled out. What exactly is going on here? I think it makes for an interesting story, and thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this.

Airlines are abandoning Tulum, one after the other

In 2023, we saw airline after airline announce flights to Tulum. Among US carriers, we saw American, Delta, JetBlue, and United, all launch flights to Tulum, while Spirit announced flights, but never launched them.

That was only a small part of the overall international service to the airport, as we also saw flights to Tulum on Air Canada, Air Transat, Avianca, Copa, Discover, and WestJet, along with flights on domestic carriers like Aeromexico, Mexicana de Aviacion, Viva, and Volaris.

Less than three years after the airport opened, where do things stand? When it comes to international year-round service, we’ve now gone from service to 12 airports, to service to four airports, which is an absolutely massive reduction:

  • Among US carriers, the only ones that are left are American and Delta, while JetBlue has already pulled out, and United has announced it will pull out as of early 2027
  • That also says nothing of how Avianca, Copa, and Discover, have pulled out, while Canadian carriers now only operate seasonal service
  • And we also won’t even get into how Aeromexico has abandoned the airport, though admittedly that was just domestic service

Just to put this into numbers, in the first half of 2026, the airport saw a 33.2% reduction in passengers. June 2026 was the worst month to date, with a 44.8% drop, as there were just 47,600 passengers, compared to 86,200 passengers the year prior.

It goes without saying that for a newly built airport, this is rather catastrophic, and not what you hope to see.

What can explain Tulum’s tourism challenges?

In some ways, it feels like the whole concept behind Tulum Airport was sort of unnecessary. That’s also easily explained by the fact that the airport was well over a decade in the making, so while I can see how it might’ve seemed like a good idea at some point, tourism trends do evolve over time.

The reality is that there was a point where Tulum was cool, edgy, and a bit off the beaten path, compared to… whatever it is now. But when it comes to the struggles that airlines have had with flying to Tulum, it seems like the problems have been endless:

  • The United States is the largest inbound tourism market for Mexico, and overall demand for travel to Mexico among Americans is down; in the first half of 2026, Mexico’s share of American trips dropped from 19.8% to 18.1%, so it’s a shrinking market at the moment
  • That’s not great when paired with the fact that Mexico has seen a massive amount of growth when it comes to new hotels in places like Cancun, Los Cabos, etc., so despite visitor numbers being down, there’s increasing competition for those fewer visitors
  • Cancun has also seen an explosion in new resorts, and that’s some pretty direct competition, especially when you consider how much more easily accessible it is from a lot of destinations
  • The Maya Train (connecting Cancun and Tulum) opened around the same time as the airport, making travel between the two places easy and affordable; arguably that reduces the need for a dedicated airport, rather than creating the need for one
  • Tulum has seen a decrease in visitors, as it has sort of lost its “cool” factor, and it has also seen an issue with sargassum; in the first six months of 2026, hotel occupancy in Tulum averaged 63.7%, compared to 72.7% the year before
  • Mexico in general is suffering from the fact that it’s no longer really a value destination, at least for those looking for luxury experiences; prices are really high, and when you add in the taxes & service charges, prices start to look a whole lot like in the United States
  • Tulum Airport offered incentives for airlines to launch service there, but those incentives were reduced year by year, with almost everything running out after three years (which coincides with now!)

It’ll be interesting to see if Tulum can reverse any of these trends, and regain visitors…

Bottom line

A few years ago Tulum Airport opened to some fanfare, as a good number of airlines rushed to add service there. Unfortunately the excitement didn’t last long, as the airport has gone from a dozen year-round international routes, to just four.

This reduction in demand particularly evident from the United States, as soon there will just be nonstop service on American and Delta, and even that will be with reduced frequencies and routes.

Tulum Airport is facing endless challenges, not the least of which is a decline in visitors to Mexico from the United States, combined with increasing competition for those fewer visitors. Mexico just isn’t a value destination in the way that it used to be in places like Cancun, Tulum, Los Cabos, etc., and that’s understandably impacting demand.

I’m curious if Tulum can find a way to turn things around, but it’s not a good situation.

What do you make of the Tulum Airport demand problem?

issues.title: Earning World Of Hyatt Elite Nights & Status With Credit Cards: Worth It?
issues.summary: Both World of Hyatt credit cards earn elite nights toward status. Here's how the earning rates work, and whether spending your way to Globalist is worth it.
issues.author: Ben Schlappig
issues.content_html:
Chase and Hyatt have two co-branded credit cards — the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Card (learn more). I’d consider these to be among the more lucrative hotel credit cards out there, particularly the personal version of the card.

One of the awesome things about Hyatt’s two credit cards is that they can earn you elite nights, making it easier to qualify for status in the World of Hyatt program. In this post, I’d like to get into the nitty-gritty of how earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards works, and discuss whether it’s worth it.

Basics of World of Hyatt’s two credit cards

Chase and Hyatt have both the World of Hyatt Credit Card (a personal card) and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (a business card). Both cards have valuable benefits, though I think the personal card is considerably more compelling than the business card. Let me start by just briefly recapping the perks of the two cards.

World of Hyatt Card benefits

The World of Hyatt Credit Card has a $95 annual fee and offers:

  • Automatic World of Hyatt Discoverist status for as long as your account is open
  • Five qualifying night credits toward your next tier status every year
  • Two qualifying night credits toward your next tier status every time you spend $5,000 on your card
  • A Category 1-4 anniversary free night award on your account anniversary every year
  • A second Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year

This means that you’re getting five elite nights toward status and a Category 1-4 free night award every year just for having the card. To me that more than justifies the annual fee, by a long shot (I consistently get $250+ of value out of the free night certificate alone). That doesn’t even factor in the incremental perks you can get for spending on the card.

World of Hyatt Business Card benefits

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card has a $199 annual fee and offers:

  • Automatic World of Hyatt Discoverist status for you and five employees for as long as your account is open
  • Five qualifying night credits toward your next tier status every time you spend $10,000 on your card in a calendar year
  • Up to $100 in Hyatt credits annually — get a $50 statement credit when you spend at least $50 at a Hyatt, and you can use this twice
  • 10% back on World of Hyatt points redemptions for the remainder of the calendar year when you spend $50,000 on the card, with a maximum credit of 20,000 points

The business version of the card isn’t quite as rewarding as the personal version of the card, especially if you’re not a big spender. However, for businesses that spend quite a bit on credit cards, this can be the best card for earning elite status.

World of Hyatt credit card status earning opportunities

Both the World of Hyatt Credit Card and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offer the ability to earn elite nights. However, the ways in which you earn elite nights differ between the two cards, so let’s go over those details.

World of Hyatt Card elite night earning rates

The World of Hyatt Credit Card offers qualifying nights toward Hyatt status in two ways. First of all, the World of Hyatt Card offers five elite nights annually just for having the card. There’s no spending required to earn these five elite nights, and you receive them for each calendar year in which you have the card, including the year in which you open the card.

Beyond that, the World of Hyatt Card offers two elite nights for every $5,000 spent on the card (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,500 of spending). There’s no limit to how many elite nights you can earn this way, and the elite nights earned through spending on this card aren’t in any way tied to the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $2,500 on the card in 2026 and then spend $2,500 on the card in 2027, you’d earn two elite nights at that point.

World of Hyatt Business Card elite night earning rates

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card offers five elite nights for every $10,000 spent on the card in a calendar year (in other words, that’s up to one elite night per $2,000 of spending). On this card, the spending counter resets at the beginning of the calendar year. In other words, if you spent $8,000 on the card in 2026, you’d still have to spend a full $10,000 in 2027 to earn five elite nights.

As you can see, this card offers elite nights for spending at an accelerated rate, though unlike the personal card, it doesn’t offer the five elite nights annually just for having the card.

World of Hyatt credit card elite nights posting timeline

How soon do elite nights post from the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card?

  • For the World of Hyatt Card’s five elite nights just for being a cardmember, the terms state that the nights will post within eight weeks of opening the card, and also within eight weeks of January 1 in subsequent years; however, in reality they post much faster than that, typically within days of opening the card, and within days of January 1 in subsequent years
  • For both the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card, the terms state that elite nights from spending will post within eight weeks of the month in which you complete eligible spending, though in practice they post much faster than that, typically within days of an eligible statement closing

Is earning Hyatt elite status with credit cards worth it?

While the above covers the basics, I’d like to now analyze the overall value proposition of earning World of Hyatt elite status by spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, including addressing some of the most common questions and scenarios that come up.

Hyatt credit card spending does count for Milestone Rewards

With Hyatt, not all elite perks are tied directly to having status, but rather some require earning a certain number of elite nights in a year, known as the Milestone Rewards program. The Milestone Rewards program is how you earn perks like suite upgrade awards, club access awards, Guest of Honor awards, and more.

Hyatt elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards would count toward Milestone Rewards the same as any hotel stays would, which adds further value to credit card spending.

Hyatt credit card Discoverist status doesn’t come with elite nights

One of the perks of both Hyatt credit cards is that you receive Discoverist status for as long as you have the card. Discoverist status ordinarily requires 10 elite qualifying nights or 25,000 base points per year. As a reminder, here are World of Hyatt’s elite thresholds:

  • Discoverist status: 10 qualifying nights or 25,000 base points (equivalent to $5,000 of spending)
  • Explorist status: 30 qualifying nights or 50,000 base points (equivalent to $10,000 of spending)
  • Globalist status: 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 base points (equivalent to $20,000 of spending)

One common point of confusion is that people assume these cards really come with up to 15 elite nights per year. They assume you already get Discoverist status, and that any elite nights are on top of that. Note that while these cards offer Discoverist status, you don’t get the elite nights that correspond to that.

This means that if you have a Hyatt credit card, you’ll receive Discoverist status on an ongoing basis (and five elite nights every year if you have the personal card), but you’ll still need to qualify for Explorist or Globalist status based on the full criteria.

Hyatt credit card spending doesn’t count for lifetime status

Hyatt’s lifetime Globalist status is based on earning one million base points in the program. World of Hyatt members earn five base points per dollar spent on Hyatt stays, meaning you essentially have to spend $200,000 at Hyatts to earn lifetime Globalist status.

Credit card spending, and any elite nights earned through Hyatt credit cards, won’t count toward lifetime Globalist status. That’s because the qualification criteria is based solely on base points, and not based on elite qualifying nights (in which case it would count).

The value of spending your way to Globalist status

World of Hyatt Globalist is my favorite top tier hotel status, and what I love is that Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards make it easier to earn that. Let’s look at the best strategy for earning Globalist status with the card. Hyatt Globalist status ordinarily requires earning 60 qualifying nights in a year. So how much would you have to spend on a Hyatt credit card to earn that status?

On the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you’d need to spend $140,000 to earn Globalist status:

  • This accounts for the five elite nights you get just for having the card, as well as the two elite nights you get for every $5,000 spent
  • $140,000 of spending earns you 56 elite nights, plus the five elite nights just for having the card, for a total of 61 elite nights

Meanwhile on the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you’d need to spend $120,000 to earn Globalist status:

  • This accounts for the five elite nights you get for every $10,000 spent
  • $120,000 of spending earns you 60 elite nights, exactly enough for Globalist status

As you can see, the personal credit card offers more elite nights upfront, while the business credit card offers elite nights at a faster pace for spending (assuming you can reach the thresholds).

When you’re analyzing the value of spending your way toward status, don’t forget that even beyond the general status perks, the Milestone Rewards perks could really add up. For example, if you make it to 60 elite nights, you could select five suite upgrade awards and four club access awards, and would also receive a Category 1-7 free night award, a Category 1-4 free night award, and three Guest of Honor awards.

Then on the personal version of the card, you also receive an additional Category 1-4 free night award when you spend $15,000 on the card in a year. The value of all of those perks really adds up.

A hybrid hotel stay & credit card spending strategy works

Hyatt counts award nights toward status, and just for having the World of Hyatt Credit Card, you get a free night every year, plus the opportunity to earn a further three free nights for spending $15,000, earning Explorist status, and earning Globalist status.

On top of that, presumably you want to earn Globalist status because you actually intend to stay at Hyatts with some frequency. Hotel status is worthless if you don’t actually stay at that brand.

To be realistic, let’s assume that long term you’re earning 30 elite nights per year through actual stays. There are so many great Globalist benefits to use (like suite upgrade awards and free night awards), so if you’re staying at Hyatts less than that I question whether Globalist is worth it for you.

If you earned 30 of the required 60 elite nights through credit card spending, you’d need to spend the following:

  • $65,000 worth of spending on the World of Hyatt Card
  • $60,000 worth of spending on the World of Hyatt Business Card

Given all the incremental perks you’re picking up with Milestone Rewards, I’d say the math could really check out.

Calculate the opportunity cost of Hyatt credit card spending

When deciding if it makes sense to spend money on the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, consider the opportunity cost of the spending. For easy math purposes, I tend to consider the opportunity cost of credit card spending to be around 3.4%.

That’s because based on my valuation of miles & points, most transferable points currencies are worth 1.7 cents each, and you have some cards offering 2x points per dollar spent. Meanwhile I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

If we were to theoretically assume you’re spending $60,000 on a Hyatt credit card per year (give or take) in order to earn Globalist status, what’s the opportunity cost of that spending? By my math, you’re looking at an opportunity cost of up to 2% (the spread between a 3.4% return and 1.4% return). That’s around $1,200, if you value things the way that I do. But that’s not factoring in the value of all the other perks mentioned above:

  • It doesn’t factor in up to two Category 1-4 free night awards you’d get if you’re spending on the personal card, as these are valid at properties costing up to 25,000 points
  • It doesn’t factor in a Category 1-7 free night, valid at properties costing up to 55,000 points
  • It doesn’t factor in up to five confirmed suite upgrades, which you could use for yourself or gift to others
  • It doesn’t factor in up to four club access awards and three Guest of Honor awards, which you can gift to others

For many, I think the above perks could more than justify the difference in return on spending otherwise.

Bottom line

There are many things to love about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Card, though the ability to get a fast track toward status is probably my favorite perk. I absolutely love Hyatt Globalist status, and credit cards have historically helped me requalify for status. If you’re a Hyatt loyalist and don’t yet have the hotel group’s co-branded credit cards, they’re seriously worth considering.

What has your experience been using World of Hyatt Credit Cards to earn elite status?

Read an Excerpt From King of Masks by Petra Lord

Ana and Nell find themselves on opposite sides of a brutal war, as an ancient horror returns…

By Petra Lord

|

Published on November 17, 2026

We’re thrilled to share an excerpt from King of Masks, sequel to Petra Lord’s young adult fantasy novel Queen of Faces—publishing with Henry Holt and Co. on January 26th, 2027.

Buy the Book

King of Masks

KPetra Lord

Nell

“Adam Weaver, the vanquishing hero.” I flicked a burnt laurel on his wreath. “By the time you showed up, Khaiovhe had already killed half the school. You weren’t even clever enough to get the Aeon Scroll back. Do not presume to know my future.”

“But I do know your future, sweet Nell.” Adam smiled. “You are going to drown. You will sink deeper than you could possibly imagine. Your soul will escape through your lips like little bubbles, floating to the surface.” His voice went quiet. “When you get to the bottom, I’ll be waiting.”

Nausea grew like mold in my stomach. I stepped away from Adam, and stumbled out of the stands. I pushed past the waiters, the guards, past the fences and barricades and into the street, my head spinning.

Cheering men and women surrounded me on all sides. A deafening orchestra blasted from the parade, making my skull throb. The panic swelled in my mind like dry leaves catching flame, my arms shaking, my breath short. Someone in the crowd bumped into me, and I fell, reeling.

Rough, steady hands caught me, scooping me up like I was weightless.

“Breathe,” said Samuel. “This way.”

He carried me through the crowd, through a servant’s door into the kitchens behind the stands. He strode past caterers and chefs, plucking a grilled shrimp from a plate. As he ate it, he took me into an empty bathroom, locking the door behind us.

Samuel set me down against the bathtub, and wrapped his coat around my shoulders.

“What’s wrong?” he said simply.

My hands shook. It felt like centipedes were crawling inside my flesh.

The words spilled out of me on an impulse. “Could we swap bodies for the night? It doesn’t mean anything, just—”

We’d never done this before. In all the years we’d known each other, I’d never asked him to swap. Our families would have been furious.

Dread crawled up my skin like a spider. He doesn’t want to swap. He found the idea repulsive.

“Never mind,” I said. “It’s quite all right, you don’t have to—”

“I’ll do it.”

“Truly, it’s fine, you’ve never been in a body like this before, and—”

“Nell.” He touched a finger to my lips. “I’ll do it.”

He leaned in and kissed me, taking my hand. I reached out for him, and he reached out for me.

Flickering green light swirled around us, the color of both our souls. I felt my essence shift inside my body, pouring out of me like water from a drain.

I saw from two sets of eyes, breathed in two sets of lungs. Strength burst in my muscles, under my rough skin, and I exhaled, my body relaxing. His body, wrapped around my soul like a warm scarf in a blizzard.

For an uncut sliver of time, the boundaries melted between us, and everything that was his became mine. The most important memories of his life tore through my mind like I was flipping through a book. His family fleeing the emperor’s persecution. Immigrating to Caimor as a boy, taking a new body, a new name. The easy laughter of meeting me when we were kids, and the hole he’d punched in his wall when I’d been Ousted. His brother, shot through the head, bleeding out on a carpet during the attack on Paragon. The sound of screams as the Black Wraith burned his classmates alive.

And something else I didn’t recognize, a tiny flickering cage in the distance, a section of his past that was locked away. I noted it for an instant, before the sensory overload dragged me back to reality.

The obvious truth slapped me in the face. He’s seeing my memories, too. My memories of the last year. Of Anabelle Gage. My breath hitched.

“You were in love with her,” said Samuel.

“It was a gap year. Things just got a bit strange.”

“You severed a man’s arm for calling her ugly.”

“Very strange.”

Samuel looked at me. “You had feelings for her.”

A choking fog flooded my skull, a grey mist so thick I could barely think. I spoke, forcing my words into the silence. “She’s dead. Anabelle Gage is dead. It doesn’t matter what I felt.”

I looked down at the slender blond chassis my mother had bought for me. It looked almost identical to hers, only a decade younger. My home, for the rest of my days.

He makes you happy. You deserve to be happy.

“You have my love,” I said. “As long as there is salt in the sea and stone in the mountains.”

Samuel stared at me, his mouth flat, his eyes cold. I thought he might shout at me, or storm off.

Then his face softened.

His smile could have lit up the bottom of the sea.

The two of us sat there together. For another minute, another hour, I lost track. Then Samuel stood, cracking his neck. “All right. I’ve had about plenty of this bloody parade.” He pulled me to my feet. “Let’s go be real soldiers.”

* * *

That was the first time Samuel and I swapped bodies. But not the last.

That evening, Caimor’s invasion fleet set out to the east, battleships and destroyers and carriers transporting hundreds of thousands of soldiers. Samuel and I slept aboard the Steel Hawk, my mother’s flagship, with a dozen other Paragon students and mages of the Eldritch Guard.

That night, I found myself writhing under the covers of my cabin, sweat coating my bedsheets. I couldn’t stop thinking of Ana, vanishing beneath the clouds. Khaiovhe’s dark eyes, black flames spreading from her palm. Adam’s smirk. Before long, I expect you’ll be popping out some very handsome grandkids.

I imagined myself pregnant, my belly swollen, my body weighed down, down, until I sank into the floor and suffocated.

Only one thing could calm me enough to sleep: swapping into Samuel’s body. And to his everlasting credit, he let me do it without complaint, every night when I stumbled into his chambers. Our separate chambers, as befitting the navy.

I never had to wake him, either. He’d mastered a Praxis spell from his parents, Lucid Daydream, letting him function without any sleep. The reward for his engagement with me. Every time I found him, he was bent over his desk, memorizing facts about some noble or another, rehearsing anecdotes to use at parties. Once, I found him in front of a mirror, laughing over and over. “Lord Winter once told me my laugh sounded like a donkey,” he said. “So now, I practice it for two hours each night. Next time I see him, they’ll all be spellbound.”

“When was the last time you slept?” I said.

“Not since I learned this Praxis spell.” He shrugged. “So about four, five years ago.”

“I didn’t realize it was that dire. You really ought to rest more.”

“Someday,” he said. “When we’re married. When I’ve worked hard enough. When my family feels welcome in this country. Just once, I’d like for people to smile when I enter a room. Until that point, sleep is optional.”

After that, I felt somewhat less insane by comparison.

Still, his father had given him that spell, passed down his Codex in a spellbook. His parents were actually proud of him. That was more than I could say.

So, I slept in his body, and swapped back into my blond, feminine form during the day. It was our quiet, delicious secret.

What a thing it was, to live outside yourself. To be something, anything other than the almighty burden of you.

This pattern continued, all the way up to the eve of the invasion. The final night, before our assault of Sunset City, the largest port on the western coast of Shenten.

It would also be the final night I swapped bodies with Samuel.

That night, my nerves were too bad to fall asleep, even while wearing his body. So, I found myself walking up the cramped metal stairways of the battleship, out onto the deck. I leaned over a railing, gazing up at the starless sky, breathing in the sea air.

That was where my mother found me. “Evening.”

I spun around, almost jumping out of my skin. Admiral Rowyna Ebbridge was pacing the deck of her ship, hands tight behind her back, fingers tapping together.

I forced calm onto my face, pulse thumping in my ears. She doesn’t know you’ve swapped. As far as she was concerned, I was Samuel Pakhem, out for a breather the night before a war.

Pale moonlight shone in my mother’s eyes. The waves crashed against the ship below us.

Then she spoke, and her voice was as hard and cold as a tomb.

“Nell,” she said. “This way. There’s something I need to show you.”

The Mummy: Book of the Dead Cast Includes Some Surprising Returning Characters

The fourth film in the franchise comes out next year

By Vanessa Armstrong

|

Published on November 17, 2026

Photo Credit: Universal Pictures

0 Share
  • The Mummy: Book of the Dead Cast Includes Some Surprising Returning Characters&url=https://reactormag.com/the-mummy-book-of-the-dead-cast-returning-characters/” target=”_blank” title=”Twitter”>
  • The Mummy: Book of the Dead Cast Includes Some Surprising Returning Characters” target=”_blank” title=”Pinterest”>

Photo Credit: Universal Pictures

Production is underway for The Mummy: The Book of the Dead, the fourth installment of the franchise starring Brendan Fraser and (for most of the movies, at least) Rachel Weisz. We’ve known for a while that Fraser and Weisz would be returning, but what wasn’t clear until recently was whether other characters from the previous films would be coming back as well.

Here’s a rundown of who else has been confirmed to return for the fourth film.

Kevin J. O’Connor will be reprising his role as the shifty Beni Gabor. In the first film, Beni double-crossed Fraser’s Rick O’Connell and apparently got eaten alive by a swarm of flesh-eating scarabs. What form he’ll take in the fourth film remains to be seen.

We’ll also see the return of Oded Fehr (who you’ve seen recently in the later seasons of Star Trek: Discovery) as the Medjai warrior Ardeth Bay. In the first film, he joined Fraser’s Rick O’Connell and Weisz’s Evy in battling the reanimated Imhotep (the Medjai have been tasked for thousands of years to prevent the mummy from returning). In the second film, he tried to stop the Scorpion King (aka Dwayne Johnson) and ultimately failed.

Speaking of Imhotep, we also know that Arnold Vosloo is returning to reprise the role of the titular mummy, and rounding out the returning cast is John Hannah as Evy’s brother, Jonathan

The Book of the Dead cast also includes some new faces to the franchise. Michael Johnston (Obsession), Numan Acar (Young Sherlock), and Egyptian actor Tara Emad were reportedly in talks to join the film in undisclosed roles.

While the plot of Book of the Dead remains murky, it appears to focus more on the first two films and will pretend, like we all do, that 2008’s The Mummy: Tomb of the Dragon Emperor doesn’t exist.

We’ll get to see it all play out firsthand when the movie premieres in theaters on October 17, 2027. [end-mark]

3 Body Problem’s Alien Invasian Arrives in Season 2 Teaser

We are bugs? No, shrimps is bugs

By Molly Templeton

|

Published on November 17, 2026

Photo Credit: Netflix

0 Share
  • 3 Body Problem’s Alien Invasian Arrives in Season 2 Teaser&url=https://reactormag.com/3-body-problem-season-2-teaser/” target=”_blank” title=”Twitter”>
  • 3 Body Problem’s Alien Invasian Arrives in Season 2 Teaser” target=”_blank” title=”Pinterest”>

Photo Credit: Netflix

It hasn’t taken the second season of 3 Body Problem quite as long to make it to Netflix as it takes the show’s aliens to make it to Earth—but it’s been a while. The first look at the alien invasion comes in a new teaser, which is light on dialogue and heavy on somewhat mixed vibes. But one thing is clear: Liam Cunningham is pissed. The San-Ti are not coming to chat (when are they ever?). They’re coming to invade. They think humans are bugs! Their intentions are not vague!

Co-creator and writer David Benioff told Netflix’s Tudum that while the first season is largely about “the mystery of what’s happening,” this changes for the second season: “By the time Season 2 starts, we have a lot more information. We know there is a hostile alien civilization out there, the San-Ti, and they’re coming our way, and they want our planet for themselves.” His co-creator Alexander Woo said that one of the season’s big topics is the question of what humanity does when a looming threat is on the horizon: “Have people become used to it? Have some people started to rationalize it, and some even embraced it?” he said.

There’s definitely some embracing in this trailer, though it goes by pretty quickly. Much of the show’s cast returns for the second season, including Jovan Adepo as Saul Durand, Liam Cunningham as Thomas Wade, Eiza González as Auggie Salazar, Jess Hong as Jin Cheng, Benedict Wong as Da Shi, Sea Shimooka as Sophon, Marlo Kelly as Tatiana Haas, and Saamer Usmani as Raj Varma.

New cast members include Claudia Doumit as Captain Van Rijn; Ellie de Lange as Ayla; and Alfie Allen, David Yip, and Jordan Sunshine in recurring roles.

This season’s logline says only, “The alien invasion nears and humanity prepares to meet them—on Earth and beyond. While a space fleet embarks on a mission that spans centuries, a secret locked inside of one man’s mind might be humanity’s only hope for survival.”

The six episodes of season two arrive January 14th, 2027, on Netflix.[end-mark]

We Finally Know When We Can Watch 3 Body Problem Season 2

Season 2 of Netflix adaptation of Liu Cixin’s novels will come out early next year

By Vanessa Armstrong

|

Published on November 16, 2026

Credit: Ed Miller/Netflix

0 Share
  • 3 Body Problem Season 2&url=https://reactormag.com/we-finally-know-when-we-can-watch-3-body-problem-season-2/” target=”_blank” title=”Twitter”>
  • 3 Body Problem Season 2″ target=”_blank” title=”Pinterest”>

Credit: Ed Miller/Netflix

Remember Netflix’s 3 Body Problem? The television series adaptation of author Liu Cixin’s novels, created by David Benioff, D. B. Weiss, and Alexander Woo? It’s understandable if not; I can’t remember yesterday, and season one dropped on Netflix way back in March 2024. That’s almost (but not quite!) three years ago.

It turns out that season two will come to Netflix before that three-year mark. At the Texas Book Festival in Austin (via The Hollywood Reporter), the streamer revealed that season two will come out on January 14, 2027. There’s also a new logline for the upcoming episodes: “The alien invasion nears and humanity prepares to meet them—on Earth and beyond. While a space fleet embarks on a mission that spans centuries, a secret locked inside of one man’s mind might be humanity’s only hope for survival.”

“The tone really changes once you get to the second season,” Benioff, Weiss, and Woo said in a statement to the Netflix website, Tudum. “It’s much bigger. Things get wilder, the conflicts get more cosmic. Once people see it on the screen, they’re going to understand why we’ve been so excited for this season, in particular.”

THR also reports that season two will be a short one: six episodes compared to season one’s eight-episode run. The upcoming episodes will feature the return of the season one cast, including Jovan Adepo as Saul Durand, John Bradley as Jack Rooney, Rosalind Chao as Older Ye Wenjie, Liam Cunningham as Thomas Wade, Eiza González as Auggie Salazar, Jess Hong as Jin Cheng, Marlo Kelly as Tatiana Haas, Alex Sharp as Will Downing, Sea Shimooka as Sophon, Zine Tseng as Young Ye Wenjie, Saamer Usmani as Raj Varma, Benedict Wong as Da Shi, and Jonathan Pryce as Mike Evans. It will also see some new characters, including Claudia Doumit (SOULM8TE, The Boys) as Captain Van Rijn, Ellie de Lange (Wolf Hall, The Serpent) as Ayla, Alfie Allen (Game of Thrones), David Yip (The Chinese Detective), and Jordan Sunshine (The Pitt).

That’s a lot of characters! If you need a refresher on who’s who (and who wouldn’t; it’s been years!), Tudum has a pretty lil’ infographic with everyone’s details. And what about season three, which has already been greenlit? No news yet, but hopefully there won’t be a two-plus-year gap between seasons. [end-mark]
